Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 1:

﴿Ṭā Sīn Mīm﴾.

In its explanation there will come, from among the interpretations, what has already been mentioned concerning all the disjoined letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginnings of the surahs, with similar meanings. The most apparent of these meanings is that the intended purpose is an allusion that stirs the souls of the deniers toward contesting some of the surahs of the Qur'an by producing the like of it in its eloquence and its fluency, and a challenge to them in that, and a reproach against them for their inability to do so.

From Ibn 'Abbas: that "Ṭā Sīn Mīm" is an oath, and it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, and the thing sworn to is His saying (﴿If We wish, We could send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4]). Al-Qurazi said: Allah swore by His bounty (tawl), His splendor (sana'), and His dominion (mulk). And it has been said: the letters are abbreviated from the names of Allah the Exalted: Dhu al-Tawl, al-Quddus, al-Malik. You have already learned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah that they are letters of spelling out (li-l-tahajji) and an exhaustive challenge (istiqsa' fi al-tahaddi) that renders them unable to contest the Qur'an, and upon this the connection of its being followed by the verse (﴿These are the verses of the Manifest Book﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 2]) becomes apparent.

The majority recited (Ṭā Sīn Mīm) as one word, and they assimilated the nun of Sīn into the Mīm. Hamza recited with clear pronunciation of the nun (izhar). Abu Ja'far recited them as separate letters, and they said: and likewise it is written in the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud as separate letters (ṭ s m).

As for not lengthening the name (Ṭā), although its original form has a final hamza: since the pause-quiescence (sukun al-sakt) had come upon it, its hamza was dropped just as it is dropped in pausing, as in the non-lengthening of (Rā) in (Alif Lam Ra) at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

The demonstrative refers to the verses of the Qur'an that were revealed earlier and are present in people's minds, and the predicate ("the verses of the Book") clarifies it.

The meaning of referring to the verses of the Qur'an is to intend the challenge (*tahaddi*, the challenge to produce the like of the Qur'an) with its parts in detail, just as the challenge was intended with the whole in summary (*ijmal*). The meaning is: these are the verses of the Qur'an being recited to you, in your language and with its letters of the alphabet, so produce a surah like them, and here it is for you to take up. The *kaf* attached to the demonstrative is for address, and it is addressed to no specific person, to anyone among their eloquent speakers who is qualified for this challenge.

﴿المُبِينِ﴾ (al-Mubin) means "the manifest," from *abana*, a synonym of *bana*. That is: these are the verses of the Book whose origin from God is clear, because of its great meanings and its inimitable composition. Since the Book is manifest, its verses that it contains are manifest verses, evidencing the truthfulness of the Messengers who brought them.

It is also possible that ﴿المُبِينِ﴾ comes from the transitive *abana*, meaning "the one that makes clear" the meanings of guidance and truth it contains. This is the use of a word in both of its meanings, like a homonym (*mushtarak*).

The meaning is: what has reached you and been recited to you is the verses of the manifest Qur'an, that is, clear in its truthfulness and in its evidence for the truth of what it brought, something that none but a obstinate denier would reject.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 3:

Page 93
﴿Perhaps you would be consuming yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾
The address has been turned from its direction toward the obstinate deniers to its direction toward the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. The statement is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering what the content of His saying, ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 2], raises of the Prophet's ﷺ inner questioning about the continued aversion of the polytheists from faith and from affirming the Qur'an, as the Exalted said: ﴿Perhaps you would be consuming yourself in grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this discourse﴾ [al-Kahf: 6], and His saying: ﴿So let not your soul go out in agonies over them﴾ [Fatir: 8].

When la'alla (perhaps) comes to express the expectation of a feared matter, it is called ishfaq (apprehension) and tawaqqu' (anticipation). The most apparent of the opinions is that the expectation (tarajji) belongs to the category of informative statements, and that it is not an performative utterance like tamanni (wishing).

Tarajji is used in the sense of a demand. The most apparent view is that it is an urging to abandon grief over their misguidance, in the manner of depicting the situation of a speaker who urges the one addressed to desist, with the condition of one who regards as near the occurrence of the destruction of the addressee if he continues in what he is in of sorrow.

Al-baakhi' means the slayer. The real meaning of bakh' is to cut deeply in slaughtering. It is said: bakha'a al-shah, al-Zamakhshari said: when one reaches with the knife the bikhaa' (with a kasra on the ba' and a single dot-less letter after it, i.e. the bikhaa'), which is a vein running along the inside of the spine. Thus he said in the Kashshaf here, and he also mentioned it in al-Fa'iq. What is in it has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿So perhaps you would be consuming yourself over their traces﴾ [al-Kahf: 6], in Surat al-Kahf. Here it is used metaphorically for swift death, and the statement about it with ﴿baakhi'﴾ is an eloquent metaphor. In ﴿baakhi'﴾ the pronoun of the addressee is the agent.

The phrase ﴿allaa yakunoo﴾ is in a position of accusative by the removal of the preposition after (an), the preposition being the lam of causation, and the estimate is: "because they will not be believers," i.e., because of the negation of their faith in the future, since (an) makes the present tense specific to the future. The meaning is: your grief over their non-belief in the past is about to cause you to perish in the future through the repetition of grief and sorrow, like the saying of Joseph's brothers to their father when he said: ﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾ [Yusuf: 84], and they said: ﴿By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become consumed or become of those who perish﴾ [Yusuf: 85]. The balance of this meaning is the balance of the meaning of His saying in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿So perhaps you would be consuming yourself over their traces if they do not believe in this discourse, in grief﴾ [al-Kahf: 6], for the conditional (in) is connected to the future. It is permissible that ﴿allaa yakunoo﴾ be made to occupy the place of the agent of ﴿baakhi'﴾, and the clause is the predicate of (la'alla). The attribution of ﴿baakhi'﴾ to ﴿allaa yakunoo mu'minin﴾ is a rational metaphor, since their non-belief is made a cause of the consuming.

The present tense of the verb "to be" is used to indicate that he does not grieve over their non-belief even if that continues into the future; so its negation in the past is more fitting for not grieving over it.

The complement of "believers" is omitted, either because what is meant is "believers" in what you have brought of monotheism, resurrection, affirming the Qur'an and affirming the Messenger, or because what is meant by "believers" is the title-sense, i.e., that they not be among the group known as the believers, who are the community of Islam. The pronoun in ﴿yakunoo﴾ refers to what is known from the context, namely the polytheists whom the Prophet ﷺ invited.

He turned away from "allaa yu'minoo" to "allaa yakunoo mu'minin", because the verb "to be" carries an indication of continuity beyond what the present-tense form conveys, so the continuity of their non-belief, which is the object of ceasing grief over it, is emphasized. In Surat al-Kahf it came as ﴿So perhaps you would be consuming yourself over their traces, if they do not believe in this discourse﴾ [al-Kahf: 6] with the negative particle of the past, lam, because Surat al-Kahf was revealed later than Surat al-Shu'ara', so their non-belief was by then established and had reached the limit of despair.

The pronoun in (yakunoo) refers to what is known from the context of the challenge conveyed by His saying: ﴿Ta Sin Mim﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 1] ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 2], since it is known that those challenged are the disbelievers who denied.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verse 4:**

﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven, and their necks would remain humbled before it.﴾

This is a *isti'naf bayani* (an explanatory resumptive clause) arising from His words: (﴿Will they not be believers?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3]). The consolation over their unbelief stirs in the soul the question of why they are granted respite without punishment in order to believe, as Musa said: (﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chieftains adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 88]). So it is answered that Allah is capable of that. This resumptive clause is thus an interjection between two sentences, one of which is conjoined to the other.

The object of (﴿nasha'﴾) is omitted, indicated by the answer of the conditional, according to the common manner of omitting the object of the verb of willing. The implied meaning is: "If We will to send down a compelling sign, We shall send it down."

The particle (*in*) is used here, which generally conveys uncertainty about the occurrence of the condition, to indicate that Allah does not will this, for a wisdom that required that He not will it.

The meaning of the negation of this willing is that divine wisdom required that faith come about through reflection and free choice, because that is more conducive to the spread of the fame of Islam at the beginning of its emergence. Thus, the "sign" (*ayah*) meant here is a token indicating a threat of destruction, a tangible threat, by which there appear to them portents that warn of the approach of punishment. This is part of the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: (﴿And if their turning away has been difficult for you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign…﴾ [al-An'am: 35]). The intended meaning is not the verses of the Qur'an, because they were not satisfied with the verses of the Qur'an.

Making the sending down of the sign from the sky at that time clearer and more intensely frightening is due to the recency of such occurrences and the expectation, for everyone under the sky, that it might strike them.

If you ask: Why did He not show them a sign as He showed the Children of Israel the lifting of the mountain over them, as if it were a canopy? I say: The Children of Israel were believers in Musa and what he brought, so showing them signs was not to compel them to faith; rather it was to increase their steadfastness, as Ibrahim said: (﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]).

Upon the sending down of the sign is built what has the sense of a qualifier of it, namely the clause (﴿so their necks would remain humbled before it﴾), connected by the conjunction *fa* of consequence.

The verb (﴿fa-zallat﴾), which is in the past tense, is conjoined to the present-tense (﴿nunazzil﴾), because the verb it is conjoined to is the answer of a conditional, so the conjoined verb has the status of the answer of the conditional. Thus the form of the present and the form of the past are equally permissible, since the conditional particle turns the past into the future. Do you not see that if it were said: "If We will, We send down," or "If We will, We sent down," it would be the same? The truth is that there is no obstacle to the verbs of the condition and the consequent differing in being present or past. Moreover, conjoined elements allow what is not allowed in the element they are conjoined to, according to the principle that what is tolerated in the subsequent parts is not tolerated in the initial parts, as in the eighth rule of the eighth chapter of *Mughni al-Labib*. However, this difference between the two verbs does not lack a particularity in the speech of an eloquent speaker, especially in inimitable speech, and here there are two matters:

Variation between the two forms, and bringing near the time of the past of what is joined by *fa* to the time of the occurrence of the consequence, such that their submission to the sign is as if the sending down had occurred. This comes about quickly, so that from the swiftness of its occurrence they imagine it to be something already past. For this reason He said (﴿fa-zallat﴾) and did not say (﴿fa-tazullu﴾). This is close to the use of the past tense in His words, Exalted is He: (﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]). Both are for threat, and a parallel of it used for arousing eagerness is: "The prayer has been established."

*Al-khudu'* means humbling and submission. It is used metaphorically for obedience, since obedience is among the causes of humility. Attributing the humbling to the necks is a *majaz 'aqli* (a metaphor of attribution, in which an action is ascribed to something other than its real agent), and it contains a *tamthil* (an analogy or representation) of the state of those who obey, fearful and abased, with the state of those who humble themselves, fearing that a crushing calamity may fall upon their heads, so they lower their heads and bend to avoid the disaster descending upon them.

*Al-a'naq* is the plural of *'unuq* (with two dammas, though the *nun* may be sukun), which means the neck, and it is feminine. It was said that the one with *damma* on the *nun* is feminine and the one with sukun on the *nun* is masculine.

Since the necks are the place where humility is manifested, humility is attributed to them, although in reality it belongs to their owners. From this is His words, Exalted is He: (﴿And the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108]), meaning the people of the voices with their voices, as in the verse of al-A'sha:

"Thus do, as long as you live, when they gather, and advance when the eyes of people are startled."

Here the "startled" (*tafraq*) is attributed to the eyes by way of *majaz 'aqli*, because the eyes are the cause of the startle when seeing hidden things. From this is His words: (﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116]). They only bewitched the people with a sorcery arising from seeing the trickery of magic with their eyes. Along with this, what His words (﴿their necks would remain humbled before it﴾) add is an indication of the representation of their state. The apparent expectation would be: "They would remain humbled before it with their necks."

In the use of the plural pronoun for rational beings in His words (﴿khadi'in﴾) with reference to the necks, there is an abstraction (*tajrid*) of the metaphor of attribution in the ascription of (﴿khadi'in﴾) to (﴿a'naquhum﴾), because the proper course of continuing the metaphor would be to say: (*khadi'atan*) for it. This humility arises from anticipating that the descending punishment will overtake them.

From Mujahid it is reported that the word *a'naq* here is the plural of *'unuq* (with two dammas), which is used for the chief and leader of a people, just as "head of the people" and "chest of the people" are used. So the meaning is: "their leaders would remain humbled," meaning those who incited them to disbelief. In this case the statement becomes a threat to their leaders who adorned for them the continuation in disbelief. This interpretation, however, is weak.

From Ibn Zayd and al-Akhfash it is reported that *al-a'naq* means groups, whose singular is *'unuq* (with two dammas), meaning a group of people. The meaning would be: "they would remain humbled in groups upon groups." This is weaker than the previous one.

Among the strange and feeble interpretations is what al-Tha'labi attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "This verse was revealed about us and about the Banu Umayyah, so that their necks would be humbled before us after difficulty, and humiliation would befall them after honour." This is one of the distortions of the words of the Qur'an from their places, and we absolve Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, from saying it, he for whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed that he be taught the interpretation. This is among the fabrications of the propagandists of the Abbasid revolution (*al-Musawwida*), such as Abu Muslim al-Khurasani; and how many fabrications they have invented! The Qur'an is far too exalted to address these trivialities.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read (﴿nunazzil﴾) with a *shaddah* on the *zay* and a fatha on the second *nun*. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ya'qub read it with a damma on the first *nun* and a lightened *zay*.

**Verse 5 of Surah al-Shu'ara' (26):** ﴿Never does there come to them a fresh reminder from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it.﴾

It is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical coordination) with the clause "﴿Perhaps you will destroy yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3]." That is, this is their habit, so do not grieve over their failure to believe in the clear Book's verses. Whatever further reminder comes to them, they will turn away from it, because they are known for turning away.

The present tense (*al-mudari'*, imperfect verb) here indicates renewal and continuity. *Al-dhikr* (the reminder) is the Qur'an, since it reminds people through proofs. Its being called a *dhikr* was explained earlier, at the words: ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely possessed."﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], in Surah al-Hijr.

*Al-muhdath* (fresh, new) means new: a reminder following another reminder, reminding them of what was sent down of the Qur'an before it. The meaning derived from describing it as *muhdath* differs from the meaning derived from the present-tense form in the words: ﴿No fresh reminder comes to them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 2]. Both points together establish that it is a reminder that is continually renewed and continuous, and that some of it follows and reinforces the rest. Earlier, in Surah al-Anbiya', He said:

[Page 98]
﴿No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord except that they listen to it while playing,﴾ [al-Anbiya': 2] ﴿their hearts distracted.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3]

The name *al-Rahman* (the Most Merciful) is mentioned here rather than the attribute *al-Rabb* (the Lord), as in Surah al-Anbiya', because the context here is consoling the Prophet (ﷺ) over his people's turning away. Describing the giver of the reminder as *al-Rahman* censures the state of those who turn away and exposes their foolishness: they turn away from what is a mercy to them. If they do not perceive their own benefit, then do not let yourself waste away in sorrow over people who have squandered their own good, when you have already guided them to it and reminded them. As the proverb says: "Do not let grief grip you over blood that its own people have spilled." And al-Nabigha said:

*If your wretchedness overcomes you, I have still striven for your good.*

The use of the verb *kanu* (they were) with its predicate, rather than saying "except that they turned away," indicates that their turning away is firmly established in them and is ancient and continuous. This is because He had already described them before this with the words: ﴿that they would not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3]. Thus the non-occurrence of their belief is itself a turning away from the Messenger's call, whose method is the reminder of the Qur'an. So when a reminder comes to them after the reminder through which they did not believe, it finds them still in their ancient turning away.

The *min* in "min dhikr" (from a reminder) is emphatic (*muakkidah*), reinforcing the generality of the negation of states.

The *min* in the words ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾ is for origin (*ibtida'iyyah*).

The exception here is from general states, so the clause ﴿they were turning away from it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*, state clause) relating to the pronoun in ﴿there comes to them a reminder﴾. The prepositional phrase has been placed first to preserve the rhyme (*fasilah*, verse-ending rhyme).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 6:

﴿So they have indeed denied, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾

The fa' in (﴿fa-qad kadhdhabu﴾) is fa' faṣīḥa (the fa' that makes explicit an implied condition), meaning: it has become clear that their turning away is the turning away of denial, after the information that their practice is turning away from the Reminder that comes to them piece by piece, for their turning away was because they had denied the Qur'an. As for the fa' in His saying (﴿fa-sa-ya'tīhim﴾), it is for the sequencing of the announcement of the threat after the announcement of the denial.

Al-anbā' (the news) is the plural of naba', which is the report of a great event. It was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: (﴿And there has certainly come to you from the news of the messengers﴾ [al-An'am: 34]) in Surat al-An'am.

Page 99
Al-anbā' refers to the manifestation of its truth. The intended meaning of "coming" here is not arrival, unlike in His saying (﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ [Sad: 21]), because the arrival of the news has already occurred, so it is not expressed with the future marker in His saying: (﴿fa-sa-ya'tīhim﴾).

The (mā) in His saying (﴿mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn﴾) may be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), in which case its referent may be the Qur'an, as in His saying, may He be exalted (﴿And do not take the signs of God in mockery﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]). In its relative clause the verb (﴿yastahzi'ūn﴾) is used rather than (yukadhdhibūn) so that the benefit of informing about them that they denied it and mocked it is achieved. The bā' in (bihi) is for transitivity of the verb (yastahzi'ūn), and the pronoun in the genitive refers back to the relative (mā). Its news is its reports of the threat. It is also possible that the referent of (mā) is the category of that about which they were known to mock, namely the threat, as they used to say: "When is this promise?" and the like.

The idafah of (﴿al-anbā'﴾) to (﴿mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn﴾) on this view is an explanatory idafah (idafah bayaniyyah), meaning: the news of that which they mocked, which is the news of what will befall them.

The plural of al-anbā' on this view is in consideration of their mocking many things, among them the Resurrection, among them punishment in this world, among them the victory of the Muslims over them (﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48]), among them the conquest of Makkah, among them the punishment of Hell and the tree of zaqqum. Abu Jahl used to say: "Zaqqimuna!" as mockery.

It is also possible that (mā) is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning: the news of the occurrence of their mockery, that is, its taking place, and the pronoun in (bihi) refers to something known from the context, namely the Qur'an or the Messenger ﷺ.

The intended meaning of the news of their mockery is the news of its requital and consequence, which is what the Qur'an threatened them with in more than one verse.

The discussion regarding the insertion of the verb (kānū) here is like the discussion regarding its insertion in His saying earlier (﴿they were turning away from it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 5]), but the present verb (﴿yastahzi'ūn﴾) was preferred over the active participle as in His saying (﴿they were turning away from it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 5]), because mockery is renewed with the renewal of their threat of punishment, whereas turning away is firmly established in them.

Page 100
The meaning of (﴿fa-sa-ya'tīhim anbā'u mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn﴾) according to the first aspect is that the coming is in the sense of realization, as in His saying (﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]), meaning it has been realized; that is, the reports of the threat with which the Qur'an threatened them, the Qur'an at which they used to mock, will surely be realized.
And according to the second aspect, the reports of their mockery of the Qur'an will surely reach them, that is, the reports of punishment for that. The singular form of the verb (ya'tīhim) was preferred, although its subject is a broken plural for a non-human masculine noun that may be feminine, because singularity is lighter in speech due to its frequent occurrence.

[p. 100]

The waw (الواوُ) is a conjunction (ʿāṭifa) joining the clause (﴿And no reminder comes to them from the Most Merciful, newly revealed, except that they turn away from it﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 5]). The interrogative hamza (الهَمْزَةُ الِاسْتِفْهامِيَّةُ) therefore comes before the conjunctive waw in wording, because interrogation has precedence (الصَّدارَة). Its purpose is to establish the proof against them, that the signs do not benefit them, because obstinacy (المُكابَرَة) diverts them from reflecting on the signs. The signs confirming the truth of what the Qur'an calls them to, namely monotheism and belief in the Resurrection, are established and manifest in the heavens and the earth, yet they were blind to them and associated partners with God. It is therefore no wonder that they go astray from the signs of the truthfulness of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. That the Qur'an was sent down from God, if these people were eager for the truth and searching for it, the signs by which they were reminded would have sufficed them in place of the signs they demand. God, exalted is He, says: (﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 185]) (﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yūnus: 101]), meaning: for a people who have not prepared themselves for faith.

What is mentioned in this verse is the varieties of plants, which are indications of God's oneness, because this wise craftsmanship proceeds only from one who has no partner. This is a proof through reason (ʿaql). It is also a proof of the possibility of the Resurrection, because the growth of plants after dryness is a likeness of the revival of the dead after their decay, as God, exalted is He, says: (﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 33]). This is an approximate proof (dalīl taqrībī) of possibility.

[p. 101]

for possibility. Thus the verse on growth contains an alert to the nullification of the two roots of their unbelief: the root of associating partners with God, and the root of denying the Resurrection.

The interrogation is a denial of their not seeing this, because the indication of the growth of plants of the one Creator is a clear indication for everyone who sees it. When they did not benefit from that sight, their seeing was placed in the position of non-seeing, so this was denied to them. The intent is to deny their failure to draw inference from it.

The clause (﴿how many We caused to grow﴾) is an inclusive apposition (badal al-ishtimāl) of the clause "yarawā" (they see), and it is thus the target of the denial. The phrase (﴿to the earth﴾) is connected to the verb "yarawā," meaning: have they not looked at the earth, while it is before their eyes?

(كَمْ) is a noun indicating abundance, and here it is declarative (khabariyya) and in the accusative governed by (﴿We caused to grow﴾). The implied sense is: We caused to grow therein much of every noble pair.

(مِن) is partitive (tabʿīḍiyya). The domain of multiplicity conveyed by (كَمْ) is the abundance of growth in many places, and the domain of comprehensiveness conveyed by (كُلِّ) is the kinds and species of plants. In both respects there is an indication of precise craftsmanship. The mention of parts of every pair dispensed with mentioning the specification (mumayyiz) of (كَمْ), because it is known from the partitive.

The zawj (الزَّوْجُ) means the kind, and the application of zawj to kind is common in non-animal matters. God, exalted is He, says: (﴿And from all fruits He made therein two mates﴾ [al-Raʿd: 3]), according to one of two possibilities discussed in Sūrat al-Raʿd, and His saying was previously mentioned in Ṭā-Hā: (﴿Then We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 53]).

The karīm (الكَرِيمُ) means the choice of its kind. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 10–11:**

﴿When your Lord called out to Musa: "Go to the wrongdoing people,"﴾ ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God?﴾

A beginning of enumerating signs that confirm the truth of the Messenger (ﷺ), by mentioning the consequences for those who denied their messengers.

[Page 103]

The purpose is to warn those addressed by the call to Islam lest they suffer what befell the deniers. Within this there is also a clarification of some of the proofs that the messengers presented.

Since these examples are among the exemplary punishments, the intention is to mention many of those that became well known, and not to restrict the account to a single incident. This is because non-rational proofs are open to the possibility that the connection (between cause and effect) does not hold, namely that what befell some of those peoples happened by chance and coincidence. When it becomes clear that similar cases recur, the probability of coincidence weakens, because qiyas al-tamthil (analogical reasoning by example) does not yield certainty except when it is joined by its supporting elements of mass transmission (tawatur) and repetition.

The account of Musa was begun before the account of Ibrahim, contrary to the usual order in which the Qur'an narrates stories, which is by chronological sequence. Perhaps this is because the surah was revealed to refute the polytheists, who insisted on the manifestation of signs of extraordinary events in the created world, claiming that they would not believe unless a sign came to them. So they were given the example of the obstinacy of Pharaoh and his people toward the signs of Musa, when they said: (﴿This is clearly a sorcerer﴾ [Yunus: 2]). The phrase (﴿When your Lord called out to Musa﴾) is joined as a clause conjoined to the entire clause (﴿Have they not looked at the earth﴾).

(Idh) may be a noun of time in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb whose estimated meaning is: "And remember when your Lord called out to Musa," following the pattern of his words in the story that comes after it: (﴿And recite to them the report of Ibrahim﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 69]). In this implied element there is a reminder to the Messenger (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, that consoles him for what he encounters from his people.

The call of God to Musa is the revelation to him through speech that he heard without the mediation of an angel.

The clause (﴿that go to the wrongdoing people﴾) explains the verb "called out," and (an) is explanatory. The purpose of relating this story is admonition through the consequence of the deniers, and this is reached at His words: (﴿So We revealed to Musa: "Strike the sea with your staff"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63]) up to His words: (﴿Indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 9]). As for what precedes that, His words (﴿When your Lord called out to Musa﴾), etc., it is a detailed account of the causes of the admonition, by mentioning Musa's call to what he was commanded to convey, and the aversion of Pharaoh and his people, and what followed from that until the conclusion.

Describing the people of Pharaoh as "the wrongdoing people" alludes to the reason for the sending (of the messenger). In this general description there is a directing of Musa's own soul to await the specification of these people by what will clarify them, and a stirring of his anger against them, so that the impulse of his anger against them joins the impulse of carrying out God's command that sent him to them. This is more effective for his speech to reach their souls. It also implies that they were well known for wrongdoing.

Then he followed this with a mention of their intrinsic description in an explanatory manner, from "the wrongdoing people," which is His words (﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾). In the repetition of the word "people" there is an effect of emphasis. So he did not say: "Go to the wrongdoing people of Pharaoh," like the verse of Jarir:

*O Taym, Taym of ʿAdi, may you have no father,*
*may ʿUmar not find you in some disgrace.*

Wrongdoing (zulm) encompasses its types. Among them is their wronging themselves by worshipping what does not deserve worship, and among them is their wronging people by denying them their rights, when they enslaved the Children of Israel and oppressed them. Its usage in both senses has been mentioned many times, as the opposite of justice: (﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114]) in al-Baqarah, and in the sense of shirk in His words: (﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82]) in al-An'am.

Know that here he has departed from mentioning what Musa's call began with, which is in Surah Ta-Ha in His words: (﴿Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals﴾ [Ta-Ha: 12]) up to His words: (﴿so that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23]). This is because the context here requires limiting the account to what explains the call of the people of Pharaoh and their aversion, so that they may take warning from their consequence. As for the context of what is in Surah Ta-Ha, it is to show Musa's honour with his Lord and his messengership together, so that context calls for elaboration, along with the difference in style in narrating one and the same story, as was mentioned in the seventh introduction among the introductions of this tafsir.

The coming that was commanded is his going to convey the message to them. This is a concise statement, clarified by His words: (﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16]) and to its end.

The clause (﴿Will they not fear God?﴾) is a resumptive explanatory clause (istin'af bayani), because when He commanded him to go to them for their call, and described them as wrongdoers, the speech would provoke a question in Musa's mind about the extent of their wrongdoing. So there came what indicates their deep immersion in wrongdoing and their persistence in it, to strengthen Musa's resolve to reach the utmost limit in the call, and to prepare him to receive their denial without surprise. Thus (ألا) in His words (ألا يتقون) is composed of two particles: the interrogative hamza and the negative (لا). The interrogation is to deny their non-fear, and to express Musa's wonder at this, for Musa was aware of their conditions, having grown up among them and known their injustices, the greatest of which was shirk and the killing of the prophets of the Children of Israel. . . .

[Page 105]

It is also possible that (ألا) is a single word, the particle of presentation and urging, so the clause (﴿Will they not fear God?﴾) is an explanation of the clause (go), and the meaning is: "Say to them: Will you not fear God?" Thus the speech is related by its meaning, not by its wording. This is permissible in reporting speech, as in His words: (﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]), where the clause (worship God) explains the clause (You commanded me). God had commanded him that they should worship God, the Lord of Musa and their Lord, so he related what God commanded him by its meaning. This presentation is similar to His words in Surah al-Nazi'at: (﴿So say: "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]).

Piety (ittiqa') is fear and caution. The object of the verb (﴿fear﴾) is omitted, because it is evident that what is meant is: "Will they not fear the consequences of their wrongdoing?" This was previously discussed at His words: (﴿those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear﴾ [al-Anfal: 56]) in Surah al-Anfal.

From the application of the description of wrongdoing and lack of piety to the people of Pharaoh in the context of commanding Musa to go to them, Musa knows that among the first things his call should begin with is that he should summon them to abandon wrongdoing and to piety.

The mention of Musa was previously made at His words: (﴿And when We appointed Musa forty nights﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51]) in al-Baqarah. And the biography of Pharaoh was previously given at His words: (﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-A'raf: 103]) in al-A'raf.

Then he followed this with a mention of their intrinsic description in an explanatory manner, from "the wrongdoing people," which is His words (﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾). In the repetition of the word "people" there is an effect of emphasis. So he did not say: "Go to the wrongdoing people of Pharaoh," like the verse of Jarir:

*O Taym, Taym of ʿAdi, may you have no father,*
*may ʿUmar not find you in some disgrace.*

Wrongdoing (zulm) encompasses its types. Among them is their wronging themselves by worshipping what does not deserve worship, and among them is their wronging people by denying them their rights, when they enslaved the Children of Israel and oppressed them. Its usage in both senses has been mentioned many times, as the opposite of justice: (﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114]) in al-Baqarah, and in the sense of shirk in His words: (﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82]) in al-An'am.

Know that here he has departed from mentioning what Musa's call began with, which is in Surah Ta-Ha in His words: (﴿Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals﴾ [Ta-Ha: 12]) up to His words: (﴿so that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23]). This is because the context here requires limiting the account to what explains the call of the people of Pharaoh and their aversion, so that they may take warning from their consequence. As for the context of what is in Surah Ta-Ha, it is to show Musa's honour with his Lord and his messengership together, so that context calls for elaboration, along with the difference in style in narrating one and the same story, as was mentioned in the seventh introduction among the introductions of this tafsir.

The coming that was commanded is his going to convey the message to them. This is a concise statement, clarified by His words: (﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16]) and to its end.

The clause (﴿Will they not fear God?﴾) is a resumptive explanatory clause (istin'af bayani), because when He commanded him to go to them for their call, and described them as wrongdoers, the speech would provoke a question in Musa's mind about the extent of their wrongdoing. So there came what indicates their deep immersion in wrongdoing and their persistence in it, to strengthen Musa's resolve to reach the utmost limit in the call, and to prepare him to receive their denial without surprise. Thus (ألا) in His words (ألا يتقون) is composed of two particles: the interrogative hamza and the negative (لا). The interrogation is to deny their non-fear, and to express Musa's wonder at this, for Musa was aware of their conditions, having grown up among them and known their injustices, the greatest of which was shirk and the killing of the prophets of the Children of Israel. . . .

[Page 105]

It is also possible that (ألا) is a single word, the particle of presentation and urging, so the clause (﴿Will they not fear God?﴾) is an explanation of the clause (go), and the meaning is: "Say to them: Will you not fear God?" Thus the speech is related by its meaning, not by its wording. This is permissible in reporting speech, as in His words: (﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]), where the clause (worship God) explains the clause (You commanded me). God had commanded him that they should worship God, the Lord of Musa and their Lord, so he related what God commanded him by its meaning. This presentation is similar to His words in Surah al-Nazi'at: (﴿So say: "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]).

Piety (ittiqa') is fear and caution. The object of the verb (﴿fear﴾) is omitted, because it is evident that what is meant is: "Will they not fear the consequences of their wrongdoing?" This was previously discussed at His words: (﴿those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear﴾ [al-Anfal: 56]) in Surah al-Anfal.

From the application of the description of wrongdoing and lack of piety to the people of Pharaoh in the context of commanding Musa to go to them, Musa knows that among the first things his call should begin with is that he should summon them to abandon wrongdoing and to piety.

The mention of Musa was previously made at His words: (﴿And when We appointed Musa forty nights﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51]) in al-Baqarah. And the biography of Pharaoh was previously given at His words: (﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-A'raf: 103]) in al-A'raf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 12–14:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me,﴾ ﴿and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be eloquent, so send for Harun.﴾ ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me."﴾

Opening his reply by calling upon God with the description of "Lord" with a pronoun attached to it conveys tenderness and submission. He feared that they would deny him because he knew that a message such as this is never received by those to whom the messenger is sent except with denial. He made himself fearful of denial because, when the message from God was bestowed upon him, concern for the success of his mission settled in his breast, so that their denial of it was something to be feared.

(﴿and my breast will be constricted﴾) Most readers recite it with a nominative ending, so it is coordinated with (﴿I fear﴾).

[Page 106]

Or the waw may be a waw of circumstance (ḥāl), making it a hypothetical circumstantial clause, meaning: "while at that time my breast is constricted because of their failure to be guided."

Constriction (ḍayq) is the opposite of expansiveness (si'ah), and here it is used metaphorically for anger and grief, because whoever is overcome by that undergoes an agitation, and from it arises a contraction of the nerves in the chest and heart, under the influence of a particular perception on the gathering of the nerves located in the brain, which is the perceiver; so he feels something like fullness in the chest. This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: (﴿He makes his breast constricted and narrow﴾ [al-An'am: 125]) and His saying: (﴿and your breast is constricted by it﴾ [Hud: 12]) in surah Hud. The meaning is that he grieves and is distressed at their denial of him, and the desire to persuade them of his truthfulness surges within him. When such thoughts arise in the mind, the preparation of proofs arises from them, and in that preparation there is strain and fatigue for the thinking faculty. When he has set them forth, he feels relief and something like expansiveness in the chest, so he called that "expansion of the breast" (sharḥ al-ṣadr). For this reason Moses asked for it in the other verse: (﴿My Lord, expand my breast for me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 25]).

Inṭilāq (fluency) is literally the reflexive form of aṭlaqahu, when he released it and did not hold it back; so it is literally used for going away. Here it is used metaphorically for the eloquence of the tongue and its clarity in speech; that is, my tongue becomes tied and is not clear when I want to argue and reason. Its coordination with (my breast will be constricted) indicates that by the constriction of the breast he meant the multiplication of thoughts of reasoning in his soul against those who denied him, so that he might persuade them of his truthfulness, until he feels as though his breast is full. The usual state is that this lessens bit by bit in proportion to what its bearer expresses of it to the listeners. If there is a stammer and an impediment in his tongue, the thoughts remain jumbled in his breast. The meaning is: "My breast will be constricted when they deny me, and my tongue will not be eloquent."

The majority recited (﴿will be constricted﴾ [al-Hijr: 97]) and (﴿and will not be eloquent﴾) in the nominative, coordinated with (﴿I fear﴾). For this reason he confirmed it with the emphatic particle, because he was certain that this would occur, since it is innate upon receiving denial, and because the trust of the message and the eagerness to carry out God's will inevitably produce this in his soul. And since the tying of his tongue was certain to him, and was so because of that certainty, the two verbs (﴿will be constricted﴾ [al-Hijr: 97]) and (﴿will not be eloquent﴾) are coordinated with what is established for him, namely the occurrence of fear of denial, and they were not coordinated with (﴿they deny me﴾), which is the feared and anticipated outcome, since its being certain to occur makes it more deserving than something merely anticipated.

[Page 107]

Ya'qub recited (﴿and will be constricted﴾) and (﴿and will not be eloquent﴾) with the verbs in the accusative, coordinated with (﴿they deny me﴾), meaning: he anticipates that his breast will be constricted and his tongue will not be eloquent. It has been said that Moses had a stammer in his tongue when he spoke. This was discussed earlier in surah Ta-Ha and will come in surah al-Zukhruf. The purpose of this statement is not to disclaim the undertaking of this great obligation, but rather to pave the way for what he built upon it, namely his request that his brother Harun be associated with him, because he is more capable than him in argument and oratory, as he said in the other verse: (﴿My brother Harun is more eloquent in tongue than I, so send him with me﴾ [al-Qasas: 34]). So his statement here: (﴿so send for Harun﴾) is general and is clarified by what is in the other verse, so it is known that there is brevity (ījāz) in the speech here, and that it is not intended to mean: "send for Harun in my place."

He asked God to send for Harun and did not ask Him to make Harun speak as He spoke to him, because Harun was far from the place of intimate conversation. The meaning is: "send an angel with the revelation to Harun, that he may be with me."

His saying: (﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me﴾) is an allusion to asking for help and support, and that God would suffice him against the evil of his enemy until he fulfils what God entrusted to him in the most complete manner. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Badr: "O God, I ask You for Your help and Your promise. O God, if You will, You will not be worshipped on earth."

Dhanb (charge) means a crime and a violation of what is obligatory according to their laws. The word dhanb is used for the act of holding someone accountable, since what they had against him was the right to demand blood for the man he struck and killed, and the Copts threatened him that if they caught him they would kill him, so he left Egypt in fear, and that was the cause of his setting out for the land of Madyan. He called it a dhanb in accordance with what was in the law of the Copts, for there was no divine law on the matter of killing a soul at that time. It is also possible that he called it a dhanb because killing someone without retaliation or self-defence is regarded as a crime in the laws of human communities since the killing of one of the two sons of Adam his brother, and He said in surah al-Qasas: (﴿He said: "This is from the work of Satan; indeed he is a manifest, misguiding enemy."﴾ [al-Qasas: 15] ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me."﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]). Whatever the case, he made it a charge against him for them.

His saying: (﴿so I fear they will kill me﴾) is not panic or dread of death, for when he had come to hold the station of messengership, he was not one who minded dying in the way of God. Rather, he feared the obstacle to completing what had been entrusted to him, in which there is a great reward and a lofty rank.

[Page 108]

The first person pronoun ya' was dropped from (﴿they will kill me﴾) for the sake of the verse-ending (fāṣila, the rhyme-closing unit of a verse) as was discussed earlier in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿and fear Me alone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]) in surah al-Baqarah.

The mention of Harun was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: (﴿and what remains of what the family of Moses and the family of Harun left behind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248]) in surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 15–17:

﴿He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, 'Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds.'﴾ ﴿[Saying], 'Send with us the Children of Israel.'﴾

(Kalla) is a particle of negation and refutation (harf ibtal). It has already been discussed in the Almighty's words, ﴿Nay! We will record what he says﴾ [Maryam: 79], in Surah Maryam. The refutation here is directed at his statement, ﴿and I fear they will kill me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 14], meaning: they will not kill you. In this refutation there is a response to what was implied in his indirect supplication when he said, ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 14].

His words, ﴿So go with Our signs﴾, are a consequence (tafri') of the meaning of the word (kalla). The command to Musa that he go, he and Harun, implies that Musa was commanded to convey this to Harun, so Musa was a messenger to Harun with prophethood. For this reason it is mentioned in the Torah that Musa informed his brother Harun of this when he met him at Horeb, when God revealed to Harun that he should meet him. The ba' here denotes accompaniment (lil-musahabah), meaning: accompanying Our signs. It is a promise of support with miracles that will appear when needed. Among the signs is the staff that turned into a serpent during the intimate conversation, and likewise the whiteness of his hand, as in the verse of Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17], the signs.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because their command to go to Pharaoh may provoke in the soul the thought that Pharaoh would ignore the signs and, on seeing them, would not desist from harming them. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 18–19:**

﴿He said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed among us for some years of your life? And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the disbelievers."﴾

The account of Musa and Harun going to Fir'awn, seeking permission to enter his presence, and conveying what Allah commanded them to say to Fir'awn has been omitted from the discourse, for the sake of brevity. Fir'awn directed his address to Musa alone, because he understood from the detailed speech of Musa and Harun that Musa was the messenger in essence, and that Harun was a helper to him in conveying the message. So he did not occupy himself with speaking to Harun. Fir'awn turned away from engaging in refuting Musa's call. Instead, he turned to reminding him of the favour the Pharaohs, his forebears, had shown him, and to frightening him about his offence, supposing that this would uproot the call from its root and restrain Musa from it. His purpose in this address was to silence Musa, so that he would be confounded out of fear of Fir'awn, since he (Fir'awn) had found for himself a pretext by which to justify killing him, and would be excused in doing so, since (Musa) had denied the blessing of upbringing and committed the crime of killing a person.

[Page 111]

The interrogation is *taqriri* (an interrogative used to affirm a fact). The affirmation was framed as a negation of upbringing, although the intended meaning was to confirm that upbringing had taken place. This is in accordance with Musa's state in Fir'awn's view, since he saw in this speech a boldness toward him that does not suit one who is indebted to his household for upbringing, because upbringing requires love and kindness. So it is as if he gives Musa free rein, inviting him to deny that he was brought up among them, so that if he admits it and does not deny it, the admission will be free from any pretext of fear or pressure. This is the reason the affirmative interrogation is applied to a negation while the thing affirmed is established. This is like when you say to a man whom you have not seen for a long time, "Are you not so-and-so?" and there are many similar examples. From it is the statement of al-Hajjaj in his sermon on the day of Dayr al-Jamajim, threatening the Kharijites: "Are you not my companions in al-Ahwaz?"

The *taqrir* is used in its implication, which is that the one being affirmed to should be met with kindness and obedience, not with harshness. It is also permissible to make the interrogation *inkari* (a rebuke or denial) directed at him, because Musa's implicit stance in Fir'awn's view was that of one who denies that he was raised among them, and one who is thought to have forgotten them because of his deed. So Fir'awn rebuked him for that. Both aspects involve placing Musa in the position of one who denies that.

*Tarbiyah* (upbringing) is the guardianship of a child and the management of his affairs. The meaning of "among us" (﴿fina﴾) is "in our family", that is, the family of the king of Egypt. *Walid* is the infant from the time of his birth and what is close to it. When he grows up, he is no longer called *walid* but is called *tifl* (child). By this he means that Musa was picked up from the Nile. That is because Musa was raised by Ramesses II (*Ra'mses al-Thani*), one of the kings of the nineteenth dynasty of the Pharaohs of Egypt according to the order of the verifying historians. Musa left Egypt after he killed the Copt, when he was forty years old, based on the verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when he reached his full strength and became mature, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Qasas: 14], up to His saying: ﴿And he entered the city﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], and the verse. He was sent as a prophet when he was eighty years old, as stated in the Torah. The Pharaoh to whom Musa was sent was Merneptah the Second, son of Ramesses II, who succeeded him in the kingship after his death, around the middle of the fifteenth century BC. Therefore, Musa was certainly raised as the child of his father, and so Fir'awn said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾. Perhaps he was brought up together with this Pharaoh, like a brother.

The years that Musa stayed among them were about forty years.

[Page 112]

*Fa'lah* (the deed) is a single occurrence of the verb, and by it he means the result of the verbal noun, as its being attached to the pronoun of the addressee requires. By "the deed" he means his killing of the Copt. It was said that he was Fir'awn's baker. It is referred to by the relative pronoun because Musa knew of it, and in that there is an exaggeration of the deed, by which he is alluded to in order to remind him of what necessitates his rebuke.

In the shift from mentioning a specific deed to mentioning it in an unspecified form, attached to his pronoun, and then describing it with something that adds nothing to the meaning of the described, there is an exaggeration intended to make it appear grave, and to show that it is well known and established, while firmly attaching to him its consequence, so that he cannot disown it.

The clause ﴿and you were of the disbelievers﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun in ﴿you did﴾. What is meant is the disbelief in Fir'awn's blessing, insofar as he (Musa) transgressed against one of Fir'awn's close associates and clients. That occurred in support of a man from the Children of Israel, whom they regarded as the slaves of Fir'awn and his people. So Fir'awn considered Musa's support of a man from his own kin to be ingratitude for Fir'awn's blessing, because in his view it was Musa's duty to regard himself as one of Fir'awn's people and not to support the Israelites. In this there is an application of the rulings of adoption and neglect of the rulings of lineage, which is an inversion of realities and a corruption of order. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He has not made your adopted sons your sons. That is your saying with your mouths, but Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. What is meant is not disbelief in Fir'awn's religion, because Musa, on the day he killed the Copt, was not openly showing that he opposed their religion, even if he was inwardly so, because the prophets are protected from disbelief both before and after prophethood.

The clause ﴿and you were of the disbelievers﴾ may also be a conjunction to the preceding sentences, which are rebuke and blame. So he rebuked him for his past shepherding of their upbringing of him, then rebuked him for being a disbeliever in their religion at present. Moreover, his saying ﴿of the disbelievers﴾ is literally in the present, since it is an active participle, and the active participle is literally in the present.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "and you are then among the disbelievers in our religion", based on what appeared to him of indications that showed Musa's contempt for their religion in the past, since their religion requires loyalty to Fir'awn and humiliating whoever humiliates them and Fir'awn. Perhaps this is the reason Fir'awn resolved to take retribution from Musa for the Copt, since the assault on him was accompanied by contempt for Fir'awn and his people.

[Page 113]

The speech as a whole conveys amazement at Musa's assumption of the position of a guide, given the faults he had committed in Fir'awn's view, which are incompatible with his claim to be a messenger from the Lord.

In the shift from mentioning a specific deed to mentioning it in an unspecified form, attached to his pronoun, and then describing it with something that adds nothing to the meaning of the described, there is an exaggeration intended to make it appear grave, and to show that it is well known and established, while firmly attaching to him its consequence, so that he cannot disown it.

The clause ﴿and you were of the disbelievers﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun in ﴿you did﴾. What is meant is the disbelief in Fir'awn's blessing, insofar as he (Musa) transgressed against one of Fir'awn's close associates and clients. That occurred in support of a man from the Children of Israel, whom they regarded as the slaves of Fir'awn and his people. So Fir'awn considered Musa's support of a man from his own kin to be ingratitude for Fir'awn's blessing, because in his view it was Musa's duty to regard himself as one of Fir'awn's people and not to support the Israelites. In this there is an application of the rulings of adoption and neglect of the rulings of lineage, which is an inversion of realities and a corruption of order. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He has not made your adopted sons your sons. That is your saying with your mouths, but Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. What is meant is not disbelief in Fir'awn's religion, because Musa, on the day he killed the Copt, was not openly showing that he opposed their religion, even if he was inwardly so, because the prophets are protected from disbelief both before and after prophethood.

The clause ﴿and you were of the disbelievers﴾ may also be a conjunction to the preceding sentences, which are rebuke and blame. So he rebuked him for his past shepherding of their upbringing of him, then rebuked him for being a disbeliever in their religion at present. Moreover, his saying ﴿of the disbelievers﴾ is literally in the present, since it is an active participle, and the active participle is literally in the present.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "and you are then among the disbelievers in our religion", based on what appeared to him of indications that showed Musa's contempt for their religion in the past, since their religion requires loyalty to Fir'awn and humiliating whoever humiliates them and Fir'awn. Perhaps this is the reason Fir'awn resolved to take retribution from Musa for the Copt, since the assault on him was accompanied by contempt for Fir'awn and his people.

[Page 113]

The speech as a whole conveys amazement at Musa's assumption of the position of a guide, given the faults he had committed in Fir'awn's view, which are incompatible with his claim to be a messenger from the Lord.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 20–22:

﴿He said: "I did it then, when I was among those who went astray. So I fled from you when I feared you, then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers. And is this a favour you hold over me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?"﴾

The composure of Musa and his reliance upon his Lord prompted him to acknowledge the deed and to mention the good that resulted from it for him, so as to show that he praised its outcome, even though he had committed it without foreseeing the good that it would bring him. He began with the admission of his deed so that Fir'awn would know that his words had found no point of entry to influence the soul of Musa. Musa delayed his answer to Fir'awn's saying: (﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed among us for years of your life?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18]), because he knew that its aim was to restrain him from confronting him with the claim that a Lord higher than Fir'awn had sent Musa to him. He began with the answer concerning the more important part of Fir'awn's speech, which is (﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 19]), because he knew that it was more effective in the aim of silencing him, and to show Fir'awn that he was not afraid that they would demand retribution for that slain man, out of confidence that God would save him from their aggression.

The word (إذًا, "then") here is a particle of answer and consequence. Its final nun is not tanwin but an original letter of the word. He placed (﴿I did it﴾) before (إذن) in order to hasten the admission, so that it would be a metaphor for his lack of fear of this admission. The sense of recompense here is what al-Zamakhshari explained in the Kashshaf: Fir'awn's saying (﴿You did your deed which you did﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 19]) implies the meaning "you have repaid our favour by what you did"; so Musa said to him: "Yes, I did it, repaying you," submitting to his words, because his favour was worthy of being repaid with such a recompense. This is the most apparent of what has been said in the interpretation of this verse. Al-Qazwini said in the marginal notes on the Kashshaf: Some of the verifiers said: (إذًا) is an adverb cut off from annexation, with fatha preferred over kasra for its lightness and frequency of use. Perhaps by "some of the verifiers" he means Radi al-Din al-Astarabadhi in his commentary on the Kafiya al-Hajibiyya, for he said in the chapter on adverbs: "The truth is that (إذ), when the annexed noun is omitted from it and tanwin is substituted for it, except in cases like yawmi'idhin, may also take fatha, and from it is the saying of the Exalted: (﴿I did it then, when I was among those who went astray﴾), that is, I did it when you raised me," for there is no meaning of recompense here. End of quote. In that case it is connected to (﴿I did it﴾), cut off from annexation in pronunciation because the governing word indicates the annexed noun. The meaning is: "I did it at a time when I did it, so my reminding you of it after a long time is of no use." This reading of (إذًا) in the verse is the preference of Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Radi in his commentary on the Hajibiyya, and al-Damamini in al-Mazj 'ala al-Mughni, and the apparent sense of al-Qazwini's words in al-Kashf 'ala al-Kashshaf indicates that he also prefers it.

The meaning of recompense in his saying (﴿I did it then﴾) is that Fir'awn's saying (﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 19]) was intended to silence and threaten Musa, so Musa made his admission of the deed a recompense for that threat, in the manner of "answering according to the premise" (al-qawl bil-mujib), that is: "I am not intimidated by what you intend."

Musa made himself one of "those who went astray" if the intended meaning of his words, which the verse relates, is the well-known sense of error in Arabic, namely the error of corruption. Then his meaning would be that the rage of anger had caused him to neglect respect for the sanctity of the soul, even though at that time there was no sharia, for the preservation of souls is something upon which human laws agree and which they have inherited in the periods between prophets. This is supported by his saying in the other verse: (﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.﴾ So He forgave him [al-Qasas: 16]). If his meaning is the sense of losing the way, that is, "I was at that time without knowledge of the truth because there was no sharia," which is the meaning of ignorance, as in the Exalted's saying: (﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7]), then the matter is clear.

On both interpretations, Musa's answer contains an acknowledgment of the apparent content of the accusation and a nullification of what follows from it, namely making it a proof for denying his message from God. For this reason he responded to Fir'awn's saying (﴿And you are among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 19]) with his saying (﴿And I am among those who went astray﴾), as a nullification, since being a disbeliever at that time would have been more important to nullify.

With this, the reason for the digression in the answer becomes clear in his saying: (﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers﴾). That is: my flight was followed by God bestowing His favour upon me, setting my affairs right, teaching me, guiding me, and sending me. This is not mere verbosity on Musa's part, but because it conveys the meaning that a person is the son of his day, not the son of his yesterday, and that circumstances are judged by their ends. So there is no wonder in what I intended, for God knows best where to place His messages.

His saying (﴿So I fled from you﴾) means: a flight originating from you, because they were the cause of his flight; this is by way of an elided annexed noun, that is, "from your fear." The pronoun refers to Fir'awn and his people who conspired to kill Musa, as the Exalted said: (﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said: "O Musa, the chiefs are conferring about you to kill you"﴾ [al-Qasas: 20]). Ḥukm means wisdom and knowledge, and by it he meant prophethood, which is the first rank, when his Lord spoke to him. Then he said: (﴿and made me one of the messengers﴾), that is, after He showed him the miracle and said to him: (﴿I have chosen you above the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 144]), He sent him with the words: (﴿Go to Fir'awn, for he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24]).

Then he returned to the beginning of the speech and turned to Fir'awn's favour upon him by raising him, nullifying it and refusing to call it a favour. So his saying (﴿And is this a favour﴾) refers to the favour which Fir'awn's gratitude implied, for gratitude can only be for a favour.

Then, if the clause (﴿that you have enslaved﴾) is taken as an explanation of the demonstrative, this serves to reinforce the meaning, together with the reversal of Fir'awn's intended aim. It is similar to the Exalted's saying: (﴿And We made known to him that matter: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]), where (﴿that the last remnant of these﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]) explains (﴿that matter﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]).

It is also possible that (﴿that you have enslaved﴾) is in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, which is the preposition of causation, the sense being: "because you have enslaved the Children of Israel."

It has also been said that the speech is an interrogative with the hamza elided, and it is an interrogative of denial. The meaning of (﴿enslaved﴾) is "subjugated/humiliated," as one says 'abbada, just as one says a'bada with the transitive hamza. The linguists cited:

"How long will my people enslave me, when among them are many camels that they do as they please, and slaves?"

Musa's speech, on all three assessments, is a refutation of Fir'awn's favour by turning the blessing into a curse, reminding him that the blessing of his upbringing was only through the humiliation of the Children of Israel, since Fir'awn had ordered the slaughter of the children of Israel, which resulted in Musa's mother casting her child into the river, whereupon Fir'awn's wife and her attendants found him. They had known that he was one of the children of Israel from the marks of his face and the colour of his skin, which is why Fir'awn's wife said: (﴿The coolness of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas: 9]). In this there is the point that kindness to him together with harm to his people does not increase it in kindness or favour.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 23–24:

Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" He said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you were certain." (Qur'an 26:23–24)

When his intimidation did not work on Musa, peace be upon him, and he knew that Musa would not cease from his call, in execution of what Allah had commanded him, he turned the course of his argument toward that call. So he asked about the reality of the Lord of the worlds, whom Musa and Harun had mentioned as the one who had sent them, when they said: ("Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds" [al-Shu'ara': 16]). The naming of Pharaoh by name, although the usual way of relating exchanges and dialogue is to suffice with the pronoun of the speakers, by the method of "he said, and he said" or "he said, so he said," was a deviation from that method toward mentioning his name, to clarify the speaker of this statement, because of the great distance between this saying of his and his other saying.

The waw is a conjunction, joining this question to the first question, after which Musa's speech came, separating between it and what was conjoined to it.

The particle (ma) in it generally serves to ask about the reality of the noun that follows it, which distinguishes it from others. For this reason it is used to ask about the specification of a tribe. Thus, in the hadith of the delegations, the Prophet ﷺ said to them: ("What are you?"). So Pharaoh asked Musa, peace be upon him, to specify the reality of this one whom he described as ("the Lord of the worlds"). The beliefs of the Copts affirmed multiple scattered gods who had divided among themselves the management of the elements of this world and the kinds of existing things, and those elements are "the worlds," and they did not adhere to one God. The plurality of gods exercising control negates the oneness of control. So when Pharaoh heard from Musa's speech the affirmation of "the Lord of the worlds," his hearing was struck by what he was not accustomed to before, because it entailed affirming one God and negating divinity from the known gods among them. Moreover, they used to claim that Pharaoh was the one chosen from among the gods to be king of Egypt. Thus he was the manifestation of the other gods in the governance of the kingdom ("He said, O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flow beneath me?" [al-Zukhruf: 51]). By this affiliation with the gods and his representation of their will on earth, Pharaoh was called a god.

The nations at that time were heedless of everything other than themselves, so they did not reflect on the varied conditions of nations and the customs of mankind. Every nation feels only itself and its distinctive features, including its gods and its kings. The king would spread among his people nothing but his own strength and his victory over the rebels, and it would appear to the people that the world is confined to that stretch of earth. Thus you find in the monuments of the Copts no depictions of nations other than the tribes whom Pharaoh raided, bringing their captives in shackles and chains, submissive and servile, so that his people imagined that, since he had overcome those, he was the subduer of all mankind. He would conceal reports of his defeat unless a great defeat befell him from a great nation, in such a way that he could not conceal it. Then the style of history among them changes, the new state adopts the customs of the past state, forgets the events of the past, and the present situation comes to dominate their imaginations. Preachers and propagators have a great effect in this. By this, the motive of Pharaoh in this question that he put to Musa becomes clear, and it is a question mingled with astonishment and denial by way of metonymy.

Among the subtleties of this disputation is that inquiry precedes in debates; for this reason Pharaoh began with a question about the reality of the One who sent Musa, peace be upon him.

Musa's answer, peace be upon him, was an explanation of the reality of the Lord of the worlds, in a way that makes the description "Lord of the worlds" a text that admits of no meaning other than what he intended from its apparent sense. So he gave an explanation of the term with what is a detailing of its meaning, when he said: ("Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them"). Thus, by mentioning the heavens and the earth and the generality of what is between them, the explanation of the reality of what was asked about by (ma) was achieved. The return of this explanation is that it is a definition of the reality of the Lord through its properties, because that is the furthest that minds reach in knowing God: that He be known through the traces of His creation. So it is a "formal definition" (ta'rif rasmi) in logical terminology.

The question and answer were arranged in the manner of asking with the word (ma) about the genus. This follows the first of three aspects in formulating the question. The answer is from the speech of al-Kashshaf, and it is also the preference of al-Sakkaki in the chapter on demand in his book al-Miftah, and the answer corresponded to the question in complete correspondence.

The author of al-Kashshaf indicated, and the author of al-Miftah stated explicitly, that Musa's answer, which explains the reality of ("the Lord of the worlds"), contained an alert that the inference toward the affirmation of the one Creator occurs by contemplating the heavens and the earth and what is between them, a contemplation that leads to knowledge of the reality of the one Lord, distinguished from the realities of created things.

For this reason he followed his explanation with his saying: ("if you were certain"), meaning: if you were prepared for certainty, seeking knowledge of realities, not obstinate. Knowledge of this was called certainty (iqan) because it is the nature of certainty that the Creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is God, to whom no other shares.

The plural pronoun in ("if you were certain") is intended to refer to all those present in Pharaoh's assembly. Musa wished to include them in the call, seeking the completion of the call, and that the blame of the speaker does not occur except after his intended meaning from his words becomes clear, since one is not held accountable for courtesies. From this, Sahnun said concerning one who utters a saying or act that entails disbelief: he is brought forward and made to stand on the necessary consequence of his saying; if he understands it and commits to what it entails, then he is regarded as an apostate and is given three days to repent after that.
