Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 25:

﴿He said to those around him: "Do you not listen?"﴾

Pharaoh turned away from addressing Musa and stirred up the feelings of the chiefs (al-mala') around him, who were the people of his assembly. He asked them a question in the manner of one expressing astonishment at their condition: how is it that they did not listen to what Musa had said? He treated them as though they had not listened, in order to provoke their feelings, so that Musa's argument would not take hold of them. Thus he directed the interrogation at the negation of their listening, as has already been explained. This astonishment at their state of listening and silence implies, by way of implication (fahwa al-khitab), an astonishment at Musa's speech, so it is a metonymy (kinayah) for another astonishment. The basis of both astonishments is that affirming one Lord for all created beings is an abomination in Pharaoh's view; since he was a polytheist, he regarded the affirmation of the oneness of God as something that must not be met with silence. And because Pharaoh's speech to those around him includes an answer to Musa's words, Pharaoh's speech is related in the form that the Qur'an customarily uses for relating exchanges of speech, as has been mentioned more than once before, as though he were answering Musa's words.

Musa's words here come in response to Pharaoh's astonishment at the silence of those around him, which is why the narration presents his speech in the manner in which exchanges are usually related. Since Pharaoh's speech turned away from addressing Musa, moving past him to address those around him, Musa directed his address to all of them. When Musa saw that none of them had come to be persuaded by the argument from God's creation of the worlds, which he had begun with, he judged that this argument, though broad in its indication of God's existence and His oneness, since in everything in the heavens and the earth and what lies between them there is a sign pointing to His oneness, [p. 119] was not reaching them. So he descended to them to argue from their own selves and from their fathers, since God brought them into existence after non-existence and then caused their fathers to cease after their existence. The states of their own selves and their fathers are closer to them and easier for them to infer their Creator from. Thus the first argument is distinguished by its generality, and the second is distinguished by its closeness to what is self-evident, for many intelligent people imagined the heavens to be eternal and necessarily existent. As for their fathers, many of the listeners had witnessed the passing away of many of their fathers through death, and this is sufficient as evidence of the negation of eternity, which indicates the negation of divinity.

The generality of "fathers" is comprehensive through its attribution to the pronoun and through its description as "the first (ancestors)", including some of those whom they regard as being in the rank of gods, such as the ancient Pharaohs, who were titled among them "Sons of the Sun", while the sun is counted among the gods, and is represented by the idol (Amun-Ra).

Al-Rabb (the Lord): the Creator, and the Master by virtue of being the Creator.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 27:

﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman."﴾

Pharaoh grew furious when Musa mentioned what included his revered forefathers, with a statement that removes them from the attribute of divinity, claiming that this contradicts reason by necessity, so that it could only come from one whose perception is impaired. He saw that arguing from their creating and the creating of their fathers was futile, because Pharaoh and his chiefs regard the human being as coming into existence through procreation, and they do not reckon that the kind of creation which indicates a Creator is anything but creation by sudden leap (ṭafra) rather than by gradual development (tadrīj). This is based on the premise that plain intellects do not notice the subtleties of familiar things. Thus they reckon the emergence of a chick from an egg to be less than the creation of thunder, and that the creation of the silkworm is more indicative of the Creator than the creation of a human being, though this is not so. Therefore he claimed that asserting that the creation of fathers and sons, and the passing away of fathers, indicates the existence of the One God, Lord of fathers and sons, is a form of madness, since it is a creation whose subtleties they have not witnessed, whereas what is familiar and well known is the birth of fetuses and the death of the dead.

He emphasized his statement with two particles of emphasis, because Musa's condition does not indicate that he is mad, so describing him as mad was open to doubt. Therefore Pharaoh emphasized that he is mad, meaning that he knew from Musa's condition what the listeners might not know.

Pharaoh intended by applying the description of "messenger" to Musa to mock him, as evidenced by his accusing him of a madness that was certain in his own view.

He attributed the "messenger" to the addressees, distancing himself from being the intended recipient of the address, and he reinforced the mockery and the distancing by describing him with the relative clause (﴿who has been sent to you﴾). The content of the relative clause and its complement is the content of "your messenger," so mentioning it served as emphasis and as an explicit statement of the intended meaning, to further incite the listeners, lest they be affected, or lest some of them be affected, by Musa's truthfulness; for Pharaoh was preparing to make ready for resisting Musa, knowing that he had a people in Egypt whom he might seek help from.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 28:

﴿He said: "Lord of the East and the West, and whatever is between them, if you would but use your reason."﴾

When Musa saw their misunderstanding and their failure to be convinced by reasoning about the Oneness (tawhid) through ordinary creation, since the familiar matter had become confused for them with a matter that has no creator, Musa moved on to something they could neither deny nor confuse: the wondrous disposition that is witnessed every day twice. This is just as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, moved from reasoning about the existence of God through giving life and causing death, when its real meaning was obscured for Nimrod, and so Ibrahim moved to reasoning through the rising of the sun, as God the Exalted related: (﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord, because God had given him the kingdom? When Ibrahim said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Ibrahim said, "Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]). Thus the argument of Musa was a Khalili argument (hujjah khalîliyyah, the argument of the Friend of God).

"Al-mashriq" (the east) and "al-maghrib" (the west) may mean the place where the sun rises and the place where it sets on the horizon. In that case it is a prompt to reason from what occurs in those places of the horizon, the rising and setting of the sun, so that "Lord of the East and the West" means the Creator of that daily order, by way of concision.

It may also be that "al-mashriq" and "al-maghrib" are mim-noun verbal nouns (al-masdar al-mimi), meaning: Lord of the rising and the setting. Then "Lord" means the Creator, that is, the one who brings about rising and setting. And "whatever is between them," on both of these readings, means whatever lies between the two states, and the pronoun in "bayn-huma" refers to the east and the west. It is as if it were said: "and whatever is between the east and the west, and whatever is between the west and the east," that is, whatever occurs in the course of these states. As for what lies between the rising and the setting, there is the forenoon, the midday, the afternoon and the yellowing (of the sun); and as for what lies between the setting and the rising, there is the twilight, the dawn and the brightening. All of these are signs of the formation of that wondrous, perfectly ordered system.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "Lord of the East and the West" is the Owner of the two directions. But this interpretation undermines the fit of the speech with the context of reasoning about a great matter, and does not accord with the concluding phrase that follows it in His words: (﴿if you would but use your reason﴾).

Those two directions are the furthest extent of the known inhabited earth for people at that time. It is as if it were said: "Lord of the two ends of the earth," which is a metonymy for the fact that the whole earth belongs to God. This is a customary argument, since at that time they did not know of any king who ruled what lies between the east and the west, and the dominion of the self-proclaimed Pharaoh in their view was only over the lands of Egypt and Sudan.

The concluding clause (﴿if you would but use your reason﴾) is an alert to their rational consideration, so that they may return to reflection and grasp the basis of the argument; that is, "if you would but employ your minds." Among the subtleties is that this is placed opposite Pharaoh's words: "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman." For madness is opposed by reason. Musa had at first spoken to them gently, but when he saw their obstinacy and they described him as mad, he answered them harshly and countered Pharaoh's words (﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 27]) by saying: (﴿if you would but use your reason﴾), that is, "if you are the sensible ones, then do not be the madmen yourselves." This is like the saying of Abu Tammam to those who said to him: "Why do you say what is not understood?" He replied: "Why do you not understand what is said?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 29:

﴿He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among those imprisoned."﴾

When Pharaoh found no success in his argument and saw the strength of Musa's resolve regarding the truth, he turned away from argument to intimidation, so that he might cut off Musa's call at its root. This is the way of one whom proof has overcome, and there is in it a kind of arrogance: to turn away from debate to threat.

The lam in his words (﴿If you take a god﴾) is the lam of preparation for an oath (lam al-muwatta'ah lil-qasam). The meaning is that Pharaoh confirmed his threat with what amounts to an implied oath, which the lam of preparation signals in the Arabic language, as if Pharaoh had said: "I swear by an oath," or "by the oaths," or "I call God to witness." The verb (اتَّخَذْتَ, "you take") is in the continuous sense, meaning: you persist in holding that you have a god who sent you, and that you remain a denier of Pharaoh as god. Pharaoh was counted as a god to his people, because he represents the gods and is the one who carries out their will among the people; he is the intermediary between them and the people.

The meaning of (﴿I will surely make you among those imprisoned﴾) is "I will surely imprison you." He employed here the method of elaboration (itnab), because it is more fitting to the context of threat; for it conveys the sense of "I will make you one of those whom you know to be in my prison," so the purpose is to remind Musa of the terror of imprisonment. It has already been noted that this kind of construction conveys the firm establishment of the predicate in the subject, at the words of the Exalted: (﴿He said, "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67]) in Surat al-Baqarah. Imprisonment among them was a cutting off of the prisoner from acting freely without end, so that he did not know when he would come out of it, as the Exalted said: (﴿But Satan caused him to forget the remembrance of his Lord, so he remained in the prison several years.﴾ [Yusuf: 42]).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 30–33:

﴿He said, "Even if I brought you something clear?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the observers.﴾

When Musa saw Fir'awn's obstinacy in refusing to acknowledge the evidence of reasoned reflection, such that there was no hope of pursuing argument further, since he was turning away from the truth, Musa turned to displaying a sign from the extraordinary events of custom (khawariq al-'ada, miracles) as proof of his truthfulness. He presented it to him before it occurred, in order to block the avenues by which Fir'awn could claim that he did not approve of it.

He put to him a question mixed with denial and astonishment, on the assumption that Fir'awn would not be satisfied with the clear sign, and that he would surely imprison him if he did not acknowledge the divinity of Fir'awn. This was to cut off his excuse before the event. This assumption is indicated by the conditional "law" (even if), which is used to suppose a particular state. The waw in his words "Even if I brought you" is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the thing questioned by the interrogative hamza is omitted, indicated by the fact that the speech is a reply to Fir'awn's words: "I will surely make you one of those imprisoned" [al-Shu'ara': 29]. The sense is: "Will you make me one of the imprisoned, while the circumstance is that I have brought you a clear sign?" The purpose of the question is the state contained in the condition of "law," namely that it is the state most likely to prevent the goal being asked about, if it occurred, which is persistence in denial. This is a genuine question.

The waw is not postponed after the interrogative hamza, because the interrogative particle has the priority of position; rather, it is the waw that conjoins the question.

The element working in the circumstance and the element to which the circumstance refers are both implied, indicated by his words "I will surely make you" [al-Shu'ara': 29], i.e., "Will you make me one of the imprisoned?"

The description of "thing" (shay') as "clear" (mubin) is the active participle of abana, the transitive form, meaning "making clear that I am a messenger from God."

Fir'awn turned away from explicitly committing himself to acknowledging what Musa would bring, and so he spoke ambiguously when he said: "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful." In his words "if you are of the truthful" there is a hint that Fir'awn's speech implies that the assumption of Musa's truthfulness is a weak one, as is generally the case with the conditional "in" (if), while also implying that he had brought something clear and would be considered truthful in what he called to. Thus the question remained open as to whether what Musa would bring was clear or not clear. Fir'awn's speech postponed this until after the event and the descent of the sign, so that he could deny it if he needed to.

The thu'ban (serpent) is the large, long snake.

The description of "serpent" (thu'ban) as "clear" (mubin), which is the active participle of abana in its intransitive form, meaning "became manifest," indicates intense manifestness, since an increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning. The sense is: a serpent that is manifestly a serpent, with no confusion or illusion about it.

Through the difference between the first "mubin" and the second "mubin," the two final rhyme-words differ in meaning, so they are of the type of paronomasia (jinas), and they are not what is called iyta' (undesirable repetition of the same rhyme-word).

The "ilqa'" (throwing) is casting from the hand to the ground, and it was discussed in surah al-A'raf.

The "naz'" (drawing out) is pulling out something from what surrounds it, as in removing clothing or drawing a bucket from a well. The drawing out of the hand is bringing it out from the garment, so the object from which it was drawn is omitted for its obviousness. The sense is: he brought his hand out from the collar of his garment.

The sudden "idha" indicates the speed with which the colour of his hand changed to white.

The lam in his words "for the observers" may be the lam that Ibn Malik and Ibn Hisham call the lam of transitivity (lam al-ta'diya), meaning the connection of what it governs to its object. The more apparent view is that the lam means "at" ('inda), and the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial element (hal). The explanation of this was given previously in the commentary on God's words in surah al-A'raf: "He drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the observers."

The meaning of "for the observers" is that its whiteness was something the observers sought out because of its wonder, while the colour of Musa's skin was tawny. The definite article in "the observers" is for comprehensive generality by custom (al-istighraq al-'urfi), i.e., all the observers in that assembly. This indicates that its whiteness was clear and manifest, differing from the colour of his skin, in a way far from the colour of leprosy.

In his words "if you are of the truthful" there is a hint that Fir'awn's speech implies that the assumption of Musa's truthfulness is a weak one, as is generally the case with the conditional "in" (if), while also implying that he had brought something clear and would be considered truthful in what he called to. Thus the question remained open as to whether what Musa would bring was clear or not clear. Fir'awn's speech postponed this until after the event and the descent of the sign, so that he could deny it if he needed to.

The thu'ban (serpent) is the large, long snake.

The description of "serpent" (thu'ban) as "clear" (mubin), which is the active participle of abana in its intransitive form, meaning "became manifest," indicates intense manifestness, since an increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning. The sense is: a serpent that is manifestly a serpent, with no confusion or illusion about it.

Through the difference between the first "mubin" and the second "mubin," the two final rhyme-words differ in meaning, so they are of the type of paronomasia (jinas), and they are not what is called iyta' (undesirable repetition of the same rhyme-word).

The "ilqa'" (throwing) is casting from the hand to the ground, and it was discussed in surah al-A'raf.

The "naz'" (drawing out) is pulling out something from what surrounds it, as in removing clothing or drawing a bucket from a well. The drawing out of the hand is bringing it out from the garment, so the object from which it was drawn is omitted for its obviousness. The sense is: he brought his hand out from the collar of his garment.

The sudden "idha" indicates the speed with which the colour of his hand changed to white.

The lam in his words "for the observers" may be the lam that Ibn Malik and Ibn Hisham call the lam of transitivity (lam al-ta'diya), meaning the connection of what it governs to its object. The more apparent view is that the lam means "at" ('inda), and the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial element (hal). The explanation of this was given previously in the commentary on God's words in surah al-A'raf: "He drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the observers."

The meaning of "for the observers" is that its whiteness was something the observers sought out because of its wonder, while the colour of Musa's skin was tawny. The definite article in "the observers" is for comprehensive generality by custom (al-istighraq al-'urfi), i.e., all the observers in that assembly. This indicates that its whiteness was clear and manifest, differing from the colour of his skin, in a way far from the colour of leprosy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 30–33:

﴿He said, "Even if I brought you something clear?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the observers.﴾

When Musa saw Fir'awn's obstinacy in refusing to acknowledge the evidence of reasoned reflection, such that there was no hope of pursuing argument further, since he was turning away from the truth, Musa turned to displaying a sign from the extraordinary events of custom (khawariq al-'ada, miracles) as proof of his truthfulness. He presented it to him before it occurred, in order to block the avenues by which Fir'awn could claim that he did not approve of it.

He put to him a question mixed with denial and astonishment, on the assumption that Fir'awn would not be satisfied with the clear sign, and that he would surely imprison him if he did not acknowledge the divinity of Fir'awn. This was to cut off his excuse before the event. This assumption is indicated by the conditional "law" (even if), which is used to suppose a particular state. The waw in his words "Even if I brought you" is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the thing questioned by the interrogative hamza is omitted, indicated by the fact that the speech is a reply to Fir'awn's words: "I will surely make you one of those imprisoned" [al-Shu'ara': 29]. The sense is: "Will you make me one of the imprisoned, while the circumstance is that I have brought you a clear sign?" The purpose of the question is the state contained in the condition of "law," namely that it is the state most likely to prevent the goal being asked about, if it occurred, which is persistence in denial. This is a genuine question.

The waw is not postponed after the interrogative hamza, because the interrogative particle has the priority of position; rather, it is the waw that conjoins the question.

The element working in the circumstance and the element to which the circumstance refers are both implied, indicated by his words "I will surely make you" [al-Shu'ara': 29], i.e., "Will you make me one of the imprisoned?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 34–35:

﴿He said to the eminent ones around him: "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer."﴾ ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land with his sorcery, so what do you advise?﴾

The discussion of the parallel of this verse has already preceded in Surat al-A'raf, except that in this verse there is an addition, "with his sorcery" (bi-sihrihi), which is clear. Also, in this verse it is stated that this is the statement of Pharaoh to the chiefs (al-mala'), whereas in the verse of al-A'raf it is: ﴿The eminent ones of Pharaoh's people said﴾ [al-A'raf: 109]. The reconciliation between them is that Pharaoh said it to those around him, and they repeated it in his exact words, out of complete agreement, such that they did not suffice with saying "Yes," but rather they repeated Pharaoh's speech so that their statement would be in full accordance with his words.

The word (hawlahu) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarfiyyah). The adverb here is stable (mustaqirr), because it is connected to an omitted verb (kawn mahdhuf) which is a circumstantial phrase (hal) of al-mala'. The reason for the expression of their counsel with the words (ta'murun) has already been explained in Surat al-A'raf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 36–37:

﴿They said: "Put him and his brother off, and send heralds to the cities,﴾ ﴿to bring you every skilled sorcerer."﴾

The discussion of its counterpart in Surah al-A'raf has already passed, except that in this verse (wab'ath, "send") replaces (arsil, "send"), and the two are synonyms; and in this verse (sahhar, "skilled sorcerer") appears, whereas there it is (sahir, "sorcerer").

Al-sahhar (the intensive form of sahir, "sorcerer") is synonymous with al-sahir in usage, because the pattern fa''al here indicates attribution denoting a craft, like najjar ("carpenter") and qassab ("butcher"). For this reason it is followed here, and there, by the attribute (alim, "knowing"), meaning one strong in knowledge of magic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 38–40:

﴿So the magicians were assembled for the appointment of a known day.﴾ ﴿And it was said to the people, "Will you gather?"﴾ ﴿"Perhaps we will follow the magicians if they are the victors."﴾

The fa' (so) indicates that the assembling of the magicians took place in the quickest time after the dispatch of the summoners, out of the eagerness of the summoners and the summoned to carry out the command of Pharaoh.

The verb forms (ju'ima, "were assembled," and qila, "it was said") are in the passive voice, because the ones who assembled and the ones who said it were not specified; that is, whoever assembles assembled, and whoever speaks spoke.

The lam in (li-mi'ad) carries the meaning of (ʿinda, "at"), like the lam in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78]). The day is the Day of the Adornment, and it is the day of the Nile's flood. The appointed time is forenoon, as in Surat Ta-Ha.

Al-mi'ad (appointment, "set time") means the time; its original sense is the name of an instrument for fixing time. The specified time was named by it, likening it to the instrument.

The definiteness in (li-l-nas, "the people") is for comprehensiveness by custom, and they are the people of Pharaoh's city, Memphis (Manfis) or Thebes (Taybah).

And (﴿Will you gather?﴾) is an urging of the people to assemble. The interrogative is used to request haste in assembling, such that they are treated as one who asks a question seeking confirmation of their resolve to assemble, as in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿So will you desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]) in Surat al-'Uqud, and in the saying of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran:

Will you send a dinar for our need, or a slave of Rabb, a brother of 'Awn ibn Mikhraq?

He means: send to us a dinar or a slave of Rabb quickly, for our need, with one of the two.

They hoped to follow the magicians, that is, to follow what the magic of the magicians supports, which is the nullification of the religion brought by Musa. So their saying (﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾) is a metonymy for hope of their support in denying the mission of Musa, so that they would not follow him. The intent is not that the magicians would become their leaders, because Pharaoh is the one who is followed. In the condition (﴿if they are the victors﴾) the particle (in) is used, because it is the root of the conditional particles, and they had no doubt that the magicians would prevail. This is the condition of those deluded by their desires, blind to considering the changing states of affairs, who only posit those possibilities that agree with their desires and do not take precautions against the opposite possibility.

When the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh, "Will there be a reward for us if we are the victors?" ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَ السَّحَرَةُ قالُوا لِفِرْعَوْنَ أئِنَّ لَنا لَأجْرًا إنْ كُنّا نَحْنُ الغالِبِينَ﴾ He said, "Yes, and you will then be among those brought near." ﴿قالَ نَعَمْ وإنَّكم إذًا لَمِنَ المُقَرَّبِينَ﴾

Its parallel has already occurred in Surat al-A'raf, with His words, "And the magicians came" (وجاءَ السَّحَرَةُ), and with the omission of the interrogative hamza, since there He said, "Indeed, for us there is surely a reward" (إنَّ لَنا لَأجْرًا). This is a variation (tafannun, the rhetorical practice of varying expression) in relating their statement when it is repeated, so that it is not repeated in exactly the same form. It also omits the word "idhan" (then/in that case). Here He related what is implied in Pharaoh's speech as a response (jaza') to the substance of their statement, "Indeed, for us there is surely a reward, if we are the victors" (﴿إنَّ لَنا لَأجْرًا إنْ كُنّا نَحْنُ الغالِبِينَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 113]), in addition to what the particle "na'am" (yes) confirms of their question about the reward. The sense of the sentence is therefore: "If you are victors, then indeed you will be among those brought near." This was omitted in Surat al-A'raf, so its mention here is an addition to the narrative of the story. Such is the manner of the Qur'an in its narratives: the return to them does not lack a benefit not mentioned in another place, renewing the listener's attentiveness, as was explained in the seventh introduction (al-muqaddimah al-sabi'ah) among the introductions of this tafsir.

Their question about entitlement to the reward reflects a presumption (idlal, confident assertion) based on their expertise and on Pharaoh's need of them, for they knew that Pharaoh was extremely eager that they should be the victors, and they feared that Pharaoh would press them into service without pay. So they stipulated their reward before beginning the work, so that he would be bound by his promise.

This was omitted in Surat al-A'raf, so its mention here is an addition to the narrative of the story. Such is the manner of the Qur'an in its narratives: the return to them does not lack a benefit not mentioned in another place, renewing the listener's attentiveness, as was explained in the seventh introduction (al-muqaddimah al-sabi'ah) among the introductions of this tafsir.

Their question about entitlement to the reward reflects a presumption (idlal, confident assertion) based on their expertise and on Pharaoh's need of them, for they knew that Pharaoh was extremely eager that they should be the victors, and they feared that Pharaoh would press them into service without pay. So they stipulated their reward before beginning the work, so that he would be bound by his promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 43–44:

﴿Musa said to them, "Throw down what you are going to throw down."﴾ ﴿So they threw down their ropes and their staffs, and said, "By the might of Pharaoh, we will surely be the victors."﴾

The speech of Musa in that assembly is related by repeating the verb (qala, "he said") separately, in the manner of narrating dialogues, because he was the intended party of the dialogue, since they had come on his account.

In Surah al-A'raf there occurs (﴿They said, "O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw." He said, "Throw."﴾ [al-A'raf: 115]), and their offering Musa the choice of initiating the actions is omitted here, and its explanation has already preceded there. So Musa's saying to them, "Throw" (alqu), as related here, is a command merely for the fact that they are the ones who begin the throwing, so that it is followed by the nullifying of their magic by what Musa will throw. This is like the disputant in the science of kalam (ilm al-kalam, the science of theological discourse) saying to the heretic, "State your doubt (shubha)," while he intends to refute it for him. And this is 'Adud al-Din in his book al-Mawaqif, who mentions the doubts of the people of deviation and error before mentioning the proofs that refute them. The throwing was mentioned just before. The object of (alqaw, "they threw") is mentioned here and omitted in Surah al-A'raf.

In the speech of Musa, peace be upon him, there is belittling of what they will throw, since he expressed it in the form of generality, i.e., whatever you are able to throw. The discussion of the ropes and staffs in magic has already preceded when discussing this story in Surah Ta-Ha.

The relating of the magicians' saying is joined with the conjunction "wa" (and), unlike the narrations that preceded it, because this is a saying not intended as a dialogue, but rather a saying they began with at the start of the magic, seeking help and blessing by the might of Pharaoh. So the ba' in their saying, "by the might of Pharaoh," is like the ba' in "bismillah" (in the name of God): they intended to seek blessing by the power of Pharaoh, as said by Ibn 'Atiyya.

It has been said that the ba' is for oath: they swore by the might of Pharaoh that they would be victors, out of confidence, based on their belief in their error, that the will of Pharaoh cannot be overcome by anyone, since it is the will of their gods. However, this is what the commentators have set aside, and the first opinion is better, because the two sentences, according to it, convey two benefits.

The "'izza" (might) means power, and it has been discussed earlier in His saying (﴿Pride led him to sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206]) in Surah al-Baqarah.

The sentence (﴿Indeed, we are surely the victors﴾) is a resumptive, declarative (insha'i) sentence following their saying (﴿by the might of Pharaoh﴾): as if the listener, whether Musa or another, says to himself, "What effect does their saying (﴿by the might of Pharaoh﴾) have?" So they say (﴿Indeed, we are surely the victors﴾), and by this they intended to instill fear in the soul of Musa so that what he would throw in his turn would come from a weakened resolve, since they knew that resolve is among the greatest causes of the success of magic and its influence on the onlookers. The sentence (﴿Indeed, we are surely the victors﴾), with the emphatic particles it contains, conveys the meaning of an oath.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 46–49:

﴿So the magicians were cast down, prostrating.﴾ ﴿They said: "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said: "Have you believed in Him before I give you permission? Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 50–51:

﴿They said, "No harm! Indeed, we are returning to our Lord.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we aspire that our Lord will forgive us our sins, since we were the first of the believers."﴾

Al-Ḍayr (ضَيْر): a synonym of al-ḍurr (harm). It is said: ḍārahu, with the rā' lightened, yaḍīruhu, and the meaning of ﴿lā ḍayra﴾ is: your threat will not harm us. The negation of harm here means: it is a harm of a moment, after which there follows lasting bliss, so in relation to what follows it is as though it were nothing. This is a mode of negation which is used when there is an indicator for it. From it is their saying: "This is nothing," meaning it does not exist, but the intended meaning is that its existence is like non-existence.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we are returning to our Lord﴾ is a reason for the negation of harm, and it is the indicator of the intended meaning of the negation.

Al-Inqilāb (الِانْقِلاب): the return, and it has been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we aspire that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾ explains the intended meaning of the clause ﴿Indeed, we are returning to our Lord﴾. Al-ṭamaʿ (الطَّمَع): it is used for weak conjecture, and it is known as seeking what is difficult to attain. It is also used to mean conjecture, as in the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿And He it is from Whom I aspire that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82]. This usage is an expression of courtesy toward God, because He does what He wills. They gave as the reason for this aspiration that they were the first of the believers in God by confirming Musa (peace be upon him). In this is an indication of the firmness of their faith in God and His promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 52:

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾

This is another narrative about the circumstances of Musa in his call to Fir'awn. The conjunction "waw" serves to connect the narrative, and it does not indicate that this narrative is close in time to the previous one. Musa remained for a period of time demanding that Fir'awn release the Children of Israel so that they might leave Egypt, while Fir'awn kept delaying in this matter, until he saw the nine signs, as has been mentioned previously in Surah al-A'raf. Part of this verse has a parallel that has been mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha. This verse adds to that with His saying: (﴿for you will be pursued﴾), meaning that Allah informed Musa that Fir'awn would pursue them with his army, as in the verse of Surah Ta-Ha. The purpose of informing him of this is to encourage him.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read (اسْرِ) with a hamzat al-wasl, as an imperative verb from (سَرى) (sara, to travel by night), and with a kasra on the nun of (أنِ) because of the meeting of two silent letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). The rest read with a hamzat al-qat' and a sukun on the nun of (أنْ). The two verbs sara and asra are synonymous, as has been mentioned previously in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Glorified is He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]).

[Page 130]

The apparent sequence of the clauses requires that the *fa'* (ف) indicates immediate consequence following the clause ﴿And We revealed to Musa﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 52]. Between the two clauses there is an omitted element, whose estimated wording is: "So Musa set out by night and departed with them, so Pharaoh sent (summoners) into the cities, gathering (people)." That is, when the Children of Israel departed, Pharaoh feared that they would spread out into the cities of Egypt, so he sent police (*shurat*) into the cities to round up the people, so that they might catch up with the Children of Israel and bring them back to the city that was the seat of the kingdom.

*Al-Madain* is the plural of *madina*, meaning a great city. The cities of the Egyptian region at that time were numerous. Among them: (Manufri or Manfis), today Mit Rahina in al-Giza; (Tiba or Tiba), today al-Uqsur (Luxor); (Abudu), also called today al-'Araba al-Madfuna; (Abu), which is (Bu), today Idfu (Edfu); (Un Ramisi); (Armint); (Sana), today Asna; (Sawarat), today al-Siyut (Asyut); (Khamunu), today al-Ashmuniyyin (Hermopolis); (Bamazit), today al-Bahnasa; (Khisuw), today Sakha; (Kariyayna), today Sadd Abi Qayra; (Sudu), today al-Fayyum; and (Kuyti), today Qift.

The definite article in *al-madain* is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), meaning all the cities of the Egyptian region. This is a customary comprehensiveness (*istighraq 'urfi*), meaning the cities subject to Pharaoh's rule, or those presumed to lie near their route. Pharaoh and his people did not know where the Children of Israel had headed, so he wished to intercept them on every road he suspected they would pass along. He did not know whether they had turned toward the Levant (*al-Sham*) or toward the western desert, and he did not imagine that they intended the shore of the Red Sea, the Sea of *al-Qulzum*, which at that time was called the Sea of *Suf*.

The clause ﴿Indeed these are a small band, few in number﴾ is a speech (*maqul*) of an omitted utterance, because *hashirin* (summoners) implies the meaning of a call. That is, they say: "Indeed these are a small band, few in number."

The demonstrative *ha'ula'* (these) refers to something present in people's minds, because the affair of the Children of Israel had spread throughout the regions of Egypt during the period between the gathering of the magicians and the departure of the Children of Israel. The reference is not specifically to the magicians, since that does not fit the narrative.

In the demonstrative there is an implication of belittling their status, which is reinforced by the explicit statement that they are a small band, few in number.

*Al-shirdhima* is a small group of people. This is how the verifying scholars among the linguists explained it. Following it with the descriptor *qalilun* (few) serves as emphasis, to remove the possibility that the word is used to belittle their status or in comparison with Pharaoh's soldiers. The number of the Children of Israel who departed was six hundred thousand, as the commentators said, and this agrees with what is in the Book of Numbers (*Sifr al-'Adad*) of the Torah, in chapter twenty-six.

*Qalilun* is a second predicate (*khabar thani*) of the demonstrative. It is therefore a descriptor in meaning of what the word *ha'ula'* denotes, not a descriptor of *shirdhima*. Rather, it is emphatic of its meaning, and for this reason it was brought in the sound plural form (*jam' al-salama*), which is not one of the plurals of multitude.

[Page 131]

When *qalil* is used as a descriptor, it may agree with the thing described, as here, or it may be kept in the singular and masculine form, as the poet al-Samaw'al or al-Harithi said:

"And it did us no harm that we are few..." (the verse continues).

Its parallel in this respect is the word *kathir* (many), and the verse of the Exalted combines them: ﴿When Allah shows them to you in your dream as few; and if He had shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 43].

*Ghaizun* is the active participle of *ghaza-hu*, which has the meaning of *aghaza-hu*, that is, made him full of anger. *Al-ghaiz* is the intensest form of anger. It was mentioned in the Exalted's saying: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119] in Al 'Imran, and in His saying ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts﴾ [al-Tawba: 15] in Surat Bara'a. That is, they are doing what angers us.

The *lam* in His saying *lana* (to us) is the *lam* of reinforcement (*lam al-taqwiya*), and the *lam* in *la-ghaizun* is the *lam* of initiation (*lam al-ibtida'*). The placing of *lana* before *la-ghaizun* is for the sake of the rhyme (*ri'aya 'ala al-fasila*).

His saying: ﴿And indeed we are all cautious﴾ is an exhortation to the people of the cities to be cautious in the most emphatic manner, since he placed himself with them in this by saying *lajami'un* (all of us). This is a metaphor (*kinaya*) for the obligation of following him in governing the kingdom. That is: we are all cautious. *Jami'un* occurs as the subject, and its predicate is *hadhirun*, and the sentence is the predicate of *inna*. *Jami'un* has the meaning of *kull* (all), as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾ [Yunus: 4] in Surat Yunus.

*Hadhirun* was read by the majority (*al-Jumhur*) without an *alif* after the *ha'*, so it is the plural of *hadhir*, which is among the forms of intensification (*mubalagha*) according to Sibawayh and the verifying scholars. Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn 'Amir and Khalaf read it with an *alif* after the *ha'*, as the plural of *hadhir* (*hadhir*, with the active participle form). The meaning is that caution is part of his character and habit, and so the nation must likewise be with him in this. That is: it is our habit to be alert to events and cautious about what may have among them evil consequences.

This is a great principle among the principles of governance, namely blocking the means to corruption (*sadd dhara'i' al-fasad*), even if the likelihood of their leading to corruption is weak. The means that are disregarded in legislation concerning private rights are not disregarded in the governance of the public. For this reason the scholars of the Sharia say: the consideration of rulers regarding the interests of the nation is broader than the consideration of judges. Caution is broader than protecting rights, and it is the fear

[Page 132]

of the occurrence of a harmful thing that may happen, and the watchfulness to prevent its occurrence. It was mentioned in His saying: ﴿The hypocrites are wary﴾ [al-Tawba: 64] in Bara'a. What is praiseworthy in it is fear of harm when its occurrence is possible, not fear of a matter whose occurrence is impossible, for caution regarding the latter is a form of obsession.

This favors the view that the thing to be guarded against was the deception by the faith of the magicians in Allah and their affirmation of Musa. It is unlikely that the intended meaning is the departure of the Children of Israel from Egypt, because at that point it had already happened, so one would not be cautious against it; rather, the effort would be toward vengeance against them.

He did not know whether they had turned toward the Levant (*al-Sham*) or toward the western desert, and he did not imagine that they intended the shore of the Red Sea, the Sea of *al-Qulzum*, which at that time was called the Sea of *Suf*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 57–60:

﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and treasures and a noble station﴾ ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them﴾ ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾.

If you follow what the exegetes have explained of His saying: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53], it becomes necessary that you make the fa' (فَ, "so") in His saying "fa-akhrajnahum" (so We expelled them) indicate that the expulsion follows from the sending of the gatherers, i.e., he began by sending the gatherers and his going out followed that. The sequence indicated by the fa' is then according to what fits the interval between the sending of the gatherers and the arrival of the prophets (i.e., the messengers of Moses) from the regions of the kingdom, with the designation of the route of the Children of Israel; for Pharaoh would not go out with his army aimlessly, not knowing their route. The pronoun of the accusative (في "-hum" in "akhrajnahum") refers to Pharaoh and those with him, understood from His saying: "Indeed, you are pursued" (إنَّكم مُتَّبَعُونَ).

And if you follow what we have explained of His exalted saying: (﴿Then Pharaoh sent﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53]), and I do not think you would be other than content with choosing that, then make the fa' in "fa-akhrajnahum" a consequence of the sentence "﴿Indeed, you are pursued﴾" [al-Shu'ara': 52]. The estimated meaning: So Moses journeyed by night with the Children of Israel, so We expelled Pharaoh and his army from their lands in pursuit of the Children of Israel, and they followed the Children of Israel.

The pronoun in "akhrajnahum" under every interpretation refers to what is understood from the context, i.e., We expelled Pharaoh and his army. The gardens (al-jannat): the palm gardens that were on the banks of the Nile. The springs (al-'uyun): sources dug along the channels of the Nile. The treasures (al-kunuz): accumulated wealth.

The maqam: its original sense is the place of standing, or the verbal noun of qama. The meaning according to the first is: noble dwellings; according to the second: their standing in their society. The karim (noble): the precious of its kind. That is what they had of security, wealth and luxury. All of that Pharaoh and his army left behind, those who went out from it to pursue the Children of Israel, for they perished and did not return to anything of what they had left.

(Thus) The discussion of its counterpart has preceded at His saying: ﴿Thus; and We had encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91] in Surat al-Kahf, so it is in the position of a parenthetical remark (i'tiradh).

And the clause ﴿and We made them inherit it, the Children of Israel﴾ is also parenthetical, and the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and it is not a conjunction of parts of the narrative, for reasons you will know. Al-iratha (inheritance): making someone an heir. Its original sense is giving the property of a dead person, and it is also applied to giving what was owned by another to the one given (with a fatha on the ta'), as He, exalted, said: ﴿And We made the people who were oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed﴾ [al-A'raf: 137], i.e., We made the Children of Israel inherit the land of al-Sham, and He said: ﴿Then We made inherit the Book those whom We chose from Our servants﴾ [Fatir: 32].

The meaning: that God deprived the enemies of Moses of the bounty they had, for He destroyed them and gave the Children of Israel good things like them that had not been theirs. The intended meaning is not that He gave the Children of Israel what had been in the hand of Pharaoh and his people of gardens, springs and treasures, because the Children of Israel had then departed the land of Egypt and did not return to it, as His saying in Surat al-Dukhan indicates: ﴿Thus; and We made other people inherit them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 28]. There is no validity to what some of the storytellers of the Qur'an's narratives say, that the Children of Israel returned and then ruled Egypt after that, for the Children of Israel did not rule Egypt after their departure from it for all time. So there is no escape from turning the verse away from its apparent sense to an interpretation indicated by history and indicated by what is in Surat al-Dukhan.

So the pronoun in (﴿wa-awrathnaha﴾) here refers to the things enumerated, considering them as generic nouns, i.e., We made the Children of Israel inherit gardens, springs and treasures. The return of the pronoun here to a word used in the generic sense is close to the figure of istikhdam and stronger than it, i.e., We gave them things that had not been theirs before and that had belonged to the Canaanites, so God empowered the Children of Israel over them and they overcame them in the land of Palestine and al-Sham. The pronoun may return to the wording rather than the meaning, as in their saying: "I have a dirham and its half," and His saying, exalted: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, then for her is half of what he leaves, and he inherits from her if she has no child﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], since the meaning is not that the man who died inherits his sister who has half of what he left, but rather the meaning is: and the man inherits a sister of his if she has no child. It is also possible that the accusative pronoun is the object of the verb (awrathna) in the sense of an eloquent simile, i.e., We made them inherit the like of them. It has also been said: the pronoun in (awrathnaha) refers specifically to the treasures, because the Children of Israel borrowed on the night of their departure from their Egyptian neighbours their ornaments of gold and silver, and went out with them, as preceded in Surat Ta-Ha.

In my view there is another possibility, namely that the clause (﴿So We expelled them from gardens﴾) up to His saying (﴿wa-awrathnaha﴾) is a quotation of a speech from God interposed between the speech of Pharaoh. The pronoun in (﴿fa-akhrajnahum﴾) refers to the people of Pharaoh understood from His saying (﴿in the cities﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53]), i.e., so We expelled the people of the cities. The second object of the verb (awrathnaha) is omitted. The estimate: and We made them inherit others, and His saying "the Children of Israel" is an explanation of the demonstrative in His saying (﴿Indeed, these﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 54]); he took the path of summary then explanation so that it would fall into the souls of the hearers in the most effective way.

The clause (fa-atba'uhum mushriqin) is a consequence of the clause (fa-akhrajnahum), and what is between them is parenthetical. The estimate: We expelled them, so they followed them. The pronoun of the nominative refers to what the pronoun of the accusative in (﴿fa-akhrajnahum﴾) referred to, and the pronoun of the accusative refers to "my servants" (ʿibadi) in His saying: (﴿Travel by night with My servants﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 52]).

And (atba'uhum) with a hamza of cutting and sukun on the ta', with the meaning of tabi'a, i.e., they overtook them.

And (﴿mushriqin﴾) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the nominative pronoun. It may mean heading toward the direction of the east; one says ashraqa, if he entered the land of the east, just as one says anjada, ataham, a'raqa and ash'ama. From this it is known that the Children of Israel turned toward the east, which is the direction of the Sea of al-Qulzum, which is the Red Sea, and it was called on that day the Sea of Suf, and it is east of Egypt. It may also mean entering the time of sunrise, i.e., they overtook them at sunrise, after they had spent a night or nights walking, so that they did not see one another until the sunrise after the nights of travel.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 61–66:

﴿So when the two groups saw each other, the companions of Musa said, "Indeed, we are going to be overtaken."﴾ ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ ﴿So We revealed to Musa, "Strike the sea with your staff." And it parted, and each part became like a great mountain.﴾ ﴿And We brought near the others there.﴾ ﴿And We saved Musa and those with him, all of them.﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others.﴾

Meaning: when Pharaoh and his soldiers drew close to the place where the groups of the Children of Israel were, such that each group could see the other. Al-tara'i (seeing one another) is a reciprocal form (tafa'ul), because the act occurs from both sides.

Their saying, ﴿Indeed, we are going to be overtaken﴾, is emphasized with the particle of emphasis (inna and lam) due to the intensity of their concern with this news, and it is used to express panic. ﴿Kalla﴾ (No!) is a rebuke. In Surat Maryam, ﴿No! We will record what he says﴾ [Maryam: 79] was used by Musa to repel their assumption that Pharaoh would overtake them, and he justified his rebuke of them with the clause ﴿Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me.﴾

Attributing the companionship (ma'iyyah) to the Lord in ﴿Indeed, with me is my Lord﴾ means the companionship of Allah's gentle kindness toward him and His care in arranging the means of his salvation from his enemy. This is because Musa was confident that Allah would save him, in accordance with His saying, ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ and His saying, ﴿Travel with My servants by night; indeed, you will be pursued﴾, as was mentioned just before, which was a promise of guaranteeing salvation.

The clause ﴿He will guide me﴾ is either a resumed (independent) sentence or a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "my Lord." The presence of the particle of future (sa-) does no harm, because the circumstantial clause is anticipatory (muqaddarah), as in His saying, quoting Ibrahim: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [al-Saffat: 99]. The meaning is: He will show me the way to our safety from Pharaoh and his army.

Musa restricted the statement to himself in ﴿Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me﴾ because they did not know what Allah had guaranteed him of the companionship of care. When they knew that, they would know that his guidance would benefit them, since he was their leader and the one sent for their benefit. The reason he restricted it to himself is also that the way to their salvation, after Pharaoh and his army had overtaken them, could only be achieved by an act that cuts off the root of the enemy, and this act was extraordinary (khariq lil-'adah), so it could only occur at the hand of the Messenger. This is the reason for the difference in the companionship between this verse and His saying in the account of the cave: ﴿When he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40]; because that was the companionship of protecting both of them by diverting the eyes of the enemies away from them.

Allah commanded him to strike the sea with his staff, and the sea split into paths through which the tribes of the Children of Israel passed. Pharaoh charged into the sea, so the sea closed over them when they were in its midst, and all of them drowned.

Al-firq, with a kasra on the fa' and a sukun on the ra', is the separated part of something, and it has the meaning of a passive participle (maf'ul), like al-falaq. Al-tawd is the mountain.

Azlafna (We brought near) means We brought close and made near; it is derived from al-zalaf with a fatha on the lam, which means nearness. The apparent form of its verb is like fariha. It is said: izdalafa: drew near; and tazallafa: drew close; so the hamzah in azlafna is for causative transitivity. The meaning is that Allah emboldened them until they wanted to enter the paths of the sea, as they saw the action of the Children of Israel, thinking that it was shallow water.

Al-akharun (the others) are the people of Pharaoh, because it occurs in opposition to the group of the Children of Israel.

Attributing the companionship (ma'iyyah) to the Lord in ﴿Indeed, with me is my Lord﴾ means the companionship of Allah's gentle kindness toward him and His care in arranging the means of his salvation from his enemy. This is because Musa was confident that Allah would save him, in accordance with His saying, ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ and His saying, ﴿Travel with My servants by night; indeed, you will be pursued﴾, as was mentioned just before, which was a promise of guaranteeing salvation.

The presence of the particle of future (sa-) does no harm, because the circumstantial clause is anticipatory (muqaddarah), as in His saying, quoting Ibrahim: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [al-Saffat: 99]. Allah commanded him to strike the sea with his staff, and the sea split into paths through which the tribes of the Children of Israel passed. Pharaoh charged into the sea, so the sea closed over them when they were in its midst, and all of them drowned.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 67–68:

﴿Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Most Merciful.﴾

The saying concerning its like was mentioned a little earlier, before the story of Musa (Moses). This story is a sign because it indicates that this great reversal in the conditions of the two groups, which departs from the customary changes of states and nations, is evidence that it was a special act of God, by which He strengthened His Messenger and his community, broke the power of their enemies and of those who disbelieved in him. It is therefore a sign of the consequences of denying God's messengers, together with the proofs of divine unity (tawhid, the affirmation of God's oneness) contained in the story.

As for the reason each argument in this surah, concerning the proofs of God's oneness (wahdaniyyah) and the truthfulness of the messengers, is concluded with the sentence (﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾) through to its end, it was explained at the opening of this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 69–77 (part 1 of 2):

Page 137

﴿And recite to them the news of Abraham, when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?" They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them." He said, "Do they hear you when you call (upon them)? Or do they benefit you or harm you?" They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing thus." He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your forefathers, the ancients? Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds."﴾

The story of Moses with Pharaoh and his people is followed by the story of Abraham. It is placed here before the story of Noah, contrary to the usual order of their stories in the Qur'an, because of the strong resemblance between the people of Abraham and the Arab polytheists in worshipping idols that neither hear nor see. In it there is also (a lesson about) their clinging to the error of their fathers, and that Abraham called them to reason out the degradation of the idols from the rank of deserving worship, so that people's faith would rest upon the evidence of the natural disposition (fitrah). And in it (there is the point) that the people of Abraham were not afflicted with the worldly punishments that were inflicted upon the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and the people of Madyan, so they resembled the Quraysh in being granted respite.

The message of Muhammad and Abraham, may Allah bless them both, rests on the pillar of the fitrah in belief and action, i.e., in creed and legislation, for God did not place this fitrah in the creation of man so that he would waste it and neglect it, but rather so that he would uphold it and put it into practice. When God struck the example for the polytheists, to refute their claim that they would not believe until signs come to them like those given to Moses — for the signs of Moses, which are the most numerous of the signs of the earlier messengers, did not effect anything in the faith of Pharaoh and his people, since their character was obstinacy and stubbornness — He followed that with the example of the call of Abraham, which is similar to the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) in calling to the application of the proof of reflection. The pronoun in (ʿalayhim) refers to something known from the context, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah in His saying (﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself that they will not be believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3]).

Al-tilawah (التلاوة) means recitation (al-qira'ah). It was mentioned in His saying (﴿what the devils recite﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]) in al-Baqarah.

Naba' Ibrahim (نبأ إبراهيم, "the news of Abraham") means his story mentioned here; i.e., recite to them what is being revealed to you now of the news of Abraham. The Messenger (ﷺ) was ordered to recite it to indicate that the speech containing the news of Abraham is a miraculous sign, and that the proof of reason it contains against the divinity of idols, which are like the idols of the Arabs, is also a sign. Thus from the totality of this there are two signs indicating the truthfulness of the Messenger. The mention of Abraham was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]) in al-Baqarah.

(Idh qala) is an adverbial clause (zarf), i.e., "when he said." The clause is an explanation of the news, because the report concerns a story that has passed, so it was fitting that it be explained by a time-noun prefixed to what conveys the story. A parallel to this was mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people, "O my people"﴾ [Yunus: 71]) in Surah Yunus.

(Ma) is an interrogative noun used to ask about the specification of the genus, as was mentioned in His saying: (﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 23]) in this surah. The interrogation is formal, for Abraham knew that they worship idols, but he intended by the question to open the debate with them, so he put this question to them so that they would themselves begin explaining the reality of their worship and what they worship, and thereby indications of its corruption would appear to them through the explanation of that; for the one who undertakes to explain falsehood becomes aware of its falsity while arranging its meanings more than the listener does. Also, he knew that their answer would give rise to what he wanted in terms of argument against the corruption of their religion. They answered his question by specifying the type of what they worship.

He included his father in the putting of the question to them, either because he was present in the assembly of his people, since he was the custodian (sadin) of the house of idols, as has been related; or because he asked him privately and asked his people a second time, so the verse gathers the account of that.

The more evident view is that Abraham began by arguing with his father, then moved on to arguing with his people, and that this was the first argument in the assembly of his father and his people, in which he put forth his call in the form of an inquiring question, not a denial, to draw in the bird of their aversion. As for his saying in the other verse: (﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 85]) (﴿Is it falsehood — gods other than Allah — that you desire?﴾ [al-Saffat: 86]), that is another station of his with his people, accompanied by what calls for wonder at their condition, by the addition of the word (dha) after the interrogative (ma) in Surat al-Saffat. When (dha) comes after (ma), it is interpreted as having the meaning of a relative pronoun, so the meaning in Surat al-Anbiya' becomes: "What is this that you worship?", and the denial becomes directed at the fact that those idols are worshipped.

Page 139

The apparent view is that he put the question to them when they were engrossed in the worship of idols, as the use of the present tense in His saying (ta'budun, "you worship") suggests; and his people did not understand from his words anything but an inquiry, so they answered: that they worship idols upon which they remain devoted to worshipping.

The tanwin in (asnaman, "idols") is for magnification, which is why it departed from definiteness, even though they knew that Abraham knows them and knows that they worship them. The name "idols" among them is a great name, for they take pride in it, contrary to the people of monotheism. This is why Abraham said to them in another station: (﴿You only worship, besides Allah, idols﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17]), in a manner of belittling their objects of worship and making them look foolish. In their reply they used the verb (na'budu, "we worship") although the usual practice is to dispense with explicit mention, since their answer was to a question containing (ta'budun). Thus there is no need to specify the genus of the objects of worship by saying "idols," as in His saying: (﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the excess﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]) (﴿What has your Lord revealed? They say: the truth﴾ [Saba': 23]) (﴿What has your Lord revealed? They say: good﴾ [al-Nahl: 30]). Rather, they departed from the customary form of the answer by repeating the verb used in the question, joyfully and boastfully. For this reason they added to their words (na'budu) something that further emphasizes the act of worship, with their words (﴿and we remain devoted to them﴾). In the verb (nazallu, "we remain") there is an indication of continuity throughout the day. Also, they were Sabians worshipping the stars, and they made the idols symbols of the stars, which would take their place during the day; when night came, they worshipped the rising stars.

(ʿAkifin, "devoted") is construed with the meaning of (ʿabidin, "worshipping"), so the verb is transitive to it with the preposition (lam, "to") rather than (ʿala, "upon"). Since it is the nature of the Lord to be turned to in need and to be the one who benefits or harms, Abraham put to them a question about the state of these idols: do they hear the supplication of those who call upon them, and do they benefit or harm? This is to alert them to the proof of the negation of divinity from them.

The pagan nations used to worship the idol out of hope for its benefit or to ward off its harm, and for this reason some of them worshipped devils.

The object of (yasmaʿunakum, "they hear you") was made the pronoun of the addressees by way of extension (tawassu'), with an omitted modifier whose estimate is: "Do they hear your supplication?", indicated by the adverbial clause in His saying (idh tad'un, "when you call"). Abraham intended to open the debate so that they would be unable to prove that the idols hear and benefit.

Page 140

The (bal, "rather") in the reported answer of the people is for a transition from the station of affirming the attributes of the idols to a station which, in their view, decisively ends the debate, namely that they inherited the worship of these idols. When they folded up the carpet of debate concerning the attributes of their gods and moved to the proof of imitation, evading the hardship of reflection and reasoning, they resorted to proof by following the predecessors.

His saying (﴿they do thus﴾) is a comparison of the fathers' action with their own action, and it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun; the estimate being: "they do an act like that act." The prepositional phrase was placed before (yaf'alun) for emphasis on the meaning of the demonstrative noun.

In this station (which we have judged to be the first station in which he stood for the call) Abraham restricted himself to showing his slight concern with these idols, saying (﴿for they are enemies to me﴾), because he was certain that his safety afterwards indicates that the idols do not harm; otherwise they would have harmed him, since he was their enemy.

The pronoun in (fa-innahum, "for they") refers to (﴿what you have been worshipping﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 92]). His saying (wa-aba'ukum, "and your fathers") is a conjunction with the subject of (kuntum, "you were"). The ʿaduww (enemy) is derived from ʿudwan, which is harming by deed or word. The ʿaduww also means one who is hated; so ʿaduww is fa'ul in the sense of fa'il, which keeps the singular and masculine form and does not take feminine markers (except rarely, as in ʿUmar's saying to women of the Ansar: "O enemies of their own selves"). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is taken as analogous to the verbal noun of the pattern fu'ul, like al-qubul and al-wulul.

The idols have no perception, so they are not described as enemies. Therefore His saying (﴿for they are enemies to me﴾) is of the type of eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), i.e., they are like an enemy to me in that I hate them and harm them. This is close to His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir: 6]), i.e., treat him as an enemy treats his enemy. By this consideration, His saying (﴿an enemy to you﴾ [Fatir: 6]) and His saying (﴿so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir: 6]) are combined.

The expression about the idols by the pronoun of the plural of rational beings in His saying (fa-innahum) rather than (fa-innaha) follows the most common expressions used among them about the idols, because they believe them to be perceptive.

The sentence (﴿Have you considered what you have been worshipping﴾) is a consequence of the sentences of the people's speech which include their worship of idols and that they follow their fathers in that. So the fa' in (afara'aytum, "have you considered") is for consequence,

Page 141

and he placed before it the interrogative hamzah, following the familiar usage, which is that interrogative particles come at the head. The verb of seeing is mental (qalbi).
