For this reason it is often followed by a statement pointing to some of the wondrous circumstances of the object of the seeing, as in His saying: (﴿Have you seen him who turns away﴾ [al-Najm: 33]) (﴿and gives a little, then withholds﴾ [al-Najm: 34]) and so on. From this is the sequence here of His saying: (﴿Have you considered what you have been worshipping﴾) with His saying (﴿for they are enemies to me﴾).

(Aba'ukum, "your fathers") is conjoined to (antum, "you") in order to increase the display of his slight concern with those idols, while knowing that the ancients worshipped them; thus this includes the refutation of their doubt regarding the idols' deserving of worship.

Describing the fathers as "the ancients" is an exaggeration in showing slight concern for imitating them, because the custom of nations is that the more distant the era of the fathers, the more binding their imitation becomes.

The particle "fa" (فَ) in His saying, ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾, is for consequence, following from what the sentence ﴿Have you considered what you have been worshipping﴾ implies of astonishment at their worship of them. It is permissible to take "ru'yah" (seeing) as visual, with one object, and to take the interrogative as one seeking affirmation (taqrir), and the speech is then used to draw attention to something the speaker wishes to talk about, so that the listener may grasp it fully. Or the "fa" is an eloquent "fa" (fa' fasihah), with the implied meaning: "If you see them, then know that they are an enemy to me." This latter aspect is more apparent.

The exception in His saying, (﴿except the Lord of the worlds﴾), is disjunctive (munqati'). "Illa" here has the meaning of "lakin" (but), since the Lord of the worlds is not included in their worship, for it is apparent that they did not acknowledge the Creator, nor did they make their gods partners with God as the polytheists of the Arabs did. Consider His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, it was done by this, their chief"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], for it is the greatest idol among them, and His saying: ﴿He said, "Do you argue with me concerning God while He has guided me?"﴾ [al-An'am: 80]. It appears that the Chaldeans (the people of Abraham) did not believe in the Creator whom eyes cannot perceive. The greatest of their gods was the star of the sun, and the idol that represents the sun was (Ba'l). Thus the function of the idols among them was the management of people's affairs in their lives. As for origination and annihilation, they were among those who say: (﴿And nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24]), and that origination is among the works of procreation, while they were heedless of the secret of the formation of those animal systems and the deposit of them within them. It may be that they acknowledged a great Lord of the cosmos, but they made the idols partners to Him in the governance of the order of those creatures, as was the case of the polytheism among the Arabs. So the exception is connected (muttasil), because God is among those they worshipped, i.e., except the Lord who created the worlds.

The idols of the people of Abraham were mentioned earlier in Surat al-Anbiya'. Refer also to what comes in Surat al-'Ankabut.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 78–82:**

﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me.﴾ ﴿And who feeds me and gives me drink.﴾ ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.﴾ ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life.﴾ ﴿And who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense.﴾

The more apparent view is that the relative pronoun (al-ladhi, "who") is in the position of a descriptive modifier (na't) for "Lord of the worlds," and that "﴿it is He who guides me﴾" is a conjunction ('atf) upon the relative clause (silah), which is a consequence of it, since whoever is the Creator is the most worthy to direct His creatures, rather than anyone else taking that charge. It is also permissible that the relative pronoun be a new subject (mubtada') and that "﴿it is He who guides me﴾" be its predicate (khabar). The fa' (then) was added to the predicate because the relative pronoun resembles a conditional (shart). In both possibilities, the relative form implies the reason for the predicate's construction, which is the exclusion (istidrak) in His saying "﴿except the Lord of the worlds﴾" [al-Shu'ara': 77], meaning: that is the One to whom I devote myself, because He created me, as in His other verse: "﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth﴾" [al-An'am: 79].

The placing of the subject (musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate in "﴿it is He who guides me﴾," instead of saying "fa-yahdini" (so He guides me), is for the purpose of restricting the guidance to Him alone, so that He is the one who takes charge of guidance and no other. This is because the context aims at refuting their belief that their idols exercise control, and this is a restriction by comparison (qasr idafi), which is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb). The pronoun here is not a separating pronoun (damir fasl), because a separating pronoun does not occur after a conjunction.

The use of the present tense in "﴿yahdini﴾" is because guidance is continually renewed for him. The verb of guidance was made to follow the verb of creation with fa' (then), because it is connected to it, since this guidance, in this sense, is a requirement of creation, as it arises from the creation of the intellect, as He, Exalted, said: "﴿Who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾" [Ta-Ha: 50]. By guidance is meant indicating the paths of knowledge, as in His, Exalted, saying: "﴿and We guided him to the two highways﴾" [al-Balad: 10]. So the meaning is: He who created me as a body and an intellect. Among the guidance mentioned is the repelling of the whisperings of falsehood from the intellect, so that the exercise of reflection is protected from error.

[p. 143]

The discussion of placing the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying "﴿and who feeds me and gives me drink﴾" and His saying "﴿it is He who cures me﴾" is like what was said regarding the two previous ones, to refute their claim that the idols determine for them the ease of what they eat and drink, and that healing from illness comes through them. These are also not separating pronouns.

"﴿And when I am ill﴾" is conjoined to "﴿feeds me and gives me drink﴾," because at the time he said this, he was not ill. The particle "idha" (when) makes the verb following it refer to the future, meaning: when an illness befalls me.

In attributing the act of falling ill to himself, there is courtesy (ta'addub) toward God, in which he observed, in the context of good manners, the attribution to apparent causes; so he attributed the causing of illness to his own self, because he is the one who brings it about. As for His saying "﴿who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾," nothing in it requires restriction, because they did not claim that the idols cause death. Rather, the idols' action is limited to assisting or hindering the affairs of people during their lives. As for death, it is from the act of time (dahr) and nature, if they were materialists (dahriyyun); and even if they knew that creation, giving life and causing death are not among the affairs of the idols, and that they are from the act of God, Exalted, as the Arab polytheists believed, then this is evident.

The repetition of the relative pronoun in the three places, although the apparent requirement would be that the clauses be conjoined to the first clause, is for the sake of giving importance to the One who possesses those three clauses, because they are a great description of God, Exalted, and so it is fitting that He be made independent in its indication.

He used the word "ṭam'" (hope/desire) for the hope of forgiveness, out of humility toward God, Exalted, and to keep himself far from the thought of deserving forgiveness; he only hoped for that because of God's promise of it.

The "khaṭi'ah" (sin) is the wrongdoing. It is said: "khati'a" when he commits a sin. It was mentioned earlier in His, Exalted, saying: "﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾" [al-Baqarah: 58], in al-Baqarah. In the language of the sacred laws, what is intended is the violation of what the Law has commanded. Since Abraham was at that time a prophet, and prophets are protected from sins, great and small, then the "khati'ah" from them is the violation of what the prophetic station requires.

Forgiveness is pardoning sins, and he restricted it by "﴿on the Day of Recompense﴾" because that is the day on which the effect of pardon becomes manifest. As for the granting of pardon by God to someone like Abraham, peace be upon him, it is in this world, and He may forgive the sins of some of the sinners on the Day of Resurrection after intercession.

[p. 144]

"Yawm al-Din" (the Day of Religion/Recompense) is the Day of Retribution. This statement is a report that contains an indirect allusion to supplication. In these descriptions, he pointed to what is among God's acts in the sensible world, in a manner that is not hidden from anyone, intending to instruct the faith of the polytheists, if they seek guidance.

In these descriptions there is also an indication that they are preparations for perfection of the soul. The words of Abraham, peace be upon him, have gathered, along with their indication of God's sole authority over those acts, which are the origin of the stages of bodily creation, another indication of all the foundations of blessings from the beginning of creation to the second creation, which is resurrection. He mentioned the creation of the body and the creation of the intellect, and the granting of what sustains the creature's existence, namely food and water, and what befalls a person of imbalance of temperament (mizaj) and its cure. He mentioned death, which is the end of the first life, and followed it with mention of the second life, to indicate that death is a state whose being a blessing does not become apparent except through deep reflection; but behind it is a life which is, without doubt, a blessing for whoever is willing to have that blessing.

The "khaṭi'ah" (sin) is the wrongdoing. It is said: "khati'a" when he commits a sin. It was mentioned earlier in His, Exalted, saying: "﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾" [al-Baqarah: 58], in al-Baqarah. In the language of the sacred laws, what is intended is the violation of what the Law has commanded. Since Abraham was at that time a prophet, and prophets are protected from sins, great and small, then the "khati'ah" from them is the violation of what the prophetic station requires.

Forgiveness is pardoning sins, and he restricted it by "﴿on the Day of Recompense﴾" because that is the day on which the effect of pardon becomes manifest. As for the granting of pardon by God to someone like Abraham, peace be upon him, it is in this world, and He may forgive the sins of some of the sinners on the Day of Resurrection after intercession.

[p. 144]

"Yawm al-Din" (the Day of Religion/Recompense) is the Day of Retribution. This statement is a report that contains an indirect allusion to supplication. In these descriptions, he pointed to what is among God's acts in the sensible world, in a manner that is not hidden from anyone, intending to instruct the faith of the polytheists, if they seek guidance.

The words of Abraham, peace be upon him, have gathered, along with their indication of God's sole authority over those acts, which are the origin of the stages of bodily creation, another indication of all the foundations of blessings from the beginning of creation to the second creation, which is resurrection. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 78–82:**

﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me.﴾ ﴿And who feeds me and gives me drink.﴾ ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.﴾ ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life.﴾ ﴿And who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense.﴾

The more apparent view is that the relative pronoun (al-ladhi, "who") is in the position of a descriptive modifier (na't) for "Lord of the worlds," and that "﴿it is He who guides me﴾" is a conjunction ('atf) upon the relative clause (silah), which is a consequence of it, since whoever is the Creator is the most worthy to direct His creatures, rather than anyone else taking that charge. It is also permissible that the relative pronoun be a new subject (mubtada') and that "﴿it is He who guides me﴾" be its predicate (khabar). The fa' (then) was added to the predicate because the relative pronoun resembles a conditional (shart). In both possibilities, the relative form implies the reason for the predicate's construction, which is the exclusion (istidrak) in His saying "﴿except the Lord of the worlds﴾" [al-Shu'ara': 77], meaning: that is the One to whom I devote myself, because He created me, as in His other verse: "﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth﴾" [al-An'am: 79].

The placing of the subject (musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate in "﴿it is He who guides me﴾," instead of saying "fa-yahdini" (so He guides me), is for the purpose of restricting the guidance to Him alone, so that He is the one who takes charge of guidance and no other. This is because the context aims at refuting their belief that their idols exercise control, and this is a restriction by comparison (qasr idafi), which is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb). The pronoun here is not a separating pronoun (damir fasl), because a separating pronoun does not occur after a conjunction.

The use of the present tense in "﴿yahdini﴾" is because guidance is continually renewed for him. The verb of guidance was made to follow the verb of creation with fa' (then), because it is connected to it, since this guidance, in this sense, is a requirement of creation, as it arises from the creation of the intellect, as He, Exalted, said: "﴿Who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾" [Ta-Ha: 50]. By guidance is meant indicating the paths of knowledge, as in His, Exalted, saying: "﴿and We guided him to the two highways﴾" [al-Balad: 10]. So the meaning is: He who created me as a body and an intellect. Among the guidance mentioned is the repelling of the whisperings of falsehood from the intellect, so that the exercise of reflection is protected from error.

[p. 143]

The discussion of placing the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying "﴿and who feeds me and gives me drink﴾" and His saying "﴿it is He who cures me﴾" is like what was said regarding the two previous ones, to refute their claim that the idols determine for them the ease of what they eat and drink, and that healing from illness comes through them. These are also not separating pronouns.

"﴿And when I am ill﴾" is conjoined to "﴿feeds me and gives me drink﴾," because at the time he said this, he was not ill. The particle "idha" (when) makes the verb following it refer to the future, meaning: when an illness befalls me.

In attributing the act of falling ill to himself, there is courtesy (ta'addub) toward God, in which he observed, in the context of good manners, the attribution to apparent causes; so he attributed the causing of illness to his own self, because he is the one who brings it about. As for His saying "﴿who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾," nothing in it requires restriction, because they did not claim that the idols cause death. Rather, the idols' action is limited to assisting or hindering the affairs of people during their lives. As for death, it is from the act of time (dahr) and nature, if they were materialists (dahriyyun); and even if they knew that creation, giving life and causing death are not among the affairs of the idols, and that they are from the act of God, Exalted, as the Arab polytheists believed, then this is evident.

When the last part of his speech, in calling to the true religion, contained a supplication for forgiveness, he moved from it to a supplication for what combines perfection of the soul through prophethood and the conveyance of the call to God to creation. The proof that he established among his people was by revelation from God, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ [al-An'am: 83]. So at that time he was in a state of nearness to God. He spoke this aloud in that assembly because it came right after finishing the most sacred duty, which is calling to the religion. So it is a supplication (ibtihal) more likely to be accepted, like supplication after the prayers, at the breaking of the fast, the supplication on the Day of 'Arafah, and supplication at the time of battle, all of which come at the completion of acts of worship. A parallel to this is his supplication upon finishing the building of the foundations of the Ka'bah, which is related in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il [with him]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], up to His saying: ﴿Our Lord, make us submissive to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128], up to ﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. He also began with himself in the works of this religion, as God, exalted is He, said, relating about Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], and as His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) was commanded when he said: ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-Zumar: 12].

Being first in virtues has a desirable rank. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "I was the first to shoot an arrow in the way of God." The opposite of this is being first in wrongdoings. In a hadith: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing."

In his supplication, Abraham responded to the five blessings that God had bestowed upon him, mentioned in His saying: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 78], up to His saying: (the Day of Judgment), which refer to sensory gifts, by asking for five blessings that refer to the perfection of the soul, as indicated by His saying: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾. Between his requests he inserted his plea for forgiveness for his father, because that falls within His saying: ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾.

So the beginning of his supplication was that he be given ḥukm, which is wisdom and prophethood. God said about Joseph: ﴿We gave him ḥukm and knowledge﴾ [Yusuf: 22], meaning prophethood. Abraham, when he made this supplication, was already a prophet, so the request was a plea for increase, since the degrees of perfection have no limit: that he be given messengership along with prophethood, or be given a sharia along with messengership, or that he ask for the continuation of that.

Then he rose higher and asked to be joined with the righteous (al-salihin). The word al-salihin includes all the righteous among the prophets and messengers. So he asked to attain the ranks of the messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm): Noah, Hud, and Salih, and the martyrs and the righteous. He placed al-salihin last because it is general, so it serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil).

Then he asked for the preservation of a good remembrance of himself among the nations and generations that come after him. This includes asking for the continuation and the conclusion of perfection, and seeking the spread of praise for him. This is what the spirit feeds upon after death, because praise of him calls forth people's supplications for him, their prayers upon him, and their greetings of peace, as a reward for what they know of the purity of his soul.

God placed among his descendants prophets and messengers who mention him, and the nations that follow them remember him, and his remembrance endures in books. Ibn al-'Arabi said: (Malik said: "There is no harm in a man loving that he be praised for being righteous and be seen in the works of the righteous, if he intends by it the face of God, and that is the good praise." God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Taha: 39]. This is the narration of Ashhab from Malik, may God have mercy on him.) The discussion of this has already been dealt with at length at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who say: Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring comfort of the eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan: 74], in Surat al-Furqan.

By "tongue" (lisan) is meant speech, by applying the name of the instrument to what is established by it. The lam in His saying (li) implies that the good remembrance is for his sake, that is, a remembrance of him with goodness. The construction of lisan with sidq is an annexation of a qualified noun to its adjective, so it carries the intensification of description by the verbal noun, meaning: a tongue that is truthful (lisanan sadiqan).

Here sidq is a metonymy (kinaya) for what is loved and desired, because it is desired that it be realized and actually occur. He asked to be among those deserving Paradise forever. The term "heirs" (warathah) is metaphorically applied to people who deserve it, because the heir receives ownership of the inherited thing merely upon the death of the former owner. Since Paradise has no previous owners, it must be that the heirs deserve it from the time the people of Paradise take up residence in it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the heirs﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10], ﴿who will inherit Paradise; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 11].

He asked for forgiveness for his father before asking that God not disgrace him on the Day of Resurrection, because he wanted that nothing befall him on that day that would break his heart. He had striven in the work that conveys this and sought God's help in it. Nothing remained in him as a grievance except the grievance over his father's disbelief. So he asked forgiveness for him, because if his father were brought with those who went astray, that would cause him breakdown, even if the rest of his supplications had been answered. So this was the last thing he feared: the humiliation of the soul that might come from his lineage, not from his own self. In a hadith: "My father Abraham will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a dhi'h (that is, a male hyena), and he will be thrown into the Fire, and the people of the place of standing will not perceive it." So this is the answer to his saying: ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾, that is, a cutting off of anything that carries a trace of disgrace.

[Page 147]

The discussion of the meaning of khizy (disgrace) has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except disgrace in the life of this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 192] in Al 'Imran.

The pronoun in (yub'athun) refers to the servants, which is known from the context.

The clause (﴿indeed, he was among those who went astray﴾) is a justification for the request of forgiveness for his father. It contains an implication that he asked for a specific forgiveness for him, which is the forgiveness of the greatest sin, namely associating partners with God. This is a request that the station of intimate friendship (khullah) required. His father was alive at that time, as indicated in another verse: ﴿He said: Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord; indeed, He has been ever gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. Perhaps Abraham knew from his father's condition that his faith was not hoped for with what his son had brought; or God revealed this to him, as indicated by the verse: ﴿And the request of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. It is also possible that in the law of Abraham at that time, the deprivation of polytheists from forgiveness had not yet been established, so this would be part of the meaning of His saying: ﴿But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. It is also possible that asking forgiveness for him is a metonymy for the cause of forgiveness, which is his being guided to faith.

As for (﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾) and so on, it appears to be part of the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him. Then (﴿the day when neither will avail﴾) is a substitute (badal) for (﴿the day they are resurrected﴾). He intended by it to show that refuge on that day is with God alone, and there is no help in it from what people have become accustomed to in this world as means of defending themselves.

Ibn 'Atiyyah maintained, as the more probable view, that the verses beginning with ﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ up to His saying: ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 102] are separate from the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, and are a report from God, exalted is He, describing the day at which Abraham stood in his supplication, that he not be disgraced on it. End of quote. This is an elegant view. So (﴿the day when neither wealth will avail﴾) is a resumed statement (isti'naf), a predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: it is a day when neither wealth nor children will avail. The fatha on (yawma) is a fatha of indeclinability (bina'), because (yawm) is an adverb annexed to a conjugated verb, so it may be declined or indeclinable on fatha. It is like His saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. On this view it becomes evident that what is meant by ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ is an indication of Abraham, peace be upon him, because God, exalted is He, described him with something like this in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿And indeed, among his followers [was Abraham]﴾ [al-Saffat: 83], that is, among the followers of Noah was Abraham, ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84].

[Page 148]

In it also is a reminder to his people that their idols will not avail them anything. The negation of the benefit of wealth is true by negating the existence of wealth on that day, by the kind of usage found in the line: "On a broad road whose landmark cannot guide one," meaning: there is no landmark on it by which one could be guided. This is an Arabic usage when the context indicates it. Among the expressions of the science of logic is: "the negative proposition is true by negating the subject."

Limiting the mention to wealth and children in the negation of those who avail follows the general state of tribes in defending a person: either by ransom (fidyah) or by support (najdah, which is help). So wealth is the means of ransom, and children are the most deserving of being helped to defend their father. That help was considered among them a covenant that must be fulfilled. Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"I avenged 'Adi and al-Khatim, and I did not waste
the guardianship of elders that were placed in their stead."

This implies that the failure of anything other than wealth and children to avail, from the means of defense, is established even more so, by the rule of implication (dalalat al-iqtida') based on custom ('urf). So the speech is of the type of sufficiency (ikhtifa'), as if it were said: the day when neither wealth nor children nor anything else will avail. His saying: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ is an exception from the object of (yanfa'u, "avails"), meaning: except one who is benefited, who has come to God with a sound heart.

This is the meaning of the verse, and it is understood by the listeners. Therefore, none of the early exegetes (salaf al-mufassirin) is reported to have counted this verse among the ambiguous in meaning (mutashabih al-ma'na). What made it difficult for the later scholars (khalaf) is the way of extracting this general meaning from the details of the parts of the structure of the speech. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned possibilities, none of which is free from an estimated omission. So we will explain how this meaning is derived from the arrangement of the verse in a way that is more fitting to its structure without strain.

Know that the verb (yanfa'u, "avails") takes a subject in the nominative and is transitive to an object. So by its transitivity to the object it requires an object, and it can also take complements with prepositions (huruf al-ta'diyah), that is, prepositions of genitive. The first complement that comes to mind is the complement of the cause of the action. So it is understood that His saying: ﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ indicates the subject of (yanfa'u), its object, and its cause by which it is accomplished. So His saying (with a sound heart) is the complement of the verb (came to God), because the subject of coming to God is the one who is benefited, so he is in meaning the object of the verb (yanfa'u). The complement attached to one of its two verbs, which is (atā, "came"), whose subject it is, is in meaning attached to its other verb, (yanfa'u), whose object is (one who comes to God). So it is known that the estimate of the speech is: the day when no one benefits by anything that he brings for the defense of himself, or the like, which conveys the generality of the negation of any benefiting agent, as indicated by (﴿wealth nor children﴾) from the generality of things, as we have established. The object of (yanfa'u) is omitted for the purpose of generality, as it is omitted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25], that is, He calls everyone. So the estimate is established as: the day when nothing that one brings for defending himself benefits anyone.

The excepted phrase, (﴿مَن أتى اللَّهَ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾), is definitely an exception (istithna’) from the object of (يَنْفَعُ) (yanfa‘u, "benefits"), and not from its subject. This is because the one who comes to God with a sound heart on that Day is one who is benefited, not one who benefits. So he is not excepted from the explicit form of either of the two preceding nouns, nor from what faith indicates of the more general meaning that we estimated as (ولا غَيْرُهُما) ("nor anything else"). It is therefore certain that this exception is excluded from the generality of the object of (يَنْفَعُ).

Its estimated form is: "except one who came to God with a sound heart," meaning, "so he is benefited." Taking the exception from the object of the verb (يَنْفَعُ) compels us to estimate a beneficial agent for (يَنْفَعُ) as its subject, meaning: "if something beneficial benefits him." Its generality is clarified by the complement of the verb (يَنْفَعُ), which is (﴿بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾). Since the sound heart is the cause of benefit, it is one of the individual members of the general subject estimated by the word (شَيْءٌ) (shay’, "a thing"), as already mentioned.

The conclusion is that the one who comes to God on that Day with a sound heart is benefited, by the indication of the exception, and he is also a beneficiary (i.e., he benefits himself), by the indication of the prepositional phrase attached to the verb (أتى) (atā, "came"). The sound heart is the heart of that benefited person, so that person becomes both beneficial and benefited, according to a different consideration. This is a kind of abstraction (tajrīd). It is close to the case where the subject becomes an object in the construction of (ظنّ) (zanna, "to think"), as in their saying: (خِلْتُنِي) (khiltunī, "I imagined myself") and (رَأيْتُنِي) (ra’aytunī, "I saw myself"). Here the sound heart is made a means through which benefit is obtained. For this reason the exception is connected (muttaṣil, i.e., a connected exception) and emptied (mufarragh) of the object. The construction of the speech in this manner yields a concision that is equal to many long sentences. Making the exception disconnected (munqaṭi‘, i.e., a disconnected exception) does not remove the difficulty.

Page 150

Al-qalb (الْقَلْبُ) is the inner perception.

Al-salīm (السَّلِيمُ) is that which is described by a strong quality of soundness. What is meant here is figurative, inner soundness, i.e., freedom from the beliefs of polytheism, which returns to the meaning of inner purification. Its opposite is the figuratively diseased heart, as God the Exalted said: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10]. The restriction to the sound heart here is because soundness is the impetus for righteous and outward deeds. Such soundness is established for hearts in this world only in view of the end, so they come with it intact on the Day of Resurrection before their Lord.

[Page 148]

In it also is a reminder to his people that their idols will not avail them anything. The negation of the benefit of wealth is true by negating the existence of wealth on that day, by the kind of usage found in the line: "On a broad road whose landmark cannot guide one," meaning: there is no landmark on it by which one could be guided. This is an Arabic usage when the context indicates it. Among the expressions of the science of logic is: "the negative proposition is true by negating the subject."

Limiting the mention to wealth and children in the negation of those who avail follows the general state of tribes in defending a person: either by ransom (fidyah) or by support (najdah, which is help). So wealth is the means of ransom, and children are the most deserving of being helped to defend their father. That help was considered among them a covenant that must be fulfilled. Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"I avenged 'Adi and al-Khatim, and I did not waste
the guardianship of elders that were placed in their stead."

This implies that the failure of anything other than wealth and children to avail, from the means of defense, is established even more so, by the rule of implication (dalalat al-iqtida') based on custom ('urf). So the speech is of the type of sufficiency (ikhtifa'), as if it were said: the day when neither wealth nor children nor anything else will avail. His saying: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ is an exception from the object of (yanfa'u, "avails"), meaning: except one who is benefited, who has come to God with a sound heart.

This is the meaning of the verse, and it is understood by the listeners. Therefore, none of the early exegetes (salaf al-mufassirin) is reported to have counted this verse among the ambiguous in meaning (mutashabih al-ma'na). What made it difficult for the later scholars (khalaf) is the way of extracting this general meaning from the details of the parts of the structure of the speech. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned possibilities, none of which is free from an estimated omission. So we will explain how this meaning is derived from the arrangement of the verse in a way that is more fitting to its structure without strain.

Know that the verb (yanfa'u, "avails") takes a subject in the nominative and is transitive to an object. So by its transitivity to the object it requires an object, and it can also take complements with prepositions (huruf al-ta'diyah), that is, prepositions of genitive. The first complement that comes to mind is the complement of the cause of the action. So it is understood that His saying: ﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ indicates the subject of (yanfa'u), its object, and its cause by which it is accomplished. So His saying (with a sound heart) is the complement of the verb (came to God), because the subject of coming to God is the one who is benefited, so he is in meaning the object of the verb (yanfa'u). The complement attached to one of its two verbs, which is (atā, "came"), whose subject it is, is in meaning attached to its other verb, (yanfa'u), whose object is (one who comes to God). So it is known that the estimate of the speech is: the day when no one benefits by anything that he brings for the defense of himself, or the like, which conveys the generality of the negation of any benefiting agent, as indicated by (﴿wealth nor children﴾) from the generality of things, as we have established. The object of (yanfa'u) is omitted for the purpose of generality, as it is omitted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25], that is, He calls everyone. So the estimate is established as: the day when nothing that one brings for defending himself benefits anyone.

This is because the one who comes to God with a sound heart on that Day is one who is benefited, not one who benefits. So he is not excepted from the explicit form of either of the two preceding nouns, nor from what faith indicates of the more general meaning that we estimated as (ولا غَيْرُهُما) ("nor anything else"). It is therefore certain that this exception is excluded from the generality of the object of (يَنْفَعُ).

Its estimated form is: "except one who came to God with a sound heart," meaning, "so he is benefited." Taking the exception from the object of the verb (يَنْفَعُ) compels us to estimate a beneficial agent for (يَنْفَعُ) as its subject, meaning: "if something beneficial benefits him." Its generality is clarified by the complement of the verb (يَنْفَعُ), which is (﴿بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾). Since the sound heart is the cause of benefit, it is one of the individual members of the general subject estimated by the word (شَيْءٌ) (shay’, "a thing"), as already mentioned.

The conclusion is that the one who comes to God on that Day with a sound heart is benefited, by the indication of the exception, and he is also a beneficiary (i.e., he benefits himself), by the indication of the prepositional phrase attached to the verb (أتى) (atā, "came"). The sound heart is the heart of that benefited person, so that person becomes both beneficial and benefited, according to a different consideration. This is a kind of abstraction (tajrīd). It is close to the case where the subject becomes an object in the construction of (ظنّ) (zanna, "to think"), as in their saying: (خِلْتُنِي) (khiltunī, "I imagined myself") and (رَأيْتُنِي) (ra’aytunī, "I saw myself"). Here the sound heart is made a means through which benefit is obtained. For this reason the exception is connected (muttaṣil, i.e., a connected exception) and emptied (mufarragh) of the object. The construction of the speech in this manner yields a concision that is equal to many long sentences. Making the exception disconnected (munqaṭi‘, i.e., a disconnected exception) does not remove the difficulty.

Limiting the mention to wealth and children in the negation of those who avail follows the general state of tribes in defending a person: either by ransom (fidyah) or by support (najdah, which is help). So wealth is the means of ransom, and children are the most deserving of being helped to defend their father. That help was considered among them a covenant that must be fulfilled. Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"I avenged 'Adi and al-Khatim, and I did not waste
the guardianship of elders that were placed in their stead."

This implies that the failure of anything other than wealth and children to avail, from the means of defense, is established even more so, by the rule of implication (dalalat al-iqtida') based on custom ('urf). So the speech is of the type of sufficiency (ikhtifa'), as if it were said: the day when neither wealth nor children nor anything else will avail. His saying: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ is an exception from the object of (yanfa'u, "avails"), meaning: except one who is benefited, who has come to God with a sound heart.

This is the meaning of the verse, and it is understood by the listeners. Therefore, none of the early exegetes (salaf al-mufassirin) is reported to have counted this verse among the ambiguous in meaning (mutashabih al-ma'na). What made it difficult for the later scholars (khalaf) is the way of extracting this general meaning from the details of the parts of the structure of the speech. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned possibilities, none of which is free from an estimated omission. So we will explain how this meaning is derived from the arrangement of the verse in a way that is more fitting to its structure without strain.

Know that the verb (yanfa'u, "avails") takes a subject in the nominative and is transitive to an object. So by its transitivity to the object it requires an object, and it can also take complements with prepositions (huruf al-ta'diyah), that is, prepositions of genitive. The first complement that comes to mind is the complement of the cause of the action. So it is understood that His saying: ﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ indicates the subject of (yanfa'u), its object, and its cause by which it is accomplished. The complement attached to one of its two verbs, which is (atā, "came"), whose subject it is, is in meaning attached to its other verb, (yanfa'u), whose object is (one who comes to God). So it is known that the estimate of the speech is: the day when no one benefits by anything that he brings for the defense of himself, or the like, which conveys the generality of the negation of any benefiting agent, as indicated by (﴿wealth nor children﴾) from the generality of things, as we have established. The object of (yanfa'u) is omitted for the purpose of generality, as it is omitted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25], that is, He calls everyone. So the estimate is established as: the day when nothing that one brings for defending himself benefits anyone.

The complement attached to one of its two verbs, which is (atā, "came"), whose subject it is, is in meaning attached to its other verb, (yanfa'u), whose object is (one who comes to God). So it is known that the estimate of the speech is: the day when no one benefits by anything that he brings for the defense of himself, or the like, which conveys the generality of the negation of any benefiting agent, as indicated by (﴿wealth nor children﴾) from the generality of things, as we have established. This is because the one who comes to God with a sound heart on that Day is one who is benefited, not one who benefits. So he is not excepted from the explicit form of either of the two preceding nouns, nor from what faith indicates of the more general meaning that we estimated as (ولا غَيْرُهُما) ("nor anything else"). It is therefore certain that this exception is excluded from the generality of the object of (يَنْفَعُ).

Its estimated form is: "except one who came to God with a sound heart," meaning, "so he is benefited." Taking the exception from the object of the verb (يَنْفَعُ) compels us to estimate a beneficial agent for (يَنْفَعُ) as its subject, meaning: "if something beneficial benefits him." When the last part of his speech, in calling to the true religion, contained a supplication for forgiveness, he moved from it to a supplication for what combines perfection of the soul through prophethood and the conveyance of the call to God to creation. So at that time he was in a state of nearness to God. He spoke this aloud in that assembly because it came right after finishing the most sacred duty, which is calling to the religion. So it is a supplication (ibtihal) more likely to be accepted, like supplication after the prayers, at the breaking of the fast, the supplication on the Day of 'Arafah, and supplication at the time of battle, all of which come at the completion of acts of worship. In a hadith: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing."

Between his requests he inserted his plea for forgiveness for his father, because that falls within His saying: ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾.

So the beginning of his supplication was that he be given ḥukm, which is wisdom and prophethood. God said about Joseph: ﴿We gave him ḥukm and knowledge﴾ [Yusuf: 22], meaning prophethood. Then he rose higher and asked to be joined with the righteous (al-salihin). The word al-salihin includes all the righteous among the prophets and messengers. So he asked to attain the ranks of the messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm): Noah, Hud, and Salih, and the martyrs and the righteous. He placed al-salihin last because it is general, so it serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil).

Then he asked for the preservation of a good remembrance of himself among the nations and generations that come after him. This includes asking for the continuation and the conclusion of perfection, and seeking the spread of praise for him. This is what the spirit feeds upon after death, because praise of him calls forth people's supplications for him, their prayers upon him, and their greetings of peace, as a reward for what they know of the purity of his soul.

God placed among his descendants prophets and messengers who mention him, and the nations that follow them remember him, and his remembrance endures in books. Ibn al-'Arabi said: (Malik said: "There is no harm in a man loving that he be praised for being righteous and be seen in the works of the righteous, if he intends by it the face of God, and that is the good praise." By "tongue" (lisan) is meant speech, by applying the name of the instrument to what is established by it. Here sidq is a metonymy (kinaya) for what is loved and desired, because it is desired that it be realized and actually occur. He asked to be among those deserving Paradise forever. The term "heirs" (warathah) is metaphorically applied to people who deserve it, because the heir receives ownership of the inherited thing merely upon the death of the former owner. Since Paradise has no previous owners, it must be that the heirs deserve it from the time the people of Paradise take up residence in it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the heirs﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10], ﴿who will inherit Paradise; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 11].

He asked for forgiveness for his father before asking that God not disgrace him on the Day of Resurrection, because he wanted that nothing befall him on that day that would break his heart. He had striven in the work that conveys this and sought God's help in it. Nothing remained in him as a grievance except the grievance over his father's disbelief. So he asked forgiveness for him, because if his father were brought with those who went astray, that would cause him breakdown, even if the rest of his supplications had been answered. So this was the last thing he feared: the humiliation of the soul that might come from his lineage, not from his own self. In a hadith: "My father Abraham will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a dhi'h (that is, a male hyena), and he will be thrown into the Fire, and the people of the place of standing will not perceive it." So this is the answer to his saying: ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾, that is, a cutting off of anything that carries a trace of disgrace.

[Page 147]

The discussion of the meaning of khizy (disgrace) has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except disgrace in the life of this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 192] in Al 'Imran.

The pronoun in (yub'athun) refers to the servants, which is known from the context.

The clause (﴿indeed, he was among those who went astray﴾) is a justification for the request of forgiveness for his father. It contains an implication that he asked for a specific forgiveness for him, which is the forgiveness of the greatest sin, namely associating partners with God. This is a request that the station of intimate friendship (khullah) required. His father was alive at that time, as indicated in another verse: ﴿He said: Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord; indeed, He has been ever gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. Perhaps Abraham knew from his father's condition that his faith was not hoped for with what his son had brought; or God revealed this to him, as indicated by the verse: ﴿And the request of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. It is also possible that in the law of Abraham at that time, the deprivation of polytheists from forgiveness had not yet been established, so this would be part of the meaning of His saying: ﴿But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. It is also possible that asking forgiveness for him is a metonymy for the cause of forgiveness, which is his being guided to faith.

As for (﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾) and so on, it appears to be part of the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him. Then (﴿the day when neither will avail﴾) is a substitute (badal) for (﴿the day they are resurrected﴾). He intended by it to show that refuge on that day is with God alone, and there is no help in it from what people have become accustomed to in this world as means of defending themselves.

Ibn 'Atiyyah maintained, as the more probable view, that the verses beginning with ﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ up to His saying: ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 102] are separate from the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, and are a report from God, exalted is He, describing the day at which Abraham stood in his supplication, that he not be disgraced on it. End of quote. This is an elegant view. So (﴿the day when neither wealth will avail﴾) is a resumed statement (isti'naf), a predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: it is a day when neither wealth nor children will avail. The fatha on (yawma) is a fatha of indeclinability (bina'), because (yawm) is an adverb annexed to a conjugated verb, so it may be declined or indeclinable on fatha. It is like His saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. On this view it becomes evident that what is meant by ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ is an indication of Abraham, peace be upon him, because God, exalted is He, described him with something like this in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿And indeed, among his followers [was Abraham]﴾ [al-Saffat: 83], that is, among the followers of Noah was Abraham, ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84].

In a hadith: "My father Abraham will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a dhi'h (that is, a male hyena), and he will be thrown into the Fire, and the people of the place of standing will not perceive it." So this is the answer to his saying: ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾, that is, a cutting off of anything that carries a trace of disgrace.

[Page 147]

The discussion of the meaning of khizy (disgrace) has already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except disgrace in the life of this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 192] in Al 'Imran.

The pronoun in (yub'athun) refers to the servants, which is known from the context.

The clause (﴿indeed, he was among those who went astray﴾) is a justification for the request of forgiveness for his father. It contains an implication that he asked for a specific forgiveness for him, which is the forgiveness of the greatest sin, namely associating partners with God. This is a request that the station of intimate friendship (khullah) required. His father was alive at that time, as indicated in another verse: ﴿He said: Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord; indeed, He has been ever gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. Perhaps Abraham knew from his father's condition that his faith was not hoped for with what his son had brought; or God revealed this to him, as indicated by the verse: ﴿And the request of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. It is also possible that in the law of Abraham at that time, the deprivation of polytheists from forgiveness had not yet been established, so this would be part of the meaning of His saying: ﴿But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. It is also possible that asking forgiveness for him is a metonymy for the cause of forgiveness, which is his being guided to faith.

As for (﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾) and so on, it appears to be part of the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him. Then (﴿the day when neither will avail﴾) is a substitute (badal) for (﴿the day they are resurrected﴾). He intended by it to show that refuge on that day is with God alone, and there is no help in it from what people have become accustomed to in this world as means of defending themselves.

Ibn 'Atiyyah maintained, as the more probable view, that the verses beginning with ﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ up to His saying: ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 102] are separate from the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, and are a report from God, exalted is He, describing the day at which Abraham stood in his supplication, that he not be disgraced on it. End of quote. This is an elegant view. So (﴿the day when neither wealth will avail﴾) is a resumed statement (isti'naf), a predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: it is a day when neither wealth nor children will avail. The fatha on (yawma) is a fatha of indeclinability (bina'), because (yawm) is an adverb annexed to a conjugated verb, so it may be declined or indeclinable on fatha. It is like His saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. On this view it becomes evident that what is meant by ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ is an indication of Abraham, peace be upon him, because God, exalted is He, described him with something like this in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿And indeed, among his followers [was Abraham]﴾ [al-Saffat: 83], that is, among the followers of Noah was Abraham, ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84].

[Page 148]

In it also is a reminder to his people that their idols will not avail them anything. The negation of the benefit of wealth is true by negating the existence of wealth on that day, by the kind of usage found in the line: "On a broad road whose landmark cannot guide one," meaning: there is no landmark on it by which one could be guided. This is an Arabic usage when the context indicates it. Among the expressions of the science of logic is: "the negative proposition is true by negating the subject."

Limiting the mention to wealth and children in the negation of those who avail follows the general state of tribes in defending a person: either by ransom (fidyah) or by support (najdah, which is help). So wealth is the means of ransom, and children are the most deserving of being helped to defend their father. That help was considered among them a covenant that must be fulfilled. Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"I avenged 'Adi and al-Khatim, and I did not waste
the guardianship of elders that were placed in their stead."

This implies that the failure of anything other than wealth and children to avail, from the means of defense, is established even more so, by the rule of implication (dalalat al-iqtida') based on custom ('urf). So the speech is of the type of sufficiency (ikhtifa'), as if it were said: the day when neither wealth nor children nor anything else will avail. His saying: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ is an exception from the object of (yanfa'u, "avails"), meaning: except one who is benefited, who has come to God with a sound heart.

This is the meaning of the verse, and it is understood by the listeners. Therefore, none of the early exegetes (salaf al-mufassirin) is reported to have counted this verse among the ambiguous in meaning (mutashabih al-ma'na). What made it difficult for the later scholars (khalaf) is the way of extracting this general meaning from the details of the parts of the structure of the speech. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned possibilities, none of which is free from an estimated omission. So we will explain how this meaning is derived from the arrangement of the verse in a way that is more fitting to its structure without strain.

Know that the verb (yanfa'u, "avails") takes a subject in the nominative and is transitive to an object. So by its transitivity to the object it requires an object, and it can also take complements with prepositions (huruf al-ta'diyah), that is, prepositions of genitive. The first complement that comes to mind is the complement of the cause of the action. So it is understood that His saying: ﴿the day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ indicates the subject of (yanfa'u), its object, and its cause by which it is accomplished. So His saying (with a sound heart) is the complement of the verb (came to God), because the subject of coming to God is the one who is benefited, so he is in meaning the object of the verb (yanfa'u). The complement attached to one of its two verbs, which is (atā, "came"), whose subject it is, is in meaning attached to its other verb, (yanfa'u), whose object is (one who comes to God). So it is known that the estimate of the speech is: the day when no one benefits by anything that he brings for the defense of himself, or the like, which conveys the generality of the negation of any benefiting agent, as indicated by (﴿wealth nor children﴾) from the generality of things, as we have established. The object of (yanfa'u) is omitted for the purpose of generality, as it is omitted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25], that is, He calls everyone. So the estimate is established as: the day when nothing that one brings for defending himself benefits anyone.

The excepted phrase, (﴿مَن أتى اللَّهَ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾), is definitely an exception (istithna’) from the object of (يَنْفَعُ) (yanfa‘u, "benefits"), and not from its subject. This is because the one who comes to God with a sound heart on that Day is one who is benefited, not one who benefits. So he is not excepted from the explicit form of either of the two preceding nouns, nor from what faith indicates of the more general meaning that we estimated as (ولا غَيْرُهُما) ("nor anything else"). It is therefore certain that this exception is excluded from the generality of the object of (يَنْفَعُ).

Its estimated form is: "except one who came to God with a sound heart," meaning, "so he is benefited." Taking the exception from the object of the verb (يَنْفَعُ) compels us to estimate a beneficial agent for (يَنْفَعُ) as its subject, meaning: "if something beneficial benefits him." Its generality is clarified by the complement of the verb (يَنْفَعُ), which is (﴿بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾). Since the sound heart is the cause of benefit, it is one of the individual members of the general subject estimated by the word (شَيْءٌ) (shay’, "a thing"), as already mentioned.

The conclusion is that the one who comes to God on that Day with a sound heart is benefited, by the indication of the exception, and he is also a beneficiary (i.e., he benefits himself), by the indication of the prepositional phrase attached to the verb (أتى) (atā, "came"). The sound heart is the heart of that benefited person, so that person becomes both beneficial and benefited, according to a different consideration. This is a kind of abstraction (tajrīd). It is close to the case where the subject becomes an object in the construction of (ظنّ) (zanna, "to think"), as in their saying: (خِلْتُنِي) (khiltunī, "I imagined myself") and (رَأيْتُنِي) (ra’aytunī, "I saw myself"). Here the sound heart is made a means through which benefit is obtained. For this reason the exception is connected (muttaṣil, i.e., a connected exception) and emptied (mufarragh) of the object. The construction of the speech in this manner yields a concision that is equal to many long sentences. Making the exception disconnected (munqaṭi‘, i.e., a disconnected exception) does not remove the difficulty.

Page 150

Al-qalb (الْقَلْبُ) is the inner perception.

Al-salīm (السَّلِيمُ) is that which is described by a strong quality of soundness. What is meant here is figurative, inner soundness, i.e., freedom from the beliefs of polytheism, which returns to the meaning of inner purification. Its opposite is the figuratively diseased heart, as God the Exalted said: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10]. The restriction to the sound heart here is because soundness is the impetus for righteous and outward deeds. Such soundness is established for hearts in this world only in view of the end, so they come with it intact on the Day of Resurrection before their Lord.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 90–95:

﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿And Hellfire will be made apparent for the misguided.﴾ ﴿And it will be said to them, "Where is that which you used to worship ﴿besides Allah﴾? Can they help you or defend themselves?"﴾ ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the misguided,﴾ ﴿and the soldiers of Iblis, all together.﴾

The apparent reading is that the waw in His saying: (﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and its governing element is (﴿Neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾), meaning: on the day when no one benefits except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart, while Paradise has been brought near for the God-fearing. The shift to depicting these states is something required by the situation of the call to faith through desire and fear, because he began the call by putting a question to his people about what they worship, to awaken their insight, and then followed that with the refutation of the divinity of their idols. The argument against their deserving divinity is by means of reflection, namely that they lack hearing and sight and are incapable of benefit and harm. Then he extended the argument of imitation (taqlid) which his people turned to when they were unable to support their religion through reasoning.

When the proof stood firm against the falsehood of the divinity of their idols, he turned to explaining the true God, the Lord of the worlds, who possesses the attributes of disposing over bodies and souls, the disposition of the Benefactor who is unique in His manifold dispositions, up to the disposition of eternal life; and that He is the One whose forgiveness we hope for on the Day of Resurrection. So let them know that if they seek Allah's forgiveness for the disbelief that has passed from them, then Allah will forgive them; and that if they do not desist from polytheism, nothing will benefit them on the Day of Resurrection. Then he depicted for them the outcome of the two states of piety and error by mentioning the abode of the recompense of good and the abode of the recompense of evil.

And since his people persisted in polytheism, and at that time no one was a believer apart from him, and apart from his wife and Lot, the son of his brother, the situation called for warning (tarhib) more fittingly. Therefore he elaborated in describing the state of the astray on the Day of Resurrection and the evil of their destination, where they will regret what they neglected in the world of faith and obedience, and wish to return to the world to make up for faith, but "it is too late for remorse."

Al-izlaf (ازلاف) means bringing near. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And We brought near the others there﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 64] in this surah. The meaning is that the God-fearing find Paradise present, so they do not undergo the hardship of being driven toward it.

The lam in (لِلْمُتَّقِينَ) is the lam of transitivity (lam al-ta'diyah).

(وبُرِّزَتْ) (buriyyat) is an intensified form of (أُبْرِزَتْ) (ubrizat), because the doubling (tadh'if) in it carries an emphasis not found in the transitivity by the hamzah. A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿And Hellfire will be made apparent to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36] in Surat al-Nazi'at. What is meant by (الغاوِينَ) (al-ghawin) are those described as misguided, that is, corrupt in judgment.

Mentioning what is said to the misguided serves to rebuke them and to show the contemptibility of their idols. So it is said to them: ﴿Where is that which you used to worship?﴾ In restricting the mention to this and not to others of what they will be addressed with on that day, there is a fitting relation to the situation of seeking their abandonment of worshipping those idols.

The verb of saying is attributed in the passive, because the purpose concerns knowing the statement, not knowing the speaker. The speaker is the angels by permission from Allah the Exalted, since the polytheists are too lowly for Allah to address them directly.

The interrogation in His saying: (﴿Where is that which you used to worship?﴾) is a question about determining the place of the idols if they are not present, or about their action if they are present at that scene; this is by treating the uselessness of them in what they used to hope from them as non-existence, as mockery, reproach and making them confront their error.

The interrogation in (﴿Can they help you?﴾) is likewise, with the denial that the idols could be helpers. Al-intisar means seeking a helper.

(أيْنَما) is written in the Mushafs joined, the nun of (أيْنَ) joined with the mim of (ما). In the standard orthographic convention, such a form is customarily written separately, because (ما) here is a relative noun and not the extra (مزيدة) (ma) after (أيْنَ) which, by its addition, makes (أيْنَ) a conditional noun for the generality of places. The script of the Mushaf is a followed tradition.

And (أوْ) is for choice in rebuke and correction, meaning: Did you err in hoping for their help to you, or, at least, can they manage to help themselves? That is when the idols are thrown into the Fire in the sight of their worshippers. Hence He said: (﴿So they will be thrown into it﴾), that is, the idols were overturned into Hell.

The meaning of (كُبْكِبُوا) (kubkibu) is they were thrown into it, one toppling upon another, for (كُبْكِبُوا) is the doubled form of (كُبُّوا) through repetition, and repetition of the word indicates repetition of the meaning, like (كَفْكَفَ الدَّمْعَ) (he wiped away the tears again and again). A parallel among nouns is (جَيْشٌ لَمْلَمٌ), meaning a large army, an intensification of gathering. That is because it has a synonymous verb containing its letters without doubling, in place of the doubling found in its synonym, for the sake of indicating an increase in the meaning of the verb.

The pronouns of (يَنْصُرُكم، ويَنْتَصِرُونَ، وكُبْكِبُوا) refer back to (ما تَعْبُدُونَ) by treating them as rational beings. (جُنُودُ إبْلِيسَ): they are his allies and the kinds of people of misguided beliefs which arise from the whisperings of Iblis. The discussion of Iblis has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 90–95:

﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿And Hellfire will be made apparent for the misguided.﴾ ﴿And it will be said to them, "Where is that which you used to worship ﴿besides Allah﴾? Can they help you or defend themselves?"﴾ ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the misguided,﴾ ﴿and the soldiers of Iblis, all together.﴾

The apparent reading is that the waw in His saying: (﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and its governing element is (﴿Neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾), meaning: on the day when no one benefits except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart, while Paradise has been brought near for the God-fearing. The shift to depicting these states is something required by the situation of the call to faith through desire and fear, because he began the call by putting a question to his people about what they worship, to awaken their insight, and then followed that with the refutation of the divinity of their idols. The argument against their deserving divinity is by means of reflection, namely that they lack hearing and sight and are incapable of benefit and harm. Then he extended the argument of imitation (taqlid) which his people turned to when they were unable to support their religion through reasoning.

When the proof stood firm against the falsehood of the divinity of their idols, he turned to explaining the true God, the Lord of the worlds, who possesses the attributes of disposing over bodies and souls, the disposition of the Benefactor who is unique in His manifold dispositions, up to the disposition of eternal life; and that He is the One whose forgiveness we hope for on the Day of Resurrection. So let them know that if they seek Allah's forgiveness for the disbelief that has passed from them, then Allah will forgive them; and that if they do not desist from polytheism, nothing will benefit them on the Day of Resurrection. Then he depicted for them the outcome of the two states of piety and error by mentioning the abode of the recompense of good and the abode of the recompense of evil.

And since his people persisted in polytheism, and at that time no one was a believer apart from him, and apart from his wife and Lot, the son of his brother, the situation called for warning (tarhib) more fittingly. Therefore he elaborated in describing the state of the astray on the Day of Resurrection and the evil of their destination, where they will regret what they neglected in the world of faith and obedience, and wish to return to the world to make up for faith, but "it is too late for remorse."

[Page 153]

It is possible that this is part of the reported speech of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who elaborated the admonition to depict the terror of that Day. In that case the clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), or it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) of the explanatory kind (*isti'naf bayani*), as will come.

It is also possible that the speech of Ibrahim ended at His words ﴿and the hosts of Iblis, all of them﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 95], or at His words, may He be exalted, ﴿the Day they are raised﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 87], as Ibn 'Atiyya inclined to believe. In that case this speech is an admonition from Allah to the polytheists who hear it, and an instruction from Him to the believers. The clause is then a parenthetical resumption (*isti'naf mu'taridah*) between the mention of the story and what follows it, and it is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*) arising from His words: ﴿so they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 94]. This is because the listener is in a position to ask about the purpose of casting the idols into the Fire, given that they neither understand nor act well. So He explains this to him, and then relates the quarrel of their worshippers among themselves. Their seeing their idols is the source of the dispute between them, for the followers saw with their own eyes the lies of those who misled them, while the misled have no means of disowning them or escaping. The humiliation of the idols and their presence with them in that punishment is the strongest witness that they own nothing, neither for them nor for themselves.

As for the clause ﴿while they dispute therein﴾, it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The clause ﴿By Allah﴾ is the object of the speech verb (*maqul al-qawl*). The clause ﴿indeed we were in clear error﴾ is the response to the oath. *In* (إنْ) is a lightened form of the heavy *inna* (إنَّ), and it has been deprived of its governing function because of the lightening, since lightening permits this deprivation. The clause following it takes the place of its subject and predicate. The prefixing of the predicate of *kana* with the *lam* in the clause following it serves to distinguish the lightened, emphatic *in* from the negating *in*. Generally, the clause following the lightened *in* does not lack a verb of the *kana* category.

In the oath the particle *ta'* (التاءُ) is used rather than *wa'* (الواوُ), because *ta'* is specific to oaths concerning something that is marvelled at, as was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you certainly know that we came not to cause corruption in the land"﴾ [Yusuf: 73], in Surat Yusuf, and in His words: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya': 57], in Surat al-Anbiya'. They marvel at their own error, since they placed their hopes for help and victory in stones that can avail them nothing. For this reason they expressed the entrenchment of error in them by using the preposition of location (حرفُ الظرفيَّةِ), *fi*, which is borrowed for the sense of close association (*mula'abah*), because the thing contained is intimately associated with its container. They reinforced this by describing the error as ﴿clear﴾, that is, evident and manifest. In this there is a self-rebuke on their part, since this error was able to take hold of them, although it could never have passed upon anyone possessed of even a measure of intellect.

﴿When We equated you﴾ (إذْ نُسَوِّيكم) is a temporal adverbial clause (*zarf*) connected to *kunna* (we were). That is: we were in error at the time when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds. The word *idh* is not used to express causation, as the Shaykh Ahmad ibn 'Alwan al-Tunisi, known as al-Misri, supposed, as reported from him by al-Maqqari in *Nafh al-Tib*, in the biography of Abu Ja'far al-Lablil, in the fifth section of the first part. He was misled by the implied meaning and so took it to be one of the meanings of *idh*. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*So overlook what you see, since there is no retrieving it.*

That is: at the time when there is no retrieving it.

*Taswiyah* means equalizing and making similar, that is: when we made you like the Lord of the worlds. The apparent meaning is that they made them equal to Him while acknowledging divinity, and this is the apparent state of their polytheism, as mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. It is also possible that they made them equal to Him in what became clear to them of His divinity on that Day, since they did not believe in Allah at all in the world. So this equalization is in terms of ultimate outcome, and they had come back to acknowledging what the words of Ibrahim to them in the world contained, when he said to them: ﴿Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77].

The pronoun of address in *nusawwikum* (we equate you) is directed to the idols. This is an instance of the one who regrets addressing an inanimate thing that was the cause of what brought about his remorse, by treating it as one who understands and hears. The purpose of this is to intensify the rebuke of oneself. From this is what al-Ghazali related in *Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din*: that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab entered upon Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and found him holding his tongue with two fingers, saying: "You have brought me to these watering places." And it is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he stood on al-Safa, reciting the talbiyah and saying: "O tongue, say good and you will profit; keep silent from evil and you will be safe." This is a style commonly used in speech, both prose and verse. Abu Tammam said:

*O tears, help me against the dwellers of Najd.*

The form *nusawwikum* is in the present tense to bring vividly before the mind this strange scene, when they turn to the idols with supplication and divine epithets.

Their words ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾ are an address by some of the common people to others. By "the criminals" they meant the leaders of disbelief who invented polytheism for them and fabricated a religion for them.

It is fitting that the definiteness in *al-mujrimun* (the criminals) be understood as expressing complete criminality, for among the meanings of the *al-* (the definite article) is that it indicates the sense of perfection.

They linked with the particle *fa* (then) the absence of intercessors to the clause ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾, since they had given them hope of the intercession of the idols on their behalf with Allah, just as the polytheists of the Arabs did, ﴿and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Then it became clear to them that these idols have no intercession. This statement is used to express regret and anguish.

[Page 154]

Al-shafi' (the intercessor) is one who serves as a means of bringing benefit to another or averting harm from him. The mention of intercession has preceded in His words: ﴿nor will intercession benefit it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123], in al-Baqarah, and the intercessor was discussed at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

As for their words ﴿nor a close friend﴾, it is a completion that arises from the bad treatment they receive from everyone they pass by or have dealings with, and from the deprivation that everyone they ask for kindness treats them with, until they know that all creation disowns them, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and they will see the punishment, and all connections between them will be severed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166]. The close friend (*sadiq*) is the one who consoles you, or comforts you, or grieves for you. On that Day the word of Allah is fulfilled: ﴿close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. The discussion of the *sadiq* has preceded in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿or your close friends﴾ in Surat al-Nur.

*Hamim* means near, an intimate one; it is on the pattern *fa'il* from *hamma* with a fatha on the *ha'*, meaning to draw near and be close. So it is more specific than *sadiq*.

The intended meaning is the negation of the category of intercessor and the category of close friend, since the two nouns occur in a context of emphatic negation reinforced by the superfluous *min* (from). In such a context the singular and the plural are equal in indicating the category.
