This *law* (لوْ) is for wishing (*tamanni*). Its origin is the conditional *law*, but its conditional sense has been forgotten. Its original form is: "If we were sent back to the world, we would believe," but when it is not intended to make the non-occurrence of one thing dependent on the non-occurrence of another, *law* becomes purely for wishing, because of the relation between the impossible thing and its being wished for. *Karrah* is a single instance from *karr*, which means returning.

The verb ﴿fa-nakuna﴾ (so that we would be) is put in the subjunctive as the answer to the wish.

[Page 153]

It is possible that this is part of the reported speech of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who elaborated the admonition to depict the terror of that Day. In that case the clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), or it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) of the explanatory kind (*isti'naf bayani*), as will come.

The clause following it takes the place of its subject and predicate. The prefixing of the predicate of *kana* with the *lam* in the clause following it serves to distinguish the lightened, emphatic *in* from the negating *in*. Generally, the clause following the lightened *in* does not lack a verb of the *kana* category.

In the oath the particle *ta'* (التاءُ) is used rather than *wa'* (الواوُ), because *ta'* is specific to oaths concerning something that is marvelled at, as was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you certainly know that we came not to cause corruption in the land"﴾ [Yusuf: 73], in Surat Yusuf, and in His words: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya': 57], in Surat al-Anbiya'. They marvel at their own error, since they placed their hopes for help and victory in stones that can avail them nothing. For this reason they expressed the entrenchment of error in them by using the preposition of location (حرفُ الظرفيَّةِ), *fi*, which is borrowed for the sense of close association (*mula'abah*), because the thing contained is intimately associated with its container. They reinforced this by describing the error as ﴿clear﴾, that is, evident and manifest. ﴿When We equated you﴾ (إذْ نُسَوِّيكم) is a temporal adverbial clause (*zarf*) connected to *kunna* (we were). That is: we were in error at the time when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds. He was misled by the implied meaning and so took it to be one of the meanings of *idh*. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*So overlook what you see, since there is no retrieving it.*

That is: at the time when there is no retrieving it.

*Taswiyah* means equalizing and making similar, that is: when we made you like the Lord of the worlds. The apparent meaning is that they made them equal to Him while acknowledging divinity, and this is the apparent state of their polytheism, as mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. It is also possible that they made them equal to Him in what became clear to them of His divinity on that Day, since they did not believe in Allah at all in the world. So this equalization is in terms of ultimate outcome, and they had come back to acknowledging what the words of Ibrahim to them in the world contained, when he said to them: ﴿Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77].

The pronoun of address in *nusawwikum* (we equate you) is directed to the idols. This is an instance of the one who regrets addressing an inanimate thing that was the cause of what brought about his remorse, by treating it as one who understands and hears. The purpose of this is to intensify the rebuke of oneself. From this is what al-Ghazali related in *Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din*: that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab entered upon Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and found him holding his tongue with two fingers, saying: "You have brought me to these watering places." And it is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he stood on al-Safa, reciting the talbiyah and saying: "O tongue, say good and you will profit; keep silent from evil and you will be safe." This is a style commonly used in speech, both prose and verse. Abu Tammam said:

*O tears, help me against the dwellers of Najd.*

The form *nusawwikum* is in the present tense to bring vividly before the mind this strange scene, when they turn to the idols with supplication and divine epithets.

Their words ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾ are an address by some of the common people to others. By "the criminals" they meant the leaders of disbelief who invented polytheism for them and fabricated a religion for them.

It is fitting that the definiteness in *al-mujrimun* (the criminals) be understood as expressing complete criminality, for among the meanings of the *al-* (the definite article) is that it indicates the sense of perfection.

They linked with the particle *fa* (then) the absence of intercessors to the clause ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾, since they had given them hope of the intercession of the idols on their behalf with Allah, just as the polytheists of the Arabs did, ﴿and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Then it became clear to them that these idols have no intercession. This statement is used to express regret and anguish.

[Page 154]

On that Day the word of Allah is fulfilled: ﴿close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. The discussion of the *sadiq* has preceded in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿or your close friends﴾ in Surat al-Nur.

The intended meaning is the negation of the category of intercessor and the category of close friend, since the two nouns occur in a context of emphatic negation reinforced by the superfluous *min* (from). In such a context the singular and the plural are equal in indicating the category. The difference between the two nouns of these two categories in the report of their speech is that *shafi'in* is used in the plural, and *sadiq* in the singular. This is because by the intercessors they meant the false deities, and they were accustomed to thinking of them as many, so their speech follows what is fixed in their imagination. As for the *sadiq*, its category is conceived without regard to the number of its individuals, since they did not mean a specific number. So it remains on the original basis of negating the category, and on the original basis of words, since there was no reason for anything other than the singular. What appears to me is that the plural *shafi'in* was preferred, because it better suits the picture of what was in their minds, as mentioned earlier. As for the singular *sadiq*, it is because they intended that the attribute *hamim* be applied to it. Then they built upon this anguish and remorse the wish to be returned to the world, so that they might make up for their failure in believing in Allah alone.

This *law* (لوْ) is for wishing (*tamanni*). Its origin is the conditional *law*, but its conditional sense has been forgotten. Its original form is: "If we were sent back to the world, we would believe," but when it is not intended to make the non-occurrence of one thing dependent on the non-occurrence of another, *law* becomes purely for wishing, because of the relation between the impossible thing and its being wished for. *Karrah* is a single instance from *karr*, which means returning.

The verb ﴿fa-nakuna﴾ (so that we would be) is put in the subjunctive as the answer to the wish.

[Page 153]

It is possible that this is part of the reported speech of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who elaborated the admonition to depict the terror of that Day. In that case the clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), or it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) of the explanatory kind (*isti'naf bayani*), as will come.

It is also possible that the speech of Ibrahim ended at His words ﴿and the hosts of Iblis, all of them﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 95], or at His words, may He be exalted, ﴿the Day they are raised﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 87], as Ibn 'Atiyya inclined to believe. In that case this speech is an admonition from Allah to the polytheists who hear it, and an instruction from Him to the believers. The clause is then a parenthetical resumption (*isti'naf mu'taridah*) between the mention of the story and what follows it, and it is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*) arising from His words: ﴿so they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 94]. This is because the listener is in a position to ask about the purpose of casting the idols into the Fire, given that they neither understand nor act well. So He explains this to him, and then relates the quarrel of their worshippers among themselves. Their seeing their idols is the source of the dispute between them, for the followers saw with their own eyes the lies of those who misled them, while the misled have no means of disowning them or escaping. The humiliation of the idols and their presence with them in that punishment is the strongest witness that they own nothing, neither for them nor for themselves.

As for the clause ﴿while they dispute therein﴾, it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The clause ﴿By Allah﴾ is the object of the speech verb (*maqul al-qawl*). The clause ﴿indeed we were in clear error﴾ is the response to the oath. *In* (إنْ) is a lightened form of the heavy *inna* (إنَّ), and it has been deprived of its governing function because of the lightening, since lightening permits this deprivation. The clause following it takes the place of its subject and predicate. The prefixing of the predicate of *kana* with the *lam* in the clause following it serves to distinguish the lightened, emphatic *in* from the negating *in*. Generally, the clause following the lightened *in* does not lack a verb of the *kana* category.

In the oath the particle *ta'* (التاءُ) is used rather than *wa'* (الواوُ), because *ta'* is specific to oaths concerning something that is marvelled at, as was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you certainly know that we came not to cause corruption in the land"﴾ [Yusuf: 73], in Surat Yusuf, and in His words: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya': 57], in Surat al-Anbiya'. They marvel at their own error, since they placed their hopes for help and victory in stones that can avail them nothing. For this reason they expressed the entrenchment of error in them by using the preposition of location (حرفُ الظرفيَّةِ), *fi*, which is borrowed for the sense of close association (*mula'abah*), because the thing contained is intimately associated with its container. They reinforced this by describing the error as ﴿clear﴾, that is, evident and manifest. In this there is a self-rebuke on their part, since this error was able to take hold of them, although it could never have passed upon anyone possessed of even a measure of intellect.

﴿When We equated you﴾ (إذْ نُسَوِّيكم) is a temporal adverbial clause (*zarf*) connected to *kunna* (we were). That is: we were in error at the time when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds. The word *idh* is not used to express causation, as the Shaykh Ahmad ibn 'Alwan al-Tunisi, known as al-Misri, supposed, as reported from him by al-Maqqari in *Nafh al-Tib*, in the biography of Abu Ja'far al-Lablil, in the fifth section of the first part. He was misled by the implied meaning and so took it to be one of the meanings of *idh*. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*So overlook what you see, since there is no retrieving it.*

That is: at the time when there is no retrieving it.

*Taswiyah* means equalizing and making similar, that is: when we made you like the Lord of the worlds. The apparent meaning is that they made them equal to Him while acknowledging divinity, and this is the apparent state of their polytheism, as mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. It is also possible that they made them equal to Him in what became clear to them of His divinity on that Day, since they did not believe in Allah at all in the world. So this equalization is in terms of ultimate outcome, and they had come back to acknowledging what the words of Ibrahim to them in the world contained, when he said to them: ﴿Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77].

The pronoun of address in *nusawwikum* (we equate you) is directed to the idols. This is an instance of the one who regrets addressing an inanimate thing that was the cause of what brought about his remorse, by treating it as one who understands and hears. The purpose of this is to intensify the rebuke of oneself. From this is what al-Ghazali related in *Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din*: that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab entered upon Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and found him holding his tongue with two fingers, saying: "You have brought me to these watering places." And it is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he stood on al-Safa, reciting the talbiyah and saying: "O tongue, say good and you will profit; keep silent from evil and you will be safe." This is a style commonly used in speech, both prose and verse. Abu Tammam said:

*O tears, help me against the dwellers of Najd.*

The form *nusawwikum* is in the present tense to bring vividly before the mind this strange scene, when they turn to the idols with supplication and divine epithets.

Their words ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾ are an address by some of the common people to others. By "the criminals" they meant the leaders of disbelief who invented polytheism for them and fabricated a religion for them.

It is fitting that the definiteness in *al-mujrimun* (the criminals) be understood as expressing complete criminality, for among the meanings of the *al-* (the definite article) is that it indicates the sense of perfection.

They linked with the particle *fa* (then) the absence of intercessors to the clause ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾, since they had given them hope of the intercession of the idols on their behalf with Allah, just as the polytheists of the Arabs did, ﴿and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Then it became clear to them that these idols have no intercession. This statement is used to express regret and anguish.

The form *nusawwikum* is in the present tense to bring vividly before the mind this strange scene, when they turn to the idols with supplication and divine epithets.

Their words ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾ are an address by some of the common people to others. By "the criminals" they meant the leaders of disbelief who invented polytheism for them and fabricated a religion for them.

It is fitting that the definiteness in *al-mujrimun* (the criminals) be understood as expressing complete criminality, for among the meanings of the *al-* (the definite article) is that it indicates the sense of perfection.

They linked with the particle *fa* (then) the absence of intercessors to the clause ﴿And none has misled us except the criminals﴾, since they had given them hope of the intercession of the idols on their behalf with Allah, just as the polytheists of the Arabs did, ﴿and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Then it became clear to them that these idols have no intercession. This statement is used to express regret and anguish.

[Page 154]

Al-shafi' (the intercessor) is one who serves as a means of bringing benefit to another or averting harm from him. The mention of intercession has preceded in His words: ﴿nor will intercession benefit it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123], in al-Baqarah, and the intercessor was discussed at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

As for their words ﴿nor a close friend﴾, it is a completion that arises from the bad treatment they receive from everyone they pass by or have dealings with, and from the deprivation that everyone they ask for kindness treats them with, until they know that all creation disowns them, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and they will see the punishment, and all connections between them will be severed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166]. The close friend (*sadiq*) is the one who consoles you, or comforts you, or grieves for you. On that Day the word of Allah is fulfilled: ﴿close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. The discussion of the *sadiq* has preceded in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿or your close friends﴾ in Surat al-Nur.

*Hamim* means near, an intimate one; it is on the pattern *fa'il* from *hamma* with a fatha on the *ha'*, meaning to draw near and be close. So it is more specific than *sadiq*.

The intended meaning is the negation of the category of intercessor and the category of close friend, since the two nouns occur in a context of emphatic negation reinforced by the superfluous *min* (from). In such a context the singular and the plural are equal in indicating the category. The difference between the two nouns of these two categories in the report of their speech is that *shafi'in* is used in the plural, and *sadiq* in the singular. This is because by the intercessors they meant the false deities, and they were accustomed to thinking of them as many, so their speech follows what is fixed in their imagination. As for the *sadiq*, its category is conceived without regard to the number of its individuals, since they did not mean a specific number. So it remains on the original basis of negating the category, and on the original basis of words, since there was no reason for anything other than the singular. What appears to me is that the plural *shafi'in* was preferred, because it better suits the picture of what was in their minds, as mentioned earlier. As for the singular *sadiq*, it is because they intended that the attribute *hamim* be applied to it. Had the qualified noun been put in the plural, its attribute would have had to be pluralized, and the plural of *hamim* carries a heaviness that does not suit the highest eloquence, nor fit the form of the verse-ending (*fasilah*), together with the variety achieved in this, which is one of the aims of the eloquent.

Then they built upon this anguish and remorse the wish to be returned to the world, so that they might make up for their failure in believing in Allah alone.

This *law* (لوْ) is for wishing (*tamanni*). Its origin is the conditional *law*, but its conditional sense has been forgotten. Its original form is: "If we were sent back to the world, we would believe," but when it is not intended to make the non-occurrence of one thing dependent on the non-occurrence of another, *law* becomes purely for wishing, because of the relation between the impossible thing and its being wished for. *Karrah* is a single instance from *karr*, which means returning.

The verb ﴿fa-nakuna﴾ (so that we would be) is put in the subjunctive as the answer to the wish.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 103–104:

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾

This is the third repetition of this sentence, as a enumeration of blessings upon the polytheists and a recording of their obstinacy. The demonstrative "that" (ism al-ishara) refers to the speech of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), for in it is clear proof of the Oneness of Allah the Exalted and the invalidity of the divinity of the idols. Just as the people of Ibrahim were not guided by it, so most of the polytheists in Makkah were not believers in it after hearing it. But conveying the message is binding upon the Messenger (ﷺ). The discussion of the like of this verse has already preceded.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 105–110:

﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Noah said to them: Will you not be mindful of God?﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) consoling the Messenger (ﷺ), arising from His saying: (﴿And most of them were not believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 8]). That is: do not grieve over them, and let it not weigh heavily upon you that they have denied you, for the people of Noah denied the messengers. The Arabs knew the message of Noah, and such is the condition of misguided minds: they know the circumstances but forget their causes.

The verb ascribed to the people of Noah is feminine because (qawm) is interpreted as (ummah) or (jama'ah), as one says: "Quraysh said," and "Banu 'Amir said." This is a rule for every collective noun that has no singular of its own form, when it refers to humans, like (nafar) and (rahT). But when it refers to non-humans, such as (ibil), it is feminine only. This is what al-Jawhari stated, and the author of al-Lisan and al-Misbah followed him.

In al-Kashshaf there occurs this expression: "al-qawm is feminine, and its diminutive is quwaymah." The apparent sense of his expression is that this word is feminine in meaning in usage only. No one other than him has said this, and his commentators remained silent about it, and al-Zamakhshari did not touch upon it in al-Asas. If it is taken according to the apparent sense of the expression, then it contradicts the statement of al-Jawhari and Ibn Sidah. It is possible that he meant the permissibility of feminizing (qawm), and that it is permissible to diminutive it as quwaymah, so that his statement is reconciled with the statements of al-Jawhari and Ibn Sidah. This is a distant possibility from the apparent sense of his words, emphasized by his saying: "and its diminutive is quwaymah," because diminution restores nouns to their origins. Whatever the case, it is clear that its feminine form is not due to interpreting it as (ummah), because interpretation is a consideration of the speaker and so has no effect on the forms of words, like diminution; for forms are results of imposition (wad') and not of usage. Do you not see that special forms are not made for metaphorical meanings?

(al-Mursalin) is pluralized, though they denied only one messenger, the first of the messengers, and there was no messenger before him, and they were the first deniers. It is pluralized because their denial was not on account of his person, but rather because they deemed it impossible that God should send a human being and that the worship of their idols should be error. Thus their denial of him necessitated the denial of every messenger, because every messenger says what Noah, peace be upon him, said. For this reason it is repeated in His saying: ﴿The people of 'Ad denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 123] and what follows it. Their denial that the messenger should be a human being has been related in His saying: ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 63] in al-A'raf.

The account of the denial of 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket will come in this same pattern, in what is repeated of His saying "denied" (kadhdhabat) and His saying "the messengers" (al-mursalin).

(Idh qala) is an adverbial clause, meaning: they denied him when he said to them: (Will you not be mindful?), whereupon they said: (﴿Shall we believe you, when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 111]). It appears that his saying "Will you not be mindful?" was uttered after he had called them earlier and repeated his call when he saw them persisting in disbelief, and their reply to him indicates this: (﴿and the lowest have followed you﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 111]).

This particular station from his stations is singled out for mention in this surah, because it is more suitable to the purpose of the surah in consoling the Messenger (ﷺ) by mentioning a similar situation of his with his people. The "brother" (akh) is used in the sense of a close kinsman from the same tribe. It has been mentioned previously in His saying: ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65] in Surah al-A'raf.

His saying (Will you not be mindful?) may be such that the word (alla) is composed of two particles: the interrogative hamzah entering upon the negative (la), so it is a resumption about the absence of their piety, used in rebuke, and it implies their refusal to comply with his call.

It may also be that (alla) is a single particle, the particle of exhortation (tahdid), like His saying: ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 13], and it implies their slowness in confirming him.

By piety (taqwa) is meant: fear of God's punishment for them, since they made partners with Him.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾ is a justification for the rebuke or for the exhortation; that is: how do you persist in polytheism when I have forbidden you from it, while I am a messenger to you and a trustworthy one concerning you.

Noah was known for trustworthiness and was not accused among his people, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) was called "the Trustworthy" among Quraysh. Al-Nabigha said:

Thus was Noah, who would not betray.

His emphasis with the particle of emphasis, although their denial of his trustworthiness had not preceded, is because he anticipated the occurrence of denial, so he argued against them by the test of his trustworthiness before conveying the message, for trustworthiness is evidence of his truthfulness in what he conveyed to them from God's message, just as Heraclius said to Abu Sufyan when he asked him: "Have you tested him, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), for lying?" Abu Sufyan said: "No, and we were in a period with him in which we did not know what he was doing in it." Heraclius then said to him: "I have known that he would not leave lying to people and lie against God." Thus, in the narration of Noah's argument from his trustworthiness among his people in this story, presented as an example for the polytheists in their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ), there is an allusion against them, since they denied him after they had called him the Trustworthy. It may also be intended that he was trustworthy from God's side to the nation to which he was sent. The emphasis is also due to the anticipation of their denial.

The clause ﴿And I do not ask you any reward for it﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾; that is: you know that I am trustworthy toward you, and you know that I do not seek from my call to faith any benefit for myself. The pronoun in (alayhi) refers to what is known from the context of the call.

His saying: ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me﴾ is an emphasis of his saying (Will you not be mindful?), and it is an interjection between the two coordinated clauses. He repeated the clause (﴿So be mindful of God and obey me﴾) for added emphasis. Thus he opened his call with the prohibition against abandoning piety, then gave its reason, then repeated what the opening clause requires, then gave its reason by saying: ﴿And I do not ask you any reward for it﴾, then repeated the clause of the call at the end of his speech, when he said: ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 144] a second time, as a conclusion to the call and as its justification.

The ya' is omitted from (atiy'uni) in both places, as it is omitted in His saying (﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 14]) at the beginning of the surah.

In His saying: ﴿My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ there is an allusion to the Day of Recompense. They used to deny resurrection, as indicated by His saying in Surah Nuh: ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17] ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth as a [final] bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 18]. The mention of Noah has preceded at His saying: ﴿Indeed, God chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33] in Al 'Imran.

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) consoling the Messenger (ﷺ), arising from His saying: (﴿And most of them were not believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 8]). That is: do not grieve over them, and let it not weigh heavily upon you that they have denied you, for the people of Noah denied the messengers. The Arabs knew the message of Noah, and such is the condition of misguided minds: they know the circumstances but forget their causes.

This is a rule for every collective noun that has no singular of its own form, when it refers to humans, like (nafar) and (rahT). But when it refers to non-humans, such as (ibil), it is feminine only. This is what al-Jawhari stated, and the author of al-Lisan and al-Misbah followed him.

In al-Kashshaf there occurs this expression: "al-qawm is feminine, and its diminutive is quwaymah." The apparent sense of his expression is that this word is feminine in meaning in usage only. No one other than him has said this, and his commentators remained silent about it, and al-Zamakhshari did not touch upon it in al-Asas. If it is taken according to the apparent sense of the expression, then it contradicts the statement of al-Jawhari and Ibn Sidah. It is possible that he meant the permissibility of feminizing (qawm), and that it is permissible to diminutive it as quwaymah, so that his statement is reconciled with the statements of al-Jawhari and Ibn Sidah. This is a distant possibility from the apparent sense of his words, emphasized by his saying: "and its diminutive is quwaymah," because diminution restores nouns to their origins. Whatever the case, it is clear that its feminine form is not due to interpreting it as (ummah), because interpretation is a consideration of the speaker and so has no effect on the forms of words, like diminution; for forms are results of imposition (wad') and not of usage. Do you not see that special forms are not made for metaphorical meanings?

(al-Mursalin) is pluralized, though they denied only one messenger, the first of the messengers, and there was no messenger before him, and they were the first deniers. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 111–115:**

﴿They said, "Shall we believe you, when the lowest of the people follow you?"﴾ ﴿He said, "And what knowledge do I have of what they used to do?"﴾ ﴿Their reckoning is only with my Lord, if you could perceive.﴾ ﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers.﴾ ﴿I am only a clear warner.﴾

The clause "They said" (*qalu*) is a clarifying resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question) responding to His saying, ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105]. It raises in the listener the expectation of learning what passed between them and Noah in the way of dialogue, and for this reason their argument is related using the forms "they said" and "he said." The speakers are the nobles of the people who took it upon themselves to argue with Noah.

[Page 160]

The interrogative in "Shall we believe" is a rejecting interrogative (*istifham inkari*), meaning: "We will not believe you when the lowest have followed you." Thus the clause "when ... have followed you" (*wa-ittaba'aka*) is a circumstantial clause (*hali*).

"The lowest" (*al-arzalun*) means the dregs of the people, described as having baseness (*radhala*), which is lowliness and insignificance. They meant by them the weak and the poor among the people, and so they were arrogant and disdainful of being equal to the weak in following Noah. This is like what the chiefs of the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ when 'Ammar, Bilal and Zayd ibn Harithah were among the believers: "Shall we be followers of these? Drive them away from you, for perhaps if you drive them away we will follow you." Then God revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face﴾ [al-An'am: 52], and the verses of surah al-An'am.

The majority of readers recited "wa-ittaba'aka" with a hamzat wasl and a doubled *ta'* (*tashdid*), as a past verb of the *ifti'al* form. The meaning is that they were among his followers, or that they were most of his followers. Ya'qub recited "wa-atba'uka" with a hamzat qat' (a full hamza), a sukun on the *ta'*, and an alif after the *ba'*, as the plural of *tabi'* (follower). The meaning is that they are his followers and no one else, so the form is a form of restriction (*qasr*).

Noah's answer to the speech of his people requires careful examination of its wording and meaning. As for its wording, the beginning of his speech is joined by the *waw* (*wa-*), which places it in the position of a clause conjoined to the speech of his people, signalling that it is connected to what they said. This is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for his hastening to respond, as in the words of God, related about Abraham (peace be upon him), when He said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people" [al-Baqarah: 124], and then Abraham said, "And from my descendants" [al-Baqarah: 124]. Ya'qub recited "wa-atba'uka" with a hamzat qat' (a full hamza), a sukun on the *ta'*, and an alif after the *ba'*, as the plural of *tabi'* (follower). The meaning is that they are his followers and no one else, so the form is a form of restriction (*qasr*).

Noah's answer to the speech of his people requires careful examination of its wording and meaning. As for its wording, the beginning of his speech is joined by the *waw* (*wa-*), which places it in the position of a clause conjoined to the speech of his people, signalling that it is connected to what they said. This is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for his hastening to respond, as in the words of God, related about Abraham (peace be upon him), when He said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people" [al-Baqarah: 124], and then Abraham said, "And from my descendants" [al-Baqarah: 124]. This is called *'atf talqin* (conjunction of prompting), in consideration of its occurrence in that verse, though it is better to call it *'atf takmil* (conjunction of completion).

As for its meaning, it is an interrogative indicating that his people had elaborated the general description of his followers as "the lowest," by stating attributes from the conditions of the needy, whom people do not regard. So he used an interrogative about his knowledge, an interrogative used to express little concern for the thing asked about. This is a metonymy for its scant benefit, because asking about a thing indicates ignorance of it, and ignorance is accompanied by little concern for the unknown and its low status. It is like when one is told, "So-and-so threatens you," and one replies, "What is So-and-so?" meaning: he is not regarded. In the report of Wahb ibn Kaysan from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that Abu 'Ubaydah used to give us a date each day, Wahb said: "I said, 'And what does a single date avail you?'"

[Page 161]

The meaning is: "What is my knowledge of what they were doing, that I should busy myself with obtaining knowledge of what they were doing and their deeds, in a way suited to their ranks? I am not concerned with what came before their faith."

"My knowledge" (*'ilmi*) is construed to include the sense of "my occupation" and "my concern," and so it is followed by the preposition *bi-*.

"What they used to do" (*ma kanu ya'maluna*) is a relative clause whose referent is the state (*al-halah*), since a state does not lack some action. So the meaning is: "And what is my knowledge of their deeds?" This is like what is said when asking about someone: "What did So-and-so do?", meaning: "What is his news and what is his condition?" From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the Ansari boy: "O Abu 'Umayr, what did the *nughayr* do?" (a bird called *al-nughar*, on the pattern of *surad*, a kind of nightingale, which the boy used to play with). From this also is his saying to one who asked him about the children of the polytheists who died: "God knows best what they used to do" [i.e., God knows best their condition], which is a refusal to answer. Close to this is the Arab saying, "What is his condition?" (*ma bal-uhu*), meaning: "What is his state?"

The verb "were" (*kanu*) is inserted between the relative *ma* and its relative clause, to add emphasis, meaning: to emphasise the implication of "What is my knowledge of what they were doing?" The meaning is: "What is my knowledge of what they do?" It is not intended to refer to what they had done before. The *waw* in His saying "bi-ma kanu" is a subject, and it is not the noun of *kana*, because the additional *kana* does not put the predicate in the accusative.

His saying "what they used to do" encompasses all their conditions in their religion and their worldly affairs, past, present and future, outward and inward.

The reckoning (*hisab*) in its reality is that God is the One who takes charge of dealing with them in accordance with what they have sent before and what they do, and with the realities of their deeds. This statement is required by His saying "And what is my knowledge of what they were doing?", since it encompasses all their deeds, outward and inward, among which are those for which they will be held accountable, and which are most important to the Messenger who legislates. Therefore, when he said, "And what is my knowledge of what they were doing?", he followed it with "Their reckoning is only with my Lord," following the custom of those who guide, of not neglecting an opportunity. This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When they say it [i.e., 'There is no god but God'], they have protected their blood and their property from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with God," meaning that the verification of the agreement of their inward with their outward is with God.

[Page 162]

Noah added, by way of explanation, his saying: "And I am not one to drive away the believers. I am only a clear warner." This meaning is explained by His saying in another verse: ﴿God knows best what is in their souls﴾ [Hud: 31], in surah Hud.

The restriction in His saying "Their reckoning is only with my Lord" is a restriction of a subject to an attribute: the subject is "their reckoning" and the attribute is "with my Lord." This is because the prepositional phrase functioning as predicate is in effect an attribute, since prepositional phrases and adverbial expressions that occur as predicates contain a sense that the subject is characterised by, namely the occurrence and establishment, which is implied in the sentence as "existing" or "settled," as the grammarians have explained. The sense is: "Their reckoning is restricted to being characterised by the meaning of 'with my Lord.'" Al-Sakkaki likewise estimated it thus in *al-Miftah*, and it is a restriction of singling out in relation to something else (*qasr ifrad idafi*), meaning: the state of being "with my Lord" does not extend beyond to being characterised as "with me." This is a rejection of what their speech implied, namely their demand that he remove those who believed, because they do not deserve to be equal to them in the faith which Noah demanded of his people.

His saying "if you could perceive" (*law tash'uruna*) is a belittling of them and a humbling of their delusion and their vain self-admiration. The response of "law" (*law*, "if") is omitted, indicated by what came before it. The sense is: "If you could perceive, you would perceive that their reckoning is with God and not with me, so [do not] ask me for what you have asked." That he regarded them as ignorant is indicated by His saying in surah Hud: ﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾ [Hud: 29]. This is the explanation that accords with the structure and meaning of the verse without the need for additions or assumptions.

The exegetes have gone in the direction of interpreting "the lowest" to mean that they are characterised by base lowliness, meaning: a slander against the sincerity of the faith of those who believed in him. They took His saying "And what is my knowledge of what they were doing?" as a disavowal of uncovering their inner thoughts and the soundness of their faith. Perhaps what led them to this is the word "reckoning" in His saying "Their reckoning is only with my Lord," so they understood it as the reckoning that takes place on the Day of Recompense, and that does not bring ease to the heart.

His saying "And I am not one to drive away the believers" is conjoined to His saying "And what is my knowledge of what they were doing?", so after nullifying the implication of their demand that he drive them away, he declared explicitly that he would not do it.

The clause "I am only a clear warner" is a resumptive clause carrying the sense of causation, meaning: "Because my description [as a warner] turns me away from agreeing with you."

[Page 163]

"Clear" (*mubin*) derives from *abana*, which is transitive, in the sense of "explained" and "made clear." The restriction is a restriction of singling out in relation to something else, namely a restriction of a subject to an attribute.

An account of a situation of Noah (peace be upon him) with his people similar to what is related here has already been mentioned in surah Hud, and there is some difference between the two accounts. Perhaps they are two situations, or they are two statements in one situation, one of which is related there and the other here, according to the custom of the Qur'anic narratives. So whatever addition is found in one of the two verses is to be understood as completing what is in the other.

When argument wearied them, they resorted to the weapon of the falsifiers (al-mubtilin), which is contention through harm (al-munadalah bil-adha).

Al-rajm means throwing stones (al-rami bil-hijarah), and its use has become predominant for killing by stoning. The phrase ﴿mina al-marjumin﴾ ("among those who are stoned") indicates among those who are punished by stoning, that is, from the category of miscreants who deserve stoning, as was mentioned previously in His words ﴿And I am not of the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56] in Surat al-An'am.

His words ﴿Indeed, my people have denied me﴾ serve as a preface to supplication against them. It is a statement used to express grief and despair at their giving up denial.

Al-fath means judgment (al-hukm). Its emphasis with ﴿fathan﴾ indicates a severe judgment, namely extermination (al-istisal). For this reason he followed it with a safeguard in His words ﴿and save me and those with me among the believers﴾.

Al-mashhun means filled (al-mamlu).

Thumma ("then") here indicates a gradation in rank in the reporting (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because the drowning of an entire community is a greater indication of the immensity of power than the rescue of a group of people.

The omission of the yā' in ﴿kadhdhabuni﴾ is for the sake of the fasilah (verse-ending rhyme), as was mentioned previously in His words ﴿So I fear they will kill me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 14].

The verb (كَذَّبَتْ) is joined with the feminine ta' (تاء التأنيث, the feminine marker), because the name 'Ad is a proper noun for a people, so it is construed as meaning "the nation."

The discussion of (ألا تَتَّقُونَ) is like the discussion of its counterpart mentioned earlier in the story of the people of Noah. His words, ﴿إنِّي لَكم رَسُولٌ أمِينٌ﴾ ("Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you"), are like Noah's words to his people, for a messenger is not sent unless he was already known for trustworthiness and good conduct before the mission. That Hud was like this among his people is shown by his people's words to him: ﴿إنْ نَقُولُ إلّا اعْتَراكَ بَعْضُ آلِهَتِنا بِسُوءٍ﴾ ("We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil") [Hud: 54] in Surah Hud, which indicates that they claimed that the change in his condition from what he had been known for before was due to the badness of his belief concerning their gods.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 128–130:**

﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, playing?﴾ ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, so that you may live forever?﴾ ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants.﴾

He saw among his people an exclusive devotion to the affairs of their worldly life, a turning away from reflection on the Hereafter, from working for it, and from considering the outcome. He saw that they associated others with God in divinity, and that they turned away from the worship of God alone, who had created them, settled them on the earth, and increased their strength over the nations. Their aspirations thus turned toward self-magnification, boasting, amusement, and play.

The 'Ad had reached a great level of might, of immense authority, and of dominion over the lands. This prompted their saying: ﴿Who is stronger than us in power?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. The Arab tribes would describe anything great of its kind as "'adiyy" (of 'Ad). They were people of sound opinion and sound judgment. Waddak ibn Thumayl al-Mazini said:

*"The judgment of 'Ad: none among their companions fears it,*
*even if the stammerers spoke, the tongue of the foreigner would be eloquent."*

And al-Nabigha said, praising Ghassan:

*"The judgment of 'Ad, and bodies made pure*
*from defects, calamities, and sins."*

A long time passed over them. They became ingenious in pursuing desire, devoted themselves to pleasures, and their self-conceit grew strong. They neglected the most important aspect of a human being, which is the aspect of religion and the purification of the soul. They also neglected to intend, in their works, beneficial purposes and the intention of pleasing God, because of their love of leadership and reputation. So they worshipped idols, made light of the side of God the Exalted, considered those who advised them to be fools, and God sent Hud to them. He confronted them with rebuke for having been afflicted with admiration for these works and for their boasting, since their rivalry in them diverted them from knowing God. They therefore rejected following the laws and denied the Messenger.

Among the prior works of 'Ad was that they had built, along the roads of their journeys, markers and beacons guiding the way, so that travelers would not go astray in those shifting sands where the traces of travelers do not remain. They also dug out and built cisterns for water, which are the reservoirs that collect rainwater in winter, so that travelers could drink from them and residents could benefit from them in times of scarce rain. They built fortresses and palaces on the heights of the land. This is, in itself, among beneficial works, because in it there is the preservation of people from perishing in the wilderness through losing the way, and from dying of thirst when they lack water at the time of need. So whenever these works were intended for the pleasure of God the Exalted by benefiting His servants, they were worthy of praise in this world and of reward in the next.

But when the pleasing of God the Exalted through them was neglected, and they were taken as a display and as vanity in grandeur, and when they were turning away from monotheism and from the worship of God, these works turned into a purely worldly grandeur, in which one does not look to the side of benefit, and which does not urge people to imitate them in establishing similar works. Their utmost purpose was self-praise for what they had found of them. Thus their existence became like futility, because they were empty of the spirit of good purposes, and so they had no weight with God, since God created this world so that it would be the locus of His worship and obedience.

Furthermore, they turned away from the Hereafter and confined themselves to provision for the life of this world, in the position of one who reckons himself to be abiding forever in this world.

When works are empty of regard for the purposes that please God the Exalted, the paths of their doers diverge into many ways, according to the differences of aspirations and the pursuit of particular interests. For this reason their Messenger denounced them by way of a denunciatory interrogation, following the method of exhortations. Exhortations are built upon observing what in works is a harm outweighing the benefit. The preacher does not draw attention to what may be a disadvantage in works if that benefit is desired by people, for the motive of desire spread among people suffices without urging them toward it. The preacher's engagement with this is superfluous and a departure from the purpose, by warning them or urging them about what lies outside that. This applies when the motive for good is absent or slight. This context was a context of admonition, as indicated by His saying the Exalted about them: ﴿They said, "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not of the admonishers."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 136]. The context of admonition is broader than the context of changing evil. Thus the admonition of Hud, peace be upon him, was directed at the spiritual ailments in their souls, and there was no command in his admonition to change the markers they had built or the reservoirs they had made.

Since the trace of the building had become a distraction from the beneficial purpose for life in the Hereafter, their act leading to futility was treated as the act whose purpose is futility at the start of doing it. So he denounced building for them by introducing the interrogative particle of denunciation (hamzat al-inkar) before the verb ﴿tabnuna﴾ ("you build"), and it was qualified by the clause ﴿ta'batun﴾ ("you play"), which is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject of ﴿tabnuna﴾. Yet when they built that, they did not intend by their act any futility. So the locus of the denunciation in the denunciatory interrogation is the building qualified by futility, because when a judgment enters upon something qualified by a condition, it applies to that condition.

Likewise, the verb conjoined to the verb questioned about, which is the clause ﴿wa-tattakhidhuna masani'a﴾ ("and you take for yourselves reservoirs"), falls within the scope of denunciation and is qualified by the same qualification as the verb it is conjoined to. This is based on the view that the intermediate circumstantial clause between the two clauses refers back to both of them, according to the opinion of many scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), especially when there is a contextual indicator for that.

The opinions of the exegetes differed concerning the identification of the building, the signs, and the reservoirs, as will come. Among what they said is that which is wholly devoted to frivolity, futility, and corruption; and among it is that whose original status is permissibility; and among it is that which is goodness and benefit, as will come.

The position of the clause ﴿Do you build﴾ is in the place of a substitution by inclusive apposition (badal al-ishtimal) for the clause ﴿Will you not fear God?﴾ [cf. 26:126 and similar], because its content is among what includes the absence of piety, upon which the denunciation falls, and which has the meaning of negation.

The word *rī'* (with a kasra on the rā') means an elevated place, that is, a high location; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said to mean a road or a wide pass between two mountains; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The word *āyah* means a sign indicating the way. The word *āyah* is also applied to a crafted thing that is impressive, because it serves as a sign of the mastery of its maker or the greatness of its owner.

The word *kull* ("every") is used for multitude, that is, on the high places overlooking the trodden roads. The word *'abath* means work that has no beneficial use in it.

The word *masani'* is the plural of *masna'* (reservoir), and its root is the pattern *maf'al* derived from *ṣana'a* (to make). It is a noun of place (mīmī noun) used as a description for emphasis. It is said that it is a basin carved out in the ground. It is related from Qatadah that it is built with plaster in which water is stored, and it is called *sihrij* (cistern) and *majil* (reservoir). It is also said that it means palaces; this is from Mujahid.

The lands of 'Ad extended from 'Oman to Hadramawt, east and west, and reached deep into the north as far as the sands, which are the *ahqaf* (sand dunes).

The clause ﴿so that you may live forever﴾ is a new, independent clause. The particle *la'alla* expresses hope (tarajji), which is the speaker's request for something whose attainment is considered near. The statement is mockery of them: that is, "I hope for you to live forever because of those reservoirs." It is also said that the 'Ad built lofty structures on the heights along the roads, where they would play and mock passersby. This statement may be explained as meaning that a nation in a state of decline transforms what was established for benefits into corruptions. They turned what was built for facilitating travel and securing wayfarers from going astray in the deadly wilderness into places of amusement and mockery, just as some monasteries of Christians in the lands of the Arabs were made into places for wine-drinking. Similarly, we have seen the cisterns at Carthage, which were storage tanks for the waters of Zaghwan flowing to them over arches, and we saw them become hiding places for thieves and storage places for animals, until the beginning of this century, in the year 1303 AH.

It is also said that the reservoirs were great palaces that they took for themselves. In that case the denunciation is directed at extravagance in spending on firm and sturdy structures, as if they would protect them from death. The statement is thus conveyed as an admonition against excessive luxury and grandeur. This is what we have extracted from scattered words in the opinions of the exegetes. They indicate a confusion in their discourse about how to understand Hud's denunciation of his people for two acts that were counted among the beneficial works of nations. I think we have dispelled that confusion.

As for His saying: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants﴾, He followed it with the admonition about their frivolity, play, and greed for the world. Their admonition regarding harshness toward creation in punishment is a lack of balance in their intellects. They build signs to guide travelers and make reservoirs to relieve the thirsty. How, then, does this way of thinking meet a way of thinking that goes to excess in harshness toward people in striking them? That is, punishing them.

The word *batsh* means striking in anger with a whip or a sword. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Do they have hands with which they strike?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 195], at the end of Surah Al-A'raf.

The word *jabbarin* ("tyrants") is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in *batashtum*. It is the plural of *jabbar*, and *jabbar* means one who is harsh in what is not right. The meaning is: when you strike, your striking happens in a state of tyranny, that is, going to excess in harm, which is injustice. God the Exalted said: ﴿You want only to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not want to be among the reformers﴾ [Al-Qasas: 19]. The nature of punishment is that it should have a limit appropriate to the offense punished, without excess or deficiency in striking. Excess is contempt for the rights of creation.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There are two groups of the people of the Fire whom I have not seen: a people who have whips like the tails of cows, with which they strike people; and women who are clothed yet naked…" [and the rest of the hadith].

The second verb, *batashtum*, came as the answer to *idhā* ("when"), and it is synonymous with the verb of its condition, because the difference between the verb of the condition and the verb of the answer is one of generality and specificity. This was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [Al-Furqan: 72] in Surah Al-Furqan. Such a construction is intended for emphasizing the importance of the act, since its repetition produces the confirmation of its meaning.

The position of the clause ﴿Do you build﴾ is in the place of a substitution by inclusive apposition (badal al-ishtimal) for the clause ﴿Will you not fear God?﴾ [cf. 26:126 and similar], because its content is among what includes the absence of piety, upon which the denunciation falls, and which has the meaning of negation.

The word *rī'* (with a kasra on the rā') means an elevated place, that is, a high location; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said to mean a road or a wide pass between two mountains; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The word *āyah* means a sign indicating the way. The word *āyah* is also applied to a crafted thing that is impressive, because it serves as a sign of the mastery of its maker or the greatness of its owner.

The word *kull* ("every") is used for multitude, that is, on the high places overlooking the trodden roads. The word *'abath* means work that has no beneficial use in it.

The word *masani'* is the plural of *masna'* (reservoir), and its root is the pattern *maf'al* derived from *ṣana'a* (to make). It is a noun of place (mīmī noun) used as a description for emphasis. It is said that it is a basin carved out in the ground. It is related from Qatadah that it is built with plaster in which water is stored, and it is called *sihrij* (cistern) and *majil* (reservoir). It is also said that it means palaces; this is from Mujahid.

The lands of 'Ad extended from 'Oman to Hadramawt, east and west, and reached deep into the north as far as the sands, which are the *ahqaf* (sand dunes).

The clause ﴿so that you may live forever﴾ is a new, independent clause. The particle *la'alla* expresses hope (tarajji), which is the speaker's request for something whose attainment is considered near. The statement is mockery of them: that is, "I hope for you to live forever because of those reservoirs." It is also said that the 'Ad built lofty structures on the heights along the roads, where they would play and mock passersby. This statement may be explained as meaning that a nation in a state of decline transforms what was established for benefits into corruptions. They turned what was built for facilitating travel and securing wayfarers from going astray in the deadly wilderness into places of amusement and mockery, just as some monasteries of Christians in the lands of the Arabs were made into places for wine-drinking. Similarly, we have seen the cisterns at Carthage, which were storage tanks for the waters of Zaghwan flowing to them over arches, and we saw them become hiding places for thieves and storage places for animals, until the beginning of this century, in the year 1303 AH.

It is also said that the reservoirs were great palaces that they took for themselves. In that case the denunciation is directed at extravagance in spending on firm and sturdy structures, as if they would protect them from death. The statement is thus conveyed as an admonition against excessive luxury and grandeur. This is what we have extracted from scattered words in the opinions of the exegetes. They indicate a confusion in their discourse about how to understand Hud's denunciation of his people for two acts that were counted among the beneficial works of nations. I think we have dispelled that confusion.

As for His saying: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants﴾, He followed it with the admonition about their frivolity, play, and greed for the world. Their admonition regarding harshness toward creation in punishment is a lack of balance in their intellects. They build signs to guide travelers and make reservoirs to relieve the thirsty. How, then, does this way of thinking meet a way of thinking that goes to excess in harshness toward people in striking them? That is, punishing them.

The word *batsh* means striking in anger with a whip or a sword. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Do they have hands with which they strike?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 195], at the end of Surah Al-A'raf.

The word *jabbarin* ("tyrants") is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in *batashtum*. It is the plural of *jabbar*, and *jabbar* means one who is harsh in what is not right. The meaning is: when you strike, your striking happens in a state of tyranny, that is, going to excess in harm, which is injustice. God the Exalted said: ﴿You want only to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not want to be among the reformers﴾ [Al-Qasas: 19]. The nature of punishment is that it should have a limit appropriate to the offense punished, without excess or deficiency in striking. Excess is contempt for the rights of creation.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There are two groups of the people of the Fire whom I have not seen: a people who have whips like the tails of cows, with which they strike people; and women who are clothed yet naked…" [and the rest of the hadith].

The second verb, *batashtum*, came as the answer to *idhā* ("when"), and it is synonymous with the verb of its condition, because the difference between the verb of the condition and the verb of the answer is one of generality and specificity. This was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [Al-Furqan: 72] in Surah Al-Furqan. Such a construction is intended for emphasizing the importance of the act, since its repetition produces the confirmation of its meaning.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 128–130:**

﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, playing?﴾ ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, so that you may live forever?﴾ ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants.﴾

He saw among his people an exclusive devotion to the affairs of their worldly life, a turning away from reflection on the Hereafter, from working for it, and from considering the outcome. He saw that they associated others with God in divinity, and that they turned away from the worship of God alone, who had created them, settled them on the earth, and increased their strength over the nations. Their aspirations thus turned toward self-magnification, boasting, amusement, and play.

The 'Ad had reached a great level of might, of immense authority, and of dominion over the lands. This prompted their saying: ﴿Who is stronger than us in power?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. The Arab tribes would describe anything great of its kind as "'adiyy" (of 'Ad). They were people of sound opinion and sound judgment. Waddak ibn Thumayl al-Mazini said:

*"The judgment of 'Ad: none among their companions fears it,*
*even if the stammerers spoke, the tongue of the foreigner would be eloquent."*

And al-Nabigha said, praising Ghassan:

*"The judgment of 'Ad, and bodies made pure*
*from defects, calamities, and sins."*

A long time passed over them. They became ingenious in pursuing desire, devoted themselves to pleasures, and their self-conceit grew strong. They neglected the most important aspect of a human being, which is the aspect of religion and the purification of the soul. They also neglected to intend, in their works, beneficial purposes and the intention of pleasing God, because of their love of leadership and reputation. So they worshipped idols, made light of the side of God the Exalted, considered those who advised them to be fools, and God sent Hud to them. He confronted them with rebuke for having been afflicted with admiration for these works and for their boasting, since their rivalry in them diverted them from knowing God. They therefore rejected following the laws and denied the Messenger.

Among the prior works of 'Ad was that they had built, along the roads of their journeys, markers and beacons guiding the way, so that travelers would not go astray in those shifting sands where the traces of travelers do not remain. They also dug out and built cisterns for water, which are the reservoirs that collect rainwater in winter, so that travelers could drink from them and residents could benefit from them in times of scarce rain. They built fortresses and palaces on the heights of the land. This is, in itself, among beneficial works, because in it there is the preservation of people from perishing in the wilderness through losing the way, and from dying of thirst when they lack water at the time of need. So whenever these works were intended for the pleasure of God the Exalted by benefiting His servants, they were worthy of praise in this world and of reward in the next.

But when the pleasing of God the Exalted through them was neglected, and they were taken as a display and as vanity in grandeur, and when they were turning away from monotheism and from the worship of God, these works turned into a purely worldly grandeur, in which one does not look to the side of benefit, and which does not urge people to imitate them in establishing similar works. Their utmost purpose was self-praise for what they had found of them. Thus their existence became like futility, because they were empty of the spirit of good purposes, and so they had no weight with God, since God created this world so that it would be the locus of His worship and obedience.

Furthermore, they turned away from the Hereafter and confined themselves to provision for the life of this world, in the position of one who reckons himself to be abiding forever in this world.

When works are empty of regard for the purposes that please God the Exalted, the paths of their doers diverge into many ways, according to the differences of aspirations and the pursuit of particular interests. For this reason their Messenger denounced them by way of a denunciatory interrogation, following the method of exhortations. Exhortations are built upon observing what in works is a harm outweighing the benefit. The preacher does not draw attention to what may be a disadvantage in works if that benefit is desired by people, for the motive of desire spread among people suffices without urging them toward it. The preacher's engagement with this is superfluous and a departure from the purpose, by warning them or urging them about what lies outside that. This applies when the motive for good is absent or slight. This context was a context of admonition, as indicated by His saying the Exalted about them: ﴿They said, "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not of the admonishers."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 136]. The context of admonition is broader than the context of changing evil. Thus the admonition of Hud, peace be upon him, was directed at the spiritual ailments in their souls, and there was no command in his admonition to change the markers they had built or the reservoirs they had made.

Since the trace of the building had become a distraction from the beneficial purpose for life in the Hereafter, their act leading to futility was treated as the act whose purpose is futility at the start of doing it. So he denounced building for them by introducing the interrogative particle of denunciation (hamzat al-inkar) before the verb ﴿tabnuna﴾ ("you build"), and it was qualified by the clause ﴿ta'batun﴾ ("you play"), which is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject of ﴿tabnuna﴾. Yet when they built that, they did not intend by their act any futility. So the locus of the denunciation in the denunciatory interrogation is the building qualified by futility, because when a judgment enters upon something qualified by a condition, it applies to that condition.

Likewise, the verb conjoined to the verb questioned about, which is the clause ﴿wa-tattakhidhuna masani'a﴾ ("and you take for yourselves reservoirs"), falls within the scope of denunciation and is qualified by the same qualification as the verb it is conjoined to. This is based on the view that the intermediate circumstantial clause between the two clauses refers back to both of them, according to the opinion of many scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), especially when there is a contextual indicator for that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 131–135:

﴿So be mindful of Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿And be mindful of He who has provided you with what you know.﴾ ﴿He provided you with livestock and children,﴾ ﴿and gardens and springs.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾

When the interrogative in His saying ﴿Do you build on every high place a landmark, in vain?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 128] implied disapproval of their building of landmarks, their taking of reservoirs (masani'), and their harshness toward people when angered, the command to be mindful of Allah was made to follow from it (fa-farra'a 'alayhi). With this sequencing there came a repetition of the sentence of command to taqwa (God-consciousness) and obedience.

The omission of the first-person ya' from (atī'ūni) is like its omission in its previous counterpart. The verb (wa-ittaqū) was repeated, though it would have been dispensable had the relative clause been limited to being a description of the Name of Majesty (ism al-Jalala). For the apparent structure of the discourse would be: "So be mindful of Allah, He who has provided you with what you know." Instead, he deviated from what the apparent form requires and constructed the speech on the conjunction of the command to taqwa with the command preceding it, as an emphasis on it and as concern for the command to taqwa, even though the interposition between the attribute and the qualified noun by the clause (wa-atī'ūni) required that the connection of the structure be restored by repeating the verb (ittaqū).

The verb (ittaqū) was brought conjunctively and not disjunctively because of the additional reminder of Allah's favour upon them in the second clause beyond what is in the first clause. So in the first clause he attached to the verb of taqwa the Name of the Sacred Essence, to indicate that He deserves taqwa in His essence. Then in the second clause he attached to the verb of taqwa the relative noun with its relative clause, which denotes His favour, to indicate that He deserves taqwa because He deserves gratitude for what He has bestowed.

Page 170
He has mentioned the favour in a general way, which prepares the listeners to receive what follows, so He said: ﴿who has provided you with what you know.﴾ Then He elaborated with His saying: ﴿He provided you with livestock and children,﴾ ﴿and gardens and springs.﴾ The verb (amaddakum) was repeated in the elaborating clause to increase concern with that provision, so it is for lexical emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi). This clause stands in the position of a partial substitute (badl al-ba'd) for the clause (amaddakum bi-ma ta'lamun), for the second verb (amaddakum), although it is equivalent to the first, became a substitute for it only in view of what is attached to it from His saying (bi-an'amin wa-banin), etc., which is part of what you know. Both considerations, emphasis and substitution, require disjunction, which is why the clause was not conjoined.

He began enumerating the favours with mention of livestock, because it is the greatest favour for the people of that land, since from it come their sustenance and clothing, and upon it their journeys depend, and they were a people of pasturage, so it is the cause of their survival. He conjoined children to it, because they are a great favour, being their companionship and their helpers in the means of life, the preservation of their remembrance after them, and the multiplication of their community. He conjoined gardens and springs, because through them comes the comfort of their condition, the expansion of their provision, and the living of their livestock.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) for the denunciation of their lack of taqwa and for the command to taqwa; that is: I fear for you a punishment if you do not become mindful, for commanding a thing necessarily entails prohibiting its opposite.

The punishment may be intended to be a punishment in this world which Allah threatened them with through his tongue, and it may be intended to be the punishment of the Day of Resurrection.

Describing (yawm) as (azim) is by way of rational metonymy (al-majaz al-'aqli), that is: tremendous is what occurs in it of terrors.
