They replied by despairing of him ever being accepted, so they made his admonition and its absence equal. That is, both are the same in that what he intended from his admonition, which is their compliance, does not come about.

[Page 171]

The hamza here is for equalization (*taswiyah*). Its explanation has already been given at the words, ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:6], in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Wa'z* (admonition) means frightening and warning against something harmful, and the noun is *maw'izah*. It was discussed earlier at the words, ﴿And guidance and admonition for those who are mindful of God﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:46], in Surat al-'Uqud.

The meaning of ﴿or you were not among those who admonish﴾ is: or you were not counted among those described as admonishers. That is, you were not among the people of this description at all. This is stronger in negating the attribute from him than if it had said, "or you did not admonish," as was explained earlier at the words of the Exalted, ﴿He said, "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:67], in Surat al-Baqarah. Its explanation was also given at the words, ﴿I am not among those who are guided﴾ [al-An'am 6:56], in Surat al-An'am. Earlier, in the story of Noah, His words were mentioned: ﴿You will surely be among those stoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:116].

The clause ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾ is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the content of the clause ﴿It is the same for us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers﴾. That is: it is the same for us, so we will not follow your admonition, because this is the custom of the ancients. The demonstrative "this" (*hadha*) refers to something known to both parties, which existed in the context of Hud's call to them, and its explanation will come.

As for His words, ﴿khuluq al-awwalin﴾, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, 'Asim and Khalaf read it with a *damma* on the *kha'* and a *damma* on the *lam*. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with a *fatha* on the *kha'* and a sukun on the *lam*.

On the reading of the first group, *khuluq* with two dammas means the disposition firmly established in the soul, which prompts an action suited to it, whether good or bad. It has been explained as "the psychological faculties," which is an inadequate explanation, since it covers both the natures of goodness and the natures of evil. For this reason, one of the two types cannot be known from the word alone, except by a qualifier added to it. One says *khuluq hasan* (good character), and for its opposite one says *su' khuluq* (bad character) or *khuluq dhamim* (blameworthy character). The Exalted said, ﴿And indeed you are of a tremendous character﴾ [al-Qalam 68:4]. In a hadith: "And treat people with good character."

When it is used without qualification, it is understood to mean good character, as al-Hariri said in the ninth *maqamah*: "My character is an excellent helper, and between me and my neighbors is a gulf," that is, in good character.

[Page 172]

In the terminology of the philosophers, *khuluq* is a *malakah*, that is, a firmly established condition in the soul, that is, one well-rooted in thought, from which the actions of its possessor issue without deliberation.

Thus a person's *khuluq* is a collection of dispositions (*gharaʾiz*), that is, psychological natures composed of an intellectual impression: either innate, from the original constitution, or acquired, arising from the habituation of thought to it and its adoption because one finds it good, either through experience of its benefit or through imitating what one observes of the motives for loving what one has seen. It should be called a choice of a saying or deed for its own sake, or because it is the conduct of one whom one loves and imitates, and it is called imitation (*taqlid*). The effort to attain it is called *takhallaq* (cultivating character). Salim ibn Wabisah said:

*"Keep to the striving in what you are doing,*
*for cultivated behavior comes without true character."*

When it becomes settled and firmly rooted in the soul, it becomes a natural disposition for him, and his actions proceed according to what it dictates to him and what his soul commands him, such that he cannot abandon acting in accordance with its requirements. If he tried to force his soul not to act on what his disposition dictates, he would belittle his soul and his will and despise his opinion. Character may change gradually, through experiencing harm arising from its motive, or through fear of an evil outcome from it, by the warning of one who is an exemplar for him, due to belief in his sincerity or fear of his punishment. The first of these is religious admonitions.

The meaning of the verse on this basis may be that those being reported had intended praise for their conditions, which they insisted on not changing. Thus they meant that these were the character of their forefathers and their models, so they would not accept any reproach or blame for it, as the Exalted said of their likes: ﴿You want to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship﴾ [Ibrahim 14:10]. So the demonstrative refers to what they were upon, which their messenger forbade them.

It may also be that they meant what their messenger was calling to, that is: this is nothing but the character of people before him, that is, their beliefs, which they accepted for themselves, and that he has crossed over to them and adopted them; that is, it is not by permission from God, the Exalted, just as the polytheists of Quraysh said: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ [al-An'am 6:25]. The demonstrative refers to what he calls them to.

As for the reading of the second group, *khalq* with a *fatha* on the *kha'* and a sukun on the *lam* is a verbal noun meaning creating and fashioning. *Khalq* is also the verbal noun of *khalaqa*, when someone lies in his report, and from it is the words of the Exalted, ﴿and you invent a lie﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:17]. The Arabs say, "So-and-so narrated to us fabricated stories (*ahadith al-khalq*)," which are invented fables, and it is called *ikhtilaq*, in the form *ifti'al* which indicates effort and invention. The Exalted said, ﴿This is nothing but fabrication (*ikhtilaq*)﴾ [Sad 38:7], because the liar invents a report that has not occurred.

So the meaning may be that what you claim of a message from God is a lie, and what you tell us of resurrection is fabrication. Thus the demonstrative refers to what Salih brought.

The meaning may also be that our life is like the life of the ancients: we live and then we die. Thus the speech is an eloquent comparison (*tashbih baligh*), and it is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for denying the resurrection, whose punishment he had warned them of in the words, ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:135]. They say: just as the ancients died and none of them was ever resurrected, so we too live and then die, and we will not be resurrected. This is like the words of the polytheists: ﴿Then bring our fathers if you are truthful﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:36]. So the demonstrative in His words, ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾, refers to the custom they were upon, as the exception indicates.

These are four meanings, one of which is praise, two are blame, and one is supplication.

The clause ﴿And we are not among those punished﴾ is, according to the first, second and third meanings, a conjunction of a different kind (*'atf mughayir*) to the clause ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾.

According to the fourth meaning, it is a conjunction of explanation (*'atf tafsir*) to their words ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾, stating explicitly after the metonymy.

The restriction (*qasr*) is a restriction relative to context (*qasr idafi*) according to all the meanings.

There is no doubt that the people of Salih spoke in their language many sentences that resolve into these meanings, and the Qur'an gathered them in His words, ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾, by the possibility of the demonstrative and the variation in pronunciation of the word *khuluq*. So to God belongs its conciseness and its inimitability.

The *fa'* in ﴿so they denied him﴾ is an explanatory *fa'* (*fa' fasihah*), that is: it became clear that by their saying, "It is the same for us whether you admonish or not," they had denied him, so We destroyed them.

His words, ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:190] to the end, are like their counterpart in the story of Noah.

If he tried to force his soul not to act on what his disposition dictates, he would belittle his soul and his will and despise his opinion. They had turned away from the worship of God, Exalted, and denied the Resurrection, and their leaders of disbelief deluded them in this. So Salih (peace be upon him) came to them as a messenger, reminding them of God's blessing upon them in what He had established for them of good things and in the great works He had made subservient to them. By ﴿the extravagant﴾ is meant the leaders of the people and their elders, who incite them to worship idols and keep them in error, exploiting their ignorance and making them serve their interests. Israf (extravagance) is excess in something, and what is meant here is the wholly blameworthy extravagance, both in wealth and in disbelief. Their description as ﴿those who spread corruption in the land﴾ links extravagance with corruption.

The conjunction of ﴿and do not set things right﴾ to the clause ﴿who spread corruption in the land﴾ is an emphasis on the occurrence of the matter by negating its opposite, like the words of God, Exalted: ﴿And Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them﴾ and the words of 'Amr ibn Murrah al-Juhani:

"The known lineage is not denied."

This indicates that their corruption is not mixed with any righteousness. It is as if it were said: they are only corrupters in the land. He departed from the form of restriction (qasr) lest it be understood as a restriction of exaggeration, because denying righteousness of them emphasizes the affirmation of corruption in them, so that this is fixed in the mind, and the meaning of their corruption is intensified by negating its opposite, like the words of al-Samaw'al or al-Harithi:

"Our souls flow over the edges of the swords, and they do not flow over anything other than the edges."

The definiteness in ﴿the land﴾ is the definiteness of previous reference (ta'rif al-'ahd).

[Page 175]

They had turned away from the worship of God, Exalted, and denied the Resurrection, and their leaders of disbelief deluded them in this. So Salih (peace be upon him) came to them as a messenger, reminding them of God's blessing upon them in what He had established for them of good things and in the great works He had made subservient to them. Their situation was treated as that of one who supposes eternal life and the perpetuity of blessing, so he addressed them with a rhetorical question of denial and reproach, which in meaning is a denial of their supposition. He directed the denial at the act of leaving (them), because their being left in those blessings does not occur. Thus the denial of its occurrence entails the denial of their belief in it.

This statement explains the denial in His words: ﴿Will you not fear God?﴾ Because the denial against them of the continuation of their state implies that they will depart from this life and go to God.

It also contains an exhortation to act to preserve those blessings, by thanking God for them, as the author of al-Hikam said: "Whoever does not thank blessings has exposed them to their removal, and whoever thanks them has bound them with their tether."

The word ﴿hahuna﴾ ("here") refers to their land, meaning: in all that you see. This is a wonderful conciseness (ijaz). The word ﴿amininin﴾ ("secure") is a circumstantial clause (hal) explaining part of what the phrase "in what is here" has left general. This is an alert to a great blessing which the demonstrative does not point to, because it cannot be pointed to, namely the blessing of security, which is among the greatest blessings, and the taste of the other blessings is not enjoyed except through it.

His words ﴿in gardens﴾ should be linked to ﴿secure﴾, so that the whole of this constitutes a detailed explanation of the general demonstrative, meaning: security and the ease of living came together for them. The word ﴿jannat﴾ (gardens) means the walled plots planted with palm trees and grapevines.

The word ﴿tal'* ﴾ (spathe, i.e., the flower sheath of the date palm): it is the sheath that emerges from the palm, in which the date cluster is in its first stages. It emerges like the blade of a sword, and inside it are the strands of the cluster. This spathe is called al-kimm (with a kasra on the kaf). A few days after its emergence, that sheath splits open to reveal the shamarikh, which are the branches bearing the fruit like small grains, then it thickens and becomes busr (unripe dates), then tamr (ripe dates).

The word ﴿hadim﴾ means "crushed" (in the sense of mahdum). The root hadm means crushing a thing until it becomes soft. It is used here metaphorically for what is fine and slender, as one says: a woman "hadim al-kashh" (slender-waisted). This is a sign that it yields good dates. The palm that bears good dates is called al-nakhl al-inath (the female palms), and its opposite is fahahil, which is the plural of fuhhal, with a damma on the fa and a shadda on the ha (meaning male). Its spathe is thick, and its dates are likewise.

The palm was singled out for mention, although it is among the things that the gardens include, in order to make clear its excellence by stating that its spathe is ﴿hadim﴾.

﴿And you hew﴾ is coordinated with ﴿secure﴾, meaning: and hewing, expressed with the present tense to bring the state vividly before the mind in their hewing houses out of the mountains. This has been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

﴿Farihin﴾ ("skilled") is an intensive form in the recitation of the majority, without an alif after the fa, derived from farahah, which means skill and shrewdness, meaning: knowledgeable and skilled in hewing houses from the mountains, such that through hewing they become as if they were built. It was recited by Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf as ﴿fariHin﴾ (with an active participle form).

[Page 177]

﴿They said, "You are only one of those who have been bewitched. You are nothing but a human being like us, so bring a sign if you are among the truthful."﴾

They met his admonition with slander: they claimed that he had lost his right judgment and that his condition had changed, and they fabricated that this was the effect of a severe sorcery. Al-Musahharun (those who have been bewitched) is the passive participle of sahharahu, used when someone has cast a sorcery on him that has taken full hold of him. The phrase ﴿مِنَ المُسَحَّرِينَ﴾ (min al-musahharin, "among those who have been bewitched") is more emphatic in describing him as bewitched than saying "innama anta musahharun" (you are only bewitched), as in their earlier words ﴿لَتَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المَرْجُومِينَ﴾ (you will surely be among those who are stoned) [al-Shu'ara': 116].

Since their statement ﴿إنَّما أنْتَ مِنَ المُسَحَّرِينَ﴾ (you are only among those who have been bewitched) implied that they denied him, they reinforced their denial by saying that he is a human being like them. In their view, this contradicts his being a messenger from God, because in their opinion a messenger can only be a created being who transcends normal custom, such as an angel or a jinn. Therefore the sentence ﴿ما أنْتَ إلّا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُنا﴾ (you are nothing but a human being like us) functions, in terms of its meaning, as an emphatic restatement of the sentence ﴿إنَّما أنْتَ مِنَ المُسَحَّرِينَ﴾.

Having denied him, they then drew a consequence: they demanded that he bring a sign confirming his truthfulness, that is, that he bring a supernatural act that would show that God had confirmed his claim to prophethood. They presented his truthfulness as a supposition by using the conditional particle ﴿إنْ﴾ (in), which is commonly used for what is doubtful.

The meaning of ﴿مِنَ الصّادِقِينَ﴾ (among the truthful) is "from the group known for truthfulness." By this they mean the truthful messengers, because it indicates that truthfulness has taken full hold of them, as in their earlier words ﴿مِنَ المَرْجُومِينَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 116].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 155–159:

﴿He said: "This is a she-camel; she has a turn to drink, and you have a turn to drink on an appointed day."﴾ ﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest the punishment of a tremendous day seize you.﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, and so they became regretful.﴾ ﴿So the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord – He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾

The demonstrative "this" refers to the she-camel, which he (Salih) made a sign for them. The account of this she-camel has preceded in Surat Hud, and it was mentioned there that Salih assigned her a shirb (share of water). It is pronounced with a kasra on the shin and a sukun on the ra': it is the turn at the water for the she-camel, a day on which she drinks, during which they do not crowd her with their livestock. The discussion of "the punishment of a tremendous day" is similar to the discussion of its counterpart in the story of 'Ad and their messenger.

﴿And they became regretful﴾: when they saw the signs of the punishment with which Salih had threatened them. For this reason, regret did not benefit them, because the punishment had descended upon them swiftly. Therefore it is joined with the fa' of immediate sequence (fa' al-ta'qib) to "regretful," so that "regretful, so the punishment seized them."

The parallel of His saying "Indeed in that is a sign" has preceded.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 26, verses 160–164:

﴿The people of Lot denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Lot said to them: "Will you not be mindful of God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

The discussion of its placement is like the discussion of the preceding passage, and the discussion of its interpretation is like the discussion of its counterpart.

He made Lot a brother to his people, though he was not of their lineage. He was only a sojourner among them, since the people of Lot were from the people of Palestine (Filasṭīn), of the Kanʿānīyūn (Canaanites), whereas Lot was an ʿIbrānī (Hebrew) and was the son of Ibrahim's brother. But when he settled in their land, lived among them, allied with them and supported them, he was made a brother to them, as in the words of Suhaym, the slave of the Banu al-Ḥasḥās:

"Your brother, and the client of your best, and your ally, and one who has dwelt among you and lived with you for a long time."

He means himself, addressing his masters, the Banu al-Ḥasḥās. God, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿And the brothers of Lot﴾ [Qaf: 13]. This is the use of "brotherhood" to denote constant attachment to a thing and engagement with it, as in the words of the poet:

"A brother of war, who wears its trappings for it, when they lack provisions, you are barren."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers were brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 27].

This is in the resumptive mode (istinaf, a new sentence that continues the narrative), like his saying (﴿Will you be left [secure] ...﴾) in the story of Thamud. The verb "coming to" (al-ityan) is a metonymy (kinaya) for sexual intercourse. Al-dhukran is the plural of dhakar, the opposite of unthā (female).

[p. 179]

His saying "from among the worlds" (min al-ʿalamin): the more apparent reading is that it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the waw in (﴿Do you come to﴾). The min here is fasliyya, meaning it indicates separation between two things that differ, such that neither resembles the other. The meaning is: separated from the worlds, no category of the worlds resembles you in this. This meaning was permitted secondarily by al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf, and it better suits the meaning of "the worlds" (al-ʿalamin), which in the preferred view is the plural of ʿalam, meaning a kind (nawʿ) of created beings, as explained earlier in Surat al-Fatiha.

They said, "If you do not desist, O Lut, you will surely be among those expelled." (167)

He said, "Indeed I am, of your deed, among those who detest it." (168)

"My Lord, deliver me and my family from what they do." (169)

So We delivered him and his family, all of them, (170)

except an old woman among those who remained behind. (171)

Then We destroyed the others. (172)

And We rained upon them a rain, and evil was the rain of those who were warned. (173)

Their saying is like the saying of the people of Nuh to Nuh, except that these said, "You will surely be among those expelled" (﴿لَتَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المُخْرَجِينَ﴾), so they threatened him with expulsion from their city, because he was not a native of the city but a migrant among them, and he had a marital relation (ṣihr) with them.

The form "min al-mukhrajīn" is more emphatic than "la-nukhrijannaka" (we will surely expel you), as has preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لَتَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المَرْجُومِينَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 116]. Lut's answer to their threat was the answer of one who makes light of their threat, when he repeated the denial: ﴿قالَ إنِّي لِعَمَلِكم مِنَ القالِينَ﴾, that is, "among those who hate (it)." His saying "min al-qaliyin" is more eloquent in description than saying "inni li-'amalikum qālin," as has preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿قالَ أعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ أنْ أكُونَ مِنَ الجاهِلِينَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] in Surat al-Baqarah. And this is more complete in jinas (paronomasia), for it is a complete jinas, and between "qālin" and "al-qāliyin" there is a jinas that is "mudhayyal" (with an added tail), and it is called "mutarraf" (with a matched end).

He turned to supplicating to God that He deliver him and his family from what his people do, that is, from the punishment of what they do; so there must be an implied omitted noun (muḍāf) as indicated by His saying "fa-najjaynāhu." It is not good to make the meaning: "deliver me from my doing their deed," because with it the allusion to a punishment that will befall them would be lost. The story has preceded in al-A'raf, in Hud, and in al-Hijr.

The fa' in His saying "fa-najjaynāhu" is for sequence, that is, his deliverance came directly after his supplication, as the context requires, within the shortest period between the supplication and God's command to him to leave with his family for the town of Sughar.

The "'ajūz" is the aged woman, and she is the wife of Lut. His saying "fi al-ghabirin" is a description of "ʿajūzan."

The "ghābir" is one who has the quality of remaining, which is staying behind after the departure of companions or of the people of the horse; that is, she remained in the punishment after the deliverance of her husband and family. What befell them of stones was called "maṭar" because it descended upon them from the air. "Sā'a" is a verb of blame with the meaning of "bi'sa" (evil was). And in His saying "al-mundharin" there is a recording against them that they were warned, but they did not heed the warning.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 176–180:**

﴿The companions of the Thicket denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When Shu'ayb said to them, "Will you not be mindful of God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (istintaf) of enumeration and repetition, as was mentioned earlier in the sentence (﴿'Ad denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 123]). The verb (kadhdhaba) here is not marked with the feminine ending, because (ashab) is the plural of (sahib), which is masculine in both meaning and form. This differs from His saying ﴿The people of Lot denied﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 160], where (qawm) carries the sense of a group and a community, as was mentioned earlier in His saying (﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 105]).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read (Layka) with an open lam, followed by a silent ya', and it is diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf) because of its status as a proper name and its feminine form. The rest of the readers read (al-Ayka) with the definite article, followed by an open hamza, and with the final vowel in the genitive case, taking it as a definite of reference (ta'rif 'ahd) to a known thicket. Al-Ayka means densely intertwined trees, and it is a thicket (ghaydah).

Abu 'Ubayd reported: "We saw it in the Imam, the Mushaf of 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, in (al-Hijr) and (Qaf) as (al-Ayka), and in (al-Shu'ara') and (Sad) as (Layka). After that, the Mushafs of all the regions converged and did not differ."

The companions of Layka are the people of Shu'ayb, or a tribe among them. It is said that their thicket was of (al-muql) trees, with the first letter vowelled with a damma, the second silent, and that this is the (nabq), which is also called (al-dawm), with the letter dal unpointed and a sukun on the waw.

The singular form is marked with the feminine ending (ta' al-wahda) to indicate the place, and the collective noun is (ayk). It became known as (al-Ayka), and by common usage it became a proper name with the definite article, like (al-'Aqaba). Then a change occurred in it so that it would become a personal proper name: the hamza was dropped, its vowel was placed on the lam of the definite article, and the sense of definiteness was forgotten.

From al-Zajjaj: it is reported in the tafsir that the name of the city to which Shu'ayb was sent was Layka. From Abu 'Ubayd: "We found in some books of tafsir that Layka is the name of the town, and al-Ayka is the whole region, like Makka and Bakka." This is a change made for the sake of naming, as they named (Shams) with a damma on the shin so that it would be a proper name, although its origin was (al-Shams) as a name by common usage. Change for the sake of transferring to proper-name status is common, as Ibn Jinni mentioned in his explanation of the difficult passages of al-Hamasa, in the verse of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran:

*Indeed I am a praiser of him, aiming with it at the son of my paternal uncle of truthfulness, Shams ibn Malik.*

He also mentioned it in al-Kashshaf in the Surah of Abu Lahab. Its explanation was given earlier, in the discussion of the basmala before the Surah al-Fatiha. When the name Layka became a proper name for the land, it became permissible not to apply tanwin to it for that reason. This is not merely because the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the lam, as al-Nahhas imagined, nor because the recitation is based on the appearance of the Mushaf's writing, as the author of al-Kashshaf strained to claim in his habit of belittling the readers by accusing them of error. You know that reliance in the recitations is on transmission before the copying of the Mushafs, as we explained in the sixth introduction of this tafsir. So do not follow the mistaken illusions.

It has been disputed whether the companions of Layka are the people of Madyan, or are another people living in Layka adjacent to Madyan, to whom Shu'ayb was sent along with the people of Madyan. Many of the mufassirun inclined to this view. 'Abd Allah ibn Wahb reported from Jubayr ibn Hazim, from Qatada, who said: "Shu'ayb was sent to two nations: to his people from the people of Madyan, and to the companions of al-Ayka." Jabir ibn Zayd said: "Shu'ayb was sent to his people, the people of Madyan, and to the people of the desert, who are the companions of al-Ayka."

In Ibn Kathir's tafsir: the hafiz Ibn 'Asakir narrated in the biography of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, through the chain of Muhammad ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi Shayba, with his chain, to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The people of Madyan and the companions of al-Ayka are two nations, to which God sent Shu'ayb the Prophet." Ibn Kathir said: "This is gharib (a weak report with a single transmitter at some stage), its attribution to the Prophet (ﷺ) is questionable, and the more likely view is that it is mawquf (ending with a Companion)." Ibn Jurayj reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the companions of al-Ayka are the people of Madyan.

The more apparent view is that the people of al-Ayka are a tribe other than Madyan, for the people of Madyan are the descendants of Shu'ayb's lineage, namely the offspring of Madyan ibn Ibrahim from his wife Qatura. Madyan settled in the east of the land of al-Khalil, as in the Torah. This implies that he found it a town inhabited by a people, so they were the companions of al-Ayka. Madyan and his descendants built the city and left the desert to its people, who were the inhabitants of the thicket.

What supports and favours this is that when the Qur'an mentioned this story regarding the people of Madyan, it described Shu'ayb as their brother. But when it mentioned it regarding the companions of Layka, it did not describe Shu'ayb as their brother, since Shu'ayb was neither a kinsman nor a relative by marriage to the companions of Layka. This is a subtle allusion to this point. Among what favours this is His saying, may He be exalted, in Surah al-Hijr: ﴿And indeed the companions of the thicket were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hijr: 78], ﴿so We took vengeance upon them; and indeed they both are on a clear highway﴾ [al-Hijr: 79]. Here He made their pronoun dual, considering that they are the combined two tribes: Madyan and the companions of Layka. We have explained this in Surah al-Hijr. Messengers are sent only from the people of towns, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿We did not send before you any but men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns﴾ [Yusuf: 109], and the message includes those around the town.

Shu'ayb began his call with words like those of the messengers before him, for the reason we mentioned earlier.

His saying (﴿Will you not be mindful?﴾) includes the prohibition of associating partners with God, for they were polytheists, as in the verse of Surah Hud.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 181–183:

﴿Give full measure and do not be among those who cause loss.﴾ ﴿And weigh with an even balance.﴾ ﴿And do not deprive people of their due, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief.﴾

This is a resumption (isti'naf) of his speech. He moves from the primary purpose of the call, his words "Will you not fear [Allah]?" and what follows, to the detailed call of establishing laws of transaction among them. Although they associated others with Allah, they used to give short measure and weight, deprive people of their goods when buying from them, and cause corruption on the earth. As for short-changing in measure and weight, it is injustice and the consuming of wealth by falsehood. Since their merchants had colluded in this, people were compelled to trade with short measure.

"Give full" (awfu) is a command to fulfil, meaning make a thing complete, i.e., make the measure not deficient. The "mukhsir" is the one who causes loss to others, i.e., the diminisher. So the meaning of "do not be among those who cause loss" is: do not be among those who give short measure. The phrasing "among those who cause loss" (min al-mukhsirin) is more emphatic than "do not be causers of loss" (la takunu mukhsirin), because it indicates a command to disavow the people who practise this conduct, as was mentioned earlier in several verses, among them His saying, in the story of Noah, ﴿You will surely be among those stoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 116].

[p. 185]

Al-qistas, with the qaf vowelled either with a damma or a kasra, is one of the names for justice and one of the names for the balance. It was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And weigh with an even balance; that is better and more suitable in outcome﴾ [al-Isra': 35] in surah al-Isra', and it is understood here in both meanings, as it was there, although the description "even" (mustaqim) favours that what is intended is the balance. The details of what this legislation refers to were already set out in its narrative in al-A'raf.

The majority of readers recite "bil-qistas" with a damma on the qaf. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the qaf.

The depriving of people of their goods (bakhs ashya' al-nas) means cheating them regarding the benefits of their goods and disparaging them with what is not in them, so that they are compelled to sell them at a loss. As for corruption (fasad), it applies to all harmful transactions.

Bakhs means diminution and disparagement. It was mentioned in His saying, ﴿and let him not diminish anything from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282] in surah al-Baqarah, and its counterpart in surah al-A'raf. The counterpart of the rest of the verse was mentioned in surah Hud. Among the depriving of goods is that they say to one who offers a sound commodity for sale, "Your commodity is defective," in order to turn the desirous away from it, so that they may buy it cheaply.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 184:

﴿And fear Him who created you and the former generations.﴾

He reinforced his statement at the beginning of his address, "So fear Allah" (fa-ittaqu Allah), with his statement here: ﴿And fear Him who created you and the former generations﴾, and he added to it the evidence of His entitlement to be feared, namely that Allah created them and created the nations before them. Because of this addition, he introduced the conjunctive particle (waw of conjunction) before the verb (ittaqu, "fear"); had it been merely an emphasis, its coordination would not have been valid. In his statement (alladhi khalaqakum, "who created you") there is an indication of rejecting the fearing of any others among their partners.

Al-jibillah (with a kasra on the jim and the ba', and a shadda on the lam) means the creation (al-khilqah), and what is meant by it is the created beings; for al-jibillah is a noun functioning like a verbal noun (masdar), and for this reason it is described with (al-awwalin, "the former"). It has been said: al-jibillah is used to refer to its people, i.e., "and the people of the former creation." The meaning is: He who created you and created the nations before you.

[Page 186]

﴿They said, "You are only one of the bewitched."﴾ ﴿"You are only a human being like us, and we think you are surely among the liars."﴾ ﴿"So make a piece of the sky fall upon us, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord knows best what you do."﴾

They denied his message from God, both by implication (*kināya*) and explicitly. They claimed that he was *masḥūran* (bewitched), meaning his perception and imagination were disordered as a result of magic that had been directed against him. This is a metonymy (*kināya*) for the falsity of the claim that what he brought was a message from God. The form *min al-musaḥḥarīn* ("among the bewitched") contains the same intensity (*mubālagha*) found in His words "among those stoned" (Q. 26:116), "among the bewitched" (Q. 26:153), and "among those expelled" (Q. 26:167).

The use of the conjunction *wāw* (*wāw al-ʿaṭf*, the conjunctive "and") in "*wa-mā anta illā basharun mithlunā*" ("and you are only a human being like us") makes his being human a second denial of his message. The omission of the conjunction in the story of Thamud makes his being human a proof that what proceeds from him is not a revelation from God but rather the effect of his being bewitched. Thus the outcome of the meanings of the two verses is one, but the way it is conveyed differs according to the manner of narrating the two accounts.

The word *ẓann* (supposition, "think") is used in the sense of certainty in "*wa-in naẓunnuka la-mina al-kādhibīn*" ("we think you are surely among the liars"). This usage is common, as in His words "those who think (*yaẓunnūna*) that they will meet their Lord" (Q. 2:46). Its indicator here is the entry of the *lām* on the second object of *ẓanna*, because its original form is the *lām* of oath.

*In* (إنْ) is a lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the *lām* in *la-mina al-kādhibīn* is the distinguishing *lām* (*al-lām al-fāriqa*). Its proper place is to enter upon what originally was a predicate (*khabar*), so that here one would say, for instance, *wa-in anta la-mina al-kādhibīn*. However, the Arabs have been liberal with the lightened form, and they often place it before the abrogating (*nāsikh*) verb, because of its strong specialization for the subject and predicate. Thus two governing words (*nāsikhān*) come together in the sentence, as in His words "and it would indeed have been a great (burden)" (Q. 2:143). The original construction in such an example would be *wa-naẓunnu anna-ka la-mina al-kādhibīn*, but the order was changed so that the particle of emphasis could come first. This is because *inna* and its sisters have precedence at the beginning of the sentence, except for the open *an* (أنْ). I think they lighten *inna* only when they intend to combine it with one of the governing verbs in the manner of *tanāzuʿ* (contention between two governors). Thus one who says *in aẓunnuka la-khāʾifan* intends to say *aẓunnu anna-ka la-khāʾifun*: he placed *inna* first, lightened it, and made its predicate an object of the verb of supposition, so it became *in aẓunnuka la-khāʾifan*. The Kufans, however, take *in* in such a position to be a particle of negation and make the *lām* mean *illā* ("except").

[Page 187]

The imperative in "*fa-asqit*" ("so make fall") is an imperative of incapacitation (*amr taʿjīz*), i.e., a challenge to show their inability.

*Al-kisf* (with a *kasra* on the *kāf* and sukun on the *sīn*, according to all readers except Ḥafṣ) means a piece of something. In *al-Kashshāf*, al-Zamakhsharī said it is the plural of *kisfa*, like *qiṭaʿ* and *sidr*. The first view is more apparent. God said, "And if they see a piece (*kisfan*) of the sky falling" (Q. 52:44).

Ḥafṣ read *kisafan* (with a *kasra* on the *kāf* and a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*), taking it as the plural of *kasf*, as in His words, "or you make the sky fall upon us in pieces (*kisafan*) as you claim" (Q. 17:92). This has been discussed in Surat al-Isra.

Their words "if you are among the truthful" are like the words of Thamud: "So bring a sign, if you are among the truthful" (Q. 26:154). However, these people specified the sign. It is possible that specifying it was their own proposal, and it is possible that Shuʿayb had warned them of a piece (of sky) in which a punishment would come. That is the Day of the Canopy (*yawm al-ẓulla*) mentioned in this verse. So Shuʿayb's reply attributed knowledge to God: He is the One who knows the punishment they deserve and its measure. The word *aʿlamu* ("knows best") here is an intensive form (*mubālagha*) for "knowing," not a comparative (*tafḍīl*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 189:

﴿So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them. Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾

Al-Zullah (the canopy): it was a cloud in which there were successive thunderbolts, which struck them and destroyed them, as has been mentioned previously in Surah al-A'raf. The punishment was of the same kind as what they had asked for, namely the dropping of something from the sky. As for His saying (fa-kadhdhabuhu, "so they denied him"), the fa' is fasihah (an explanatory fa', introducing a consequence that is implied), meaning: it becomes clear from their saying (﴿You are only one of those bewitched﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 185]) that they denied him; that is, the denial and their persistence in it became evident through what their intention to defeat him indicated, when they said: ﴿So drop upon us fragments from the sky if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 187]. The repetition of the verb of denial serves as a warning to the polytheists that their state is like the state of the companions of Shu'ayb, so their punishment may well be similar.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 190–191:

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord – He is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾

That is: in that there is a sign for the disbelievers of Quraysh, since their condition was like the condition of the People of the Thicket (Aṣḥāb Laykah), for they were among those who cheated in measure (al-Muṭaffifūn) while also associating partners with Allah. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Woe to those who give less [than due]﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 1] up to His saying ﴿for a tremendous Day﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 5]. The discussion of its like has already passed. We have mentioned at the opening of this surah the reason for the repetition of the verse ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 103], etc.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 190–191:

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord – He is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Woe to those who give less [than due]﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 1] up to His saying ﴿for a tremendous Day﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 5]. The discussion of its like has already passed. We have mentioned at the opening of this surah the reason for the repetition of the verse ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 103], etc.

And truly, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The Trustworthy Spirit (Jibril) has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be one of the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue.

This is a return to what the surah opened with, namely the praise and exaltation of the Qur'an and its being the greatest sign, in accordance with what His words implied: "These are the verses of the clear Book" [al-Shu'ara': 2], as mentioned earlier. The surah thus concludes with an extended praise of the Qur'an, just as it began with a concise praise of it, and with an alert that it is the greatest sign God chose to be the miracle of the best of the messengers. The pronoun in "And truly, it" refers to something known from the context after the mention of the signs of the earlier messengers. Thus, through the conjunction particle (wa, "and"), the sentence is connected to the sentences before it, and through the pronoun referring to the Qur'an, its purpose is connected to the purpose of the opening of the surah.

The sentence "And truly, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds" is conjoined to the preceding sentences, in which the reports of the messengers are related, whose peoples' circumstances resemble the situation of the people of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the signs with which God supported them, so that it may be known that the Qur'an is God's sign for this community. Its conjunction to the sentences that are similar to it is like the conjunction of one story to another, for that reason. However, this sentence is connected in meaning to the sentence "These are the verses of the clear Book" [al-Shu'ara': 2], such that, were it not for the long discourse separating them from the other, it would be conjoined to it. The address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), because in praising the Qur'an there is consolation for him regarding what he encounters of the disbelievers' turning away from accepting it and their disobedience concerning it.

The emphasis with (inna, "truly") and the lam of initiation serves to refute the denial of those who deny.

Tanzil is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (mafʿul), for the sake of intensifying the description, to the extent that the thing revealed seems to be the very act of revelation. The sentence "The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down" is an explanation of "a revelation from the Lord of the worlds," meaning: its revelation was in this manner.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs and Abu Ja'far read the zay of nazala (نَزَلَ) lightly, with the nominative of al-ruh (الرُّوحُ). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, Ya'qub and Khalaf read nazzala (نَزَّلَ) with the zay doubled, and the accusative of al-Ruha al-Amin, meaning: God caused it to be brought down by him.

"The Trustworthy Spirit" is Jibril, and it is his title in the Qur'an. He was called a spirit (ruh) because the angels belong to the world of spiritual beings, which are the immaterial ones. The discussion of the spirit was mentioned in Surah al-Isra', and "the Holy Spirit" was mentioned in al-Baqarah. Jibril's descent is by God's permission, so his descent is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.

"Trustworthy" (al-amin) is an attribute of Jibril, because God entrusted him with His revelation. The bâ' in His words "brought it down by him" denotes accompaniment.

The word "heart" (qalb) is applied to that by which knowledge is received, as the Exalted said: "Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart" [Qaf: 37], meaning: perception and intellect.

His words "upon your heart" are connected to the verb "brought down," and "upon" ('ala) denotes figurative elevation, because descent is arrival from a high place, so it necessarily implies the settling of the one descending upon a place.

The meaning of Jibril's descent upon the heart of the Prophet, upon them both be peace, is his connection with the Prophet's power of perception, to cast the divine revelation into his receptive faculty, which receives speech revealed in its words. Thus the verb "brought down" is literal.

The particle "upon" ('ala) is used metaphorically to indicate firm settling in that which is called the heart of the Prophet, like its metaphorical use in the Exalted's words: "They are upon guidance from their Lord" [al-Baqarah: 5].

The Prophet (ﷺ) described this in the hadith of the two Sahihs, from 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her), that al-Harith ibn Hisham asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying: "O Messenger of God, how does revelation come to you?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and it leaves me, and I have retained what it said. And sometimes the angel appears to me in the form of a man and speaks to me, and I retain what he says."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 196–197:**

﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*, coordination with the preceding sentence) on ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192]. The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, as the pronoun in ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ does. This is another commendation of the Qur'an: the books of the earlier prophets confirm it by agreeing with what it contains, especially in its accounts of the nations and their prophets.

[p. 191]

The phrase ﴿in the scriptures of the earlier peoples﴾ means in the books of the earlier messengers. That is, the Qur'an is found in the books of the earlier prophets, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the other prophetic books that we know of in general terms. It is well known that the pronoun for the Qur'an does not mean the essence of the Qur'an, that is, its words as revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), since the surahs and verses of the Qur'an are not written in the scriptures of the earlier peoples in their entire wording. It is therefore necessary that the pronoun refer to the Qur'an either in terms of its name and specific description, or in terms of its meanings.

As for the first consideration, the pronoun is interpreted as referring to the name of the Qur'an, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿the messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. That is, they find his name and the description that identifies him. The meaning, then, is that the mention of the Qur'an occurs in the books of the earlier peoples, that is, that there came tidings of Muhammad (ﷺ) and that he is a messenger who would come with a book. In the Book of Deuteronomy, from the books of Moses (peace be upon him), in chapter eighteen, there is the saying of Moses: (The Lord said to me: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like you, and I will put My words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.") There is no doubt that the brethren of the Children of Israel are the Arabs, as is mentioned in the Book of Genesis, chapter sixteen, at the mention of the conception of Ishmael: ﴿he will dwell in the presence of all his brethren﴾, that is, he will not dwell with them but opposite them. No prophet came with a revelation like that of Moses, with a law like the law of Moses, other than Muhammad (ﷺ), and the word of God placed in his mouth is the Qur'an, which was revealed to him and which he recites.

In the Gospel of Matthew, chapter fourteen, Jesus (peace be upon him) said: "Many false prophets will arise and will mislead many. . . But the one who endures to the end (that is, who lasts until the end of time, that is, his religion, since individuals do not live forever) will be saved, and he will preach (that is, call) with this good news of the kingdom in all the inhabited world (that is, the inhabited earth) as a witness to all nations, a general message; then the end will come (that is, the end of the world)."

So the good news is the revelation, which is the Qur'an, and it is the book that called all the nations. The Exalted said: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darknesses into the light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1], and He said: ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾ [al-Isra': 89].

In the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen, the saying of the Messiah: "And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Comforter (that is, a messenger), that He may abide with you forever (this is the perpetuity of the law), the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive (an allusion to the denial of the deniers), because it neither sees Him nor knows Him." Then he said: "But the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name (that is, the description of the message), He will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all things that I said to you (and this teaching of all things is the Qur'an, ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾)."

[p. 192]

As for the second consideration, the pronoun is interpreted in terms of its referent (*musamma*), as in the saying of people: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning half of a dirham. Just as the name of a thing is applied to its meaning, as in the Exalted's saying ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10], and His saying ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham﴾ [Maryam: 41], meaning his circumstances, so too the pronoun of the name is applied to its meaning. The meaning, then, is that what the Qur'an brought is present in the books of the earlier peoples. This is like the saying of the Gospel just mentioned: (and bring to your remembrance all things that I said to you). You will not find anything of the words of the Messiah (peace be upon him) written in the Gospels, unaltered from him, except that it is mentioned in the Qur'an. So the pronoun is taken in terms of part of it, like His saying ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13], and so on.

The purpose is that this is a sign of the truth that it is from God. This is the meaning of the Qur'an's confirming what is before it.

As for His saying ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾, it is a third commendation of the Qur'an and an argument for the second commendation, which is the testimony of the books of the prophets to its truthfulness. That is, the scholars of the Children of Israel know what is in the Qur'an that pertains to their knowledge. Because this sentence is another commendation of the Qur'an, it is coordinated with the sentence before it; otherwise, given that it is an argument for the truth of the Qur'an, it should not have been coordinated.

The verb (*ya'lamahu*, "know it") covers knowledge of the description of the Qur'an, that is, the certainty of the truthfulness of the attributes ascribed to the one who came after him, and it also covers knowledge of what their books contain.

The pronoun in (*an ya'lamahu*, "that they know it") refers to the Qur'an, on the assumption of (*an ya'lama dhikrahu*, "that they know its mention"). It is also possible that it refers to the ruling mentioned in the saying ﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 196–197:**

﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples.﴾ ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*, coordination with the preceding sentence) on ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192]. The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, as the pronoun in ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ does. This is another commendation of the Qur'an: the books of the earlier prophets confirm it by agreeing with what it contains, especially in its accounts of the nations and their prophets.

[p. 191]

The phrase ﴿in the scriptures of the earlier peoples﴾ means in the books of the earlier messengers. That is, the Qur'an is found in the books of the earlier prophets, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the other prophetic books that we know of in general terms. It is well known that the pronoun for the Qur'an does not mean the essence of the Qur'an, that is, its words as revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), since the surahs and verses of the Qur'an are not written in the scriptures of the earlier peoples in their entire wording. It is therefore necessary that the pronoun refer to the Qur'an either in terms of its name and specific description, or in terms of its meanings.

As for the first consideration, the pronoun is interpreted as referring to the name of the Qur'an, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿the messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. That is, they find his name and the description that identifies him. The meaning, then, is that the mention of the Qur'an occurs in the books of the earlier peoples, that is, that there came tidings of Muhammad (ﷺ) and that he is a messenger who would come with a book. In the Book of Deuteronomy, from the books of Moses (peace be upon him), in chapter eighteen, there is the saying of Moses: (The Lord said to me: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like you, and I will put My words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.") There is no doubt that the brethren of the Children of Israel are the Arabs, as is mentioned in the Book of Genesis, chapter sixteen, at the mention of the conception of Ishmael: ﴿he will dwell in the presence of all his brethren﴾, that is, he will not dwell with them but opposite them. No prophet came with a revelation like that of Moses, with a law like the law of Moses, other than Muhammad (ﷺ), and the word of God placed in his mouth is the Qur'an, which was revealed to him and which he recites.

In the Gospel of Matthew, chapter fourteen, Jesus (peace be upon him) said: "Many false prophets will arise and will mislead many. . . But the one who endures to the end (that is, who lasts until the end of time, that is, his religion, since individuals do not live forever) will be saved, and he will preach (that is, call) with this good news of the kingdom in all the inhabited world (that is, the inhabited earth) as a witness to all nations, a general message; then the end will come (that is, the end of the world)."

So the good news is the revelation, which is the Qur'an, and it is the book that called all the nations. The Exalted said: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darknesses into the light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1], and He said: ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾ [al-Isra': 89].

In the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen, the saying of the Messiah: "And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Comforter (that is, a messenger), that He may abide with you forever (this is the perpetuity of the law), the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive (an allusion to the denial of the deniers), because it neither sees Him nor knows Him." Then he said: "But the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name (that is, the description of the message), He will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all things that I said to you (and this teaching of all things is the Qur'an, ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾)."

[p. 192]

As for the second consideration, the pronoun is interpreted in terms of its referent (*musamma*), as in the saying of people: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning half of a dirham. Just as the name of a thing is applied to its meaning, as in the Exalted's saying ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10], and His saying ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham﴾ [Maryam: 41], meaning his circumstances, so too the pronoun of the name is applied to its meaning. The meaning, then, is that what the Qur'an brought is present in the books of the earlier peoples. This is like the saying of the Gospel just mentioned: (and bring to your remembrance all things that I said to you). You will not find anything of the words of the Messiah (peace be upon him) written in the Gospels, unaltered from him, except that it is mentioned in the Qur'an. So the pronoun is taken in terms of part of it, like His saying ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13], and so on.

The purpose is that this is a sign of the truth that it is from God. This is the meaning of the Qur'an's confirming what is before it.

As for His saying ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾, it is a third commendation of the Qur'an and an argument for the second commendation, which is the testimony of the books of the prophets to its truthfulness. That is, the scholars of the Children of Israel know what is in the Qur'an that pertains to their knowledge. Because this sentence is another commendation of the Qur'an, it is coordinated with the sentence before it; otherwise, given that it is an argument for the truth of the Qur'an, it should not have been coordinated.

The verb (*ya'lamahu*, "know it") covers knowledge of the description of the Qur'an, that is, the certainty of the truthfulness of the attributes ascribed to the one who came after him, and it also covers knowledge of what their books contain.

The pronoun in (*an ya'lamahu*, "that they know it") refers to the Qur'an, on the assumption of (*an ya'lama dhikrahu*, "that they know its mention"). It is also possible that it refers to the ruling mentioned in the saying ﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples﴾.

[p. 193]

﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabic-speaking (ajam)﴾ ﴿and he had recited it to them, they would not have been believers in it.﴾ Among the criticisms the polytheists made of the Qur'an was that it is not from God. They said: "Muhammad invented it from himself," and they said: (﴿tales of the ancients which he has had written down﴾ [al-Furqan: 5]). So God confounded them by challenging them to produce its like, and they were unable to do so.

God has exposed their slander in this verse. They only said this because the Qur'an was brought to them by an Arab messenger. Had it been brought to them by a non-Arab messenger who does not know Arabic, with God revealing these words to a messenger who neither understands them nor can compose them well, and he recited it to them, then his recitation of it, while he does not even know the language well, would also be a departure from custom (kharq 'adah, a miraculous breach of the normal order). Even if that had happened, they would not have believed that he was a messenger, although that is a departure from custom. So the phrase "to them" (ʿalayhim) adds clarification to the breach of custom. The meaning is that the polytheists, by the criticisms they throw out, do not seek the truth. Rather, they persisted in denial and began to invent excuses for their denial, out of obstinacy toward the truth and to hide from those who blame them.

The clause ﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabic-speaking﴾ is joined (ma'tufah) to the clause ﴿The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193] up to His saying ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 195]. This is because His saying "upon your heart" indicates that he was given it from God, and that it is not the words of the Prophet, unlike what the polytheists claim, that he invented it, as we indicated just above.

When He had finished arguing from their inability (to produce its like), He exposed their intentions, that they would not believe in it in any circumstance. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96] ﴿even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yunus: 97].

Al-A'jamin is the plural of a'jam. The a'jam is one who is very strongly non-Arabic in speech, meaning he does not speak a single word of Arabic well. Here it is a synonym of a'jami, with the nisba ya' (the ya' of relative adjectives). Thus, in its plural a'jamin, it is valid to consider that there is no deletion, by taking it as the plural of a'jam, as Humayd ibn Thawr said describing a dove:

I have not seen anyone like me, whom the call of one like her has moved, nor an Arab whom the call of a non-Arab (a'jam) has moved.

It is also valid to consider that the nisba ya' has been deleted for lightness. The original is al-a'jamiyyin, as in the verse attributed to Abu Talib:

And where the Ash'arites halt their saddles, at the meeting place of the torrents, between Saf and Na'il.

That is, al-Ash'ariyyun (the Ash'arites). It is upon these two considerations that the saying of al-Nabighah is to be understood:

Ghassan lie in wait for him, hoping for his return, and Turk, and the clan of the a'jamin, and Kabul.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 200–203:

﴿Thus We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿So it will come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive.﴾ ﴿Then they will say, "Will we be reprieved?"﴾

The like of the beginning of this verse has preceded in Surah al-Hijr, except that in the verse of al-Hijr it is said: ﴿Thus We cause it to enter﴾ [al-Hijr: 12] (nuslukuhu, in the present tense), whereas in this verse it is said: (salaknahu, in the past tense). The meaning in both verses is one and the purpose of both is one. The reason for choosing the present tense in the verse of al-Hijr is that it indicates renewal (al-tajaddud), lest it be imagined that the intended meaning is a past conveyance, which was conveyed to the earlier sects because their mention has preceded, and thus it is imagined that they are the intended referent of "the criminals," whereas the intended referents are the disbelievers of Quraysh. As for this verse, no mention of anyone other than the disbelievers of Quraysh has preceded in it, so it is fitting that it narrates the occurrence of this conveyance since a time past, and they remain persistent in non-belief.

The clause (Thus We caused it to enter) and what follows is a resumptive explanatory clause (jumla mustaanifa bayaniyya), meaning: if you ask about the persistence of their denial of the Qur'an, although it was revealed in clear Arabic tongue, then do not be surprised; thus, the entering (al-sulook) — We caused it to enter into the hearts of the polytheists. It is a comparison of the entering derived from (salaknahu) with itself because of its strangeness. This is similar to what preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made you a midmost nation﴾ [al-Baqara: 143] in Surah al-Baqara, meaning: it is an entering that has no parallel, namely that it entered their hearts with its clarity, and they recognised the proofs of its truthfulness from the reports of the scholars of the Children of Israel, and despite that they did not believe in it.

The meaning of (salaknahu) is "We caused it to enter." Al-A'sha said:

As the sakki enters into the door of the fayq

He expressed the polytheists by "the criminals" because their disbelief after the revelation of the Qur'an is a crime. The clause (they do not believe in it) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the criminals."

The limit in (until they see the painful punishment) is a threat of a punishment that will befall them, and an urging to hasten to faith before the punishment befalls them. The punishment applies both to the punishment of the Hereafter for those who perish before the punishment of this world befalls them, and to the punishment of the sword on the day of Badr. It is known that "faith will not benefit a soul whose faith it did not previously have" [al-An'am: 158].

His saying (﴿So it will come upon them suddenly﴾) is suitable for both punishments: the punishment of the Hereafter comes after death, and death occurs suddenly; and the punishment of this world by the sword occurs suddenly at the moment of striking with the sword.

The fa' in His saying (fa-ya'tiyahum) is conjunctive, linking the verb (ya'tiyahum) to the verb (yaraw), as indicated by the accusative case of (ya'tiyahum), and this is what the meaning of conjunction necessitates in conveying sequence (al-ta'qib). This raises a difficulty, that the coming of the punishment does not occur after their seeing it, but rather both are present together. Thus an interpretation of the meaning of the verse became necessary. The author of al-Kashshaf and those who wrote on it attempted to interpret it in ways that the soul is not content with.

In my view there is no way of interpreting it except that the clause (fa-ya'tiyahum baghta) is a substitutive clause of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause (yaraw al-'adhab al-alim), and the fa' was introduced to explain the form of inclusion, meaning: the seeing of the punishment includes its occurrence suddenly, i.e., they see it all at once without prior signs preceding it.

As for the fa' in His saying (fa-yaqulu), it serves to convey sequence in existence, and it is applicable to the swiftest punishment, so that it becomes a thought in their souls before they perish in this world; or they say that and repeat it on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment and when they are cast into it.

(Hal) is used in an interrogative sense intended as a figurative wish (tamanni), and after it came the nominal sentence indicating permanence, meaning: they wish for a long respite in which they may be enabled to attain faith and righteous deeds.

The fa' in His saying (fa-ya'tiyahum) is conjunctive, linking the verb (ya'tiyahum) to the verb (yaraw), as indicated by the accusative case of (ya'tiyahum), and this is what the meaning of conjunction necessitates in conveying sequence (al-ta'qib). This raises a difficulty, that the coming of the punishment does not occur after their seeing it, but rather both are present together. Thus an interpretation of the meaning of the verse became necessary. The author of al-Kashshaf and those who wrote on it attempted to interpret it in ways that the soul is not content with.

In my view there is no way of interpreting it except that the clause (fa-ya'tiyahum baghta) is a substitutive clause of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause (yaraw al-'adhab al-alim), and the fa' was introduced to explain the form of inclusion, meaning: the seeing of the punishment includes its occurrence suddenly, i.e., they see it all at once without prior signs preceding it.

As for the fa' in His saying (fa-yaqulu), it serves to convey sequence in existence, and it is applicable to the swiftest punishment, so that it becomes a thought in their souls before they perish in this world; or they say that and repeat it on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment and when they are cast into it.

(Hal) is used in an interrogative sense intended as a figurative wish (tamanni), and after it came the nominal sentence indicating permanence, meaning: they wish for a long respite in which they may be enabled to attain faith and righteous deeds.

﴿Are they, then, seeking to hasten Our punishment?﴾ ﴿Have you considered: if We let them enjoy for years,﴾ ﴿and then there comes to them what they were promised,﴾ ﴿what they had been enjoying will not avail them?﴾

This follows from His saying: ﴿so that it will come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 202]. It is an implied answer to their repeated question: ﴿When will this promise be, if you are truthful?﴾ [Yunus: 48]. The interrogative is used to express wonder at their delusion. The meaning is: Do they seek to hasten Our punishment, when its delay is nothing but a granting of enjoyment to them? They used to mock, saying: ﴿When will this promise be?﴾ [Yunus: 48], and they sought to hasten the punishment: ﴿And they said, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share [of punishment] before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ [Sad: 16]. Muqatil said: The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, how long will you threaten us with punishment without bringing it?" The "ma" in His saying (﴿what ... will not avail them﴾) is interrogative, and this interrogative is used for denial, meaning: it did not avail them anything. The seeing in (ara'ayta, "have you considered") is cognitive, meaning: have you known? The address is to an unspecified addressee, encompassing every addressee, including the criminals.

The clause (﴿if We let them enjoy for years﴾) is a parenthetical insertion, and the answer of the conditional is omitted, indicated by what fills the place of the two objects of (ra'ayta). The phrase (﴿and then there comes to them﴾) is conjoined to the parenthetical conditional clause, and the "thumma" (then) in it indicates sequence and delay, meaning: it came to them after years. In it there is an allusion that the punishment is coming to them and will befall them without doubt. The phrase (﴿what they were promised﴾) is a relative clause, with its relative element and the returning pronoun omitted; its estimated form is: they were promised it.

[p. 197]

The clause (﴿what ... will not avail them﴾) occupies the place of the two objects of (ra'ayta), because it is suspended from operating due to the interrogative preceding it. The phrase (﴿what they had been enjoying﴾) is a relative clause with its relative element. Its returning pronoun is omitted; its estimated form is: they were enjoying it.

The meaning is: Have you known that their being granted safety and the delay of the punishment, even if it is supposed to extend for many years, will not avail them anything if the punishment comes to them after that? This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We defer from them the punishment to a limited community, they will surely say, "What is it that holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and there will befall them what they used to mock.﴾ [Hud: 8]. This is because matters are judged by their endings.

In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi: Ibn Shihab narrated that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, whenever he woke up in the morning, would take hold of his beard, then recite: ﴿Have you considered: if We let them enjoy for years,﴾ ﴿and then there comes to them what they were promised,﴾ ﴿what they had been enjoying will not avail them,﴾ and then he would weep and say:

Your day, O deluded one, is heedlessness and negligence,
and your night is sleep, while death is bound to you.

You are neither alert and resolute when awake,
nor among the sleepers are you saved and safe.

You are pleased with what perishes and rejoice in wishes,
as the dreamer is pleased with pleasures in sleep.

You strive toward what you will later hate in its outcome;
thus in this world the beasts live.

I have not found out who the author of these verses is. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu Ja'far al-Mansur also had an account concerning this verse. Perhaps what is narrated from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz was also narrated similarly about al-Mansur.
