This is a commentary on Qur'an 26:208, and I have translated it below.

﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners﴾.

It is a reminder to the Quraysh that the towns which God destroyed, and those whose mention has preceded in this surah, had messengers who warned them of God's punishment, so that they might compare their own condition with the conditions of the nations that came before them.

The exception (al-istithna') is from omitted circumstances (ahwal mahdhufah). The implied sense is: "And We did not destroy any town in any circumstance except in a circumstance in which it had warners." The circumstantial clause has been stripped of the waw (al-waw), being dispensed with by the exceptive particle (illa). Had the waw been mentioned, it would have been permissible, as in His saying in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿except that it had a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4]. He expressed the messengers by the attribute of warning, because it is the fitting description for a threat of destruction.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 209:**

﴿A reminder, and We were never unjust.﴾

That is, this is a reminder (*dhikra*). *Dhikra* is in the nominative position as a predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), which the context indicates. Compare His words in Surat al-Ahqaf, (*balagh*), meaning "this is a message," and in Surat Ibrahim, (﴿This is a message for mankind﴾ [Ibrahim: 52]), and in Surat Sad, (*hadha dhikr*, "this is a reminder"). The meaning is: this is a reminder for you, O assembly of Quraysh. This meaning is the best of the interpretations for the placement of His words (*dhikra*). It is the view of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj and al-Farra', although they differ on the estimated omitted element. Ibn al-Anbari said: Some exegetes said, "There is no complete pause (*waqf tamm*) in al-Shu'ara' except His words (﴿except that to it are warners﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 208])."

Al-Zamakhshari hesitated over the placement of His words (*dhikra*) and offered several possibilities, all of which treat His words (*dhikra*) as a supplement (*takmila*) to the preceding discourse. These are not free of artificiality. *Al-dhikra* is a verbal noun (*ism masdar*) of *dhakkara*.

The clause (﴿and We were never unjust﴾) may be coordinated (*ma'tufa*) with (*dhikra*), since it functions like a verbal noun that requires a subject. On both readings, the import of (*wa ma kunna zalimin*, "and We were never unjust") is to give a warning (*i'dhar*) to the disbelievers of Quraysh and to alert them (*indhar*) that destruction will befall them.

The omission of the object of (*zalimin*, "unjust") is intended to generalize it, as in His words: ﴿And your Lord wrongs no one﴾ [al-Kahf: 49].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 210–212:**

﴿The devils did not bring it down.﴾ ﴿It is not fitting for them, nor are they able to do so.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are removed far from hearing it.﴾

[Page 199]

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) on the sentence ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192]. What lies between them is an interjection (*i'tiraḍ*, a parenthetical insertion), which the coherence of the meanings required, and the linking of some meanings to others, as a variation in the purpose. This is a refutation of their saying about the Prophet ﷺ that he is a soothsayer (*kahin*). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur: 29]. It also refutes their claim that the one who comes to him is a devil (*shaytan*). Al-'Awra' bint Harb, the wife of Abu Lahab, said when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ abstained from the night prayer for two nights due to illness: "I hope that your devil has forsaken you." For this reason, among the things that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira replied with when the polytheists consulted him about how to describe the Prophet ﷺ, and they said: "We will say that his speech is the speech of a soothsayer," he said: "By Allah, it is not his murmuring (*zamzama*)." The speech of soothsayers, according to their claims, is what the jinn cast to them, whereas it is merely the thoughts of their own souls, which they attribute to their supposed devils. The Qur'an is negated from being of that kind; that is, soothsayers do not have speech in their souls like the Qur'an. Thus the devils of soothsayers could not pour upon the souls of their allies anything like this Qur'an. Soothsaying is therefore from the lies and deceptions of soothsayers, and all the reports of soothsayers are tales that the transmitters have expanded.

The definite article in (*al-sam'*, "the hearing") is for a known reference (*'ahd*), and it refers to what the Arabs believed: that the devils eavesdrop (*yastariqūn al-sam'*), that is, they contrive to obtain knowledge of what occurs in the Higher Assembly (*al-mala' al-a'la*). This is because the soothsayers claimed that the jinn bring them news of what is decreed in the Higher Assembly and what will manifest in the terrestrial world. Therefore the descent of devils with the speech of the Qur'an is negated here, on the basis that the polytheists claimed that devils descend from the sky with news of what will be. The explanation of this was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Hijr and will come in Surah al-Saffat.

The meaning of ﴿It is not fitting for them﴾ is: it is not proper or correct for them. That is, it is not appropriate for them to receive the speech of Allah the Exalted, which the Trustworthy Spirit (*al-Ruh al-Amin*) is meant to receive, nor are they able to receive it. This is because satanic souls are dark and inherently wicked, so they do not accept being imprinted with the forms of what occurs in the world of the unseen. The reception of the overflow of Truth is conditioned on a correspondence (*munasaba*) between the source and the receptor.

The pronoun in (*yanbaghī*, "it is fitting") refers to what the pronoun in (*bihi*, "with it") refers to; that is, it is not fitting that the Qur'an be brought down to them, as the polytheists claimed. The object of (*yastaṭī'ūn*, "they are able") is omitted; that is, they are not able to do it. The pronouns were restated in the form used for rational beings, after they had been referred to with the pronoun for non-rational beings in His saying (*wa-mā tanazzalat*, "nor did they bring it down"), in consideration of the association of that with the soothsayers. It was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Hijr that a category of devils prepares itself for reception through what is called eavesdropping (*istiraq al-sam'*), and that it is repelled from it by shooting stars.

The statement ﴿Indeed, they are removed far from hearing it﴾ is introduced as a resumption (*isti'naf*), so it serves as a summation (*fadhlaka*) of what came before it. Its generality places it in the position of a concluding completion (*tadhyil*).

The one who is removed (*al-ma'zul*) is one who is distanced from a matter, so he is in seclusion from it. In this there is a refutation of soothsaying from its very origin. Although it contained some connection to spiritual powers in earlier times, that has ceased since the rise of Islam.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 210–212:**

﴿The devils did not bring it down.﴾ ﴿It is not fitting for them, nor are they able to do so.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are removed far from hearing it.﴾

[Page 199]

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) on the sentence ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192]. What lies between them is an interjection (*i'tiraḍ*, a parenthetical insertion), which the coherence of the meanings required, and the linking of some meanings to others, as a variation in the purpose. This is a refutation of their saying about the Prophet ﷺ that he is a soothsayer (*kahin*). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur: 29]. It also refutes their claim that the one who comes to him is a devil (*shaytan*). Al-'Awra' bint Harb, the wife of Abu Lahab, said when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ abstained from the night prayer for two nights due to illness: "I hope that your devil has forsaken you." For this reason, among the things that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira replied with when the polytheists consulted him about how to describe the Prophet ﷺ, and they said: "We will say that his speech is the speech of a soothsayer," he said: "By Allah, it is not his murmuring (*zamzama*)." The speech of soothsayers, according to their claims, is what the jinn cast to them, whereas it is merely the thoughts of their own souls, which they attribute to their supposed devils. The Qur'an is negated from being of that kind; that is, soothsayers do not have speech in their souls like the Qur'an. Thus the devils of soothsayers could not pour upon the souls of their allies anything like this Qur'an. Soothsaying is therefore from the lies and deceptions of soothsayers, and all the reports of soothsayers are tales that the transmitters have expanded.

The definite article in (*al-sam'*, "the hearing") is for a known reference (*'ahd*), and it refers to what the Arabs believed: that the devils eavesdrop (*yastariqūn al-sam'*), that is, they contrive to obtain knowledge of what occurs in the Higher Assembly (*al-mala' al-a'la*). This is because the soothsayers claimed that the jinn bring them news of what is decreed in the Higher Assembly and what will manifest in the terrestrial world. Therefore the descent of devils with the speech of the Qur'an is negated here, on the basis that the polytheists claimed that devils descend from the sky with news of what will be. The explanation of this was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Hijr and will come in Surah al-Saffat.

The meaning of ﴿It is not fitting for them﴾ is: it is not proper or correct for them. That is, it is not appropriate for them to receive the speech of Allah the Exalted, which the Trustworthy Spirit (*al-Ruh al-Amin*) is meant to receive, nor are they able to receive it. This is because satanic souls are dark and inherently wicked, so they do not accept being imprinted with the forms of what occurs in the world of the unseen. The reception of the overflow of Truth is conditioned on a correspondence (*munasaba*) between the source and the receptor.

The pronoun in (*yanbaghī*, "it is fitting") refers to what the pronoun in (*bihi*, "with it") refers to; that is, it is not fitting that the Qur'an be brought down to them, as the polytheists claimed. The object of (*yastaṭī'ūn*, "they are able") is omitted; that is, they are not able to do it. The pronouns were restated in the form used for rational beings, after they had been referred to with the pronoun for non-rational beings in His saying (*wa-mā tanazzalat*, "nor did they bring it down"), in consideration of the association of that with the soothsayers. It was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Hijr that a category of devils prepares itself for reception through what is called eavesdropping (*istiraq al-sam'*), and that it is repelled from it by shooting stars.

The statement ﴿Indeed, they are removed far from hearing it﴾ is introduced as a resumption (*isti'naf*), so it serves as a summation (*fadhlaka*) of what came before it. Its generality places it in the position of a concluding completion (*tadhyil*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 213:

﴿So do not invoke another god alongside Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾

When the address turned to the Prophet ﷺ from His saying, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193] up to here, in verses that extolled the descent of the Qur'an from Allah the Exalted and affirmed its truthfulness by stating that it is mentioned in the books of the earlier prophets, and that the scholars of the Children of Israel bore witness to it, and that it confounded the polytheists by refuting the calumny they attached to the Qur'an, it necessarily followed that what the Qur'an brought is established. The root of all this is the refutation of the religion of polytheism to which the Quraysh and others clung, and for which they contended with falsehoods. Thus it was fitting that a prohibition against associating partners with Allah and a warning against it should follow from this.

As for His saying, ﴿So do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾, it is an address to an unspecified person, so it encompasses everyone who hears this speech. It is also possible that the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, because he is the one who conveys from Allah the Exalted. Out of concern for this prohibition, it was directed to the Prophet ﷺ, even though it is established that he is already refraining from that. Therefore it is determined that the prohibition is for those who are engaged in associating partners with Allah. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should associate others with Allah, your work will surely be nullified, and you will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. The intended meaning of such an address is someone other than the one addressed, namely whoever the address reaches.

So the meaning is: ﴿So do not invoke another god alongside Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾ In this there is an indirect allusion to the polytheists, that they will be punished, since it is known that the Prophet ﷺ and his companions do not associate partners with Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 214:**

﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾.

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His words: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [Ash-Shuʿara’: 193] ﴿upon your heart, that you may be among the warners﴾ [Ash-Shuʿara’: 194]. It is a specification after a generalization, for the sake of giving attention to this particular group. The reason for this attention is that they are the people most worthy of accepting his advice and strengthening his position, and so that it does not occur to their minds that the severity of the Messenger's warning and the terrors of the threat do not apply to them, because they are the kin and the close companions of this warner. The Prophet's (ﷺ) words in his call to them confirm this: ("I cannot avail you anything against God"). They also contain an implicit rebuke of the many among them who neglected the due of kinship, since many of them harmed him and disobeyed him, like Abu Lahab. So they should not think that they will be saved in either case, and they should know that from their believers, faith alone is not accepted unless they add righteous deeds to it. This is among the things included in warning. For this reason, the Prophet (ﷺ), when this verse was revealed, called his kin, both believers and disbelievers.

In the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Hurayrah, in the Sahihayn of al-Bukhari and Muslim, which combine them, is the statement: "When (﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾) was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood upon al-Safa and called Quraysh. He began calling: 'O Banu Fihr! O Banu ʿAdi!' for the clans of Quraysh, until they gathered. If a man could not come out himself, he sent a messenger to see what it was. He said: '(O assembly of Quraysh!)' generally and specifically: 'O Banu Kaʿb ibn Luayy, save yourselves from the Fire! O Banu Murrah ibn Kaʿb, save yourselves from the Fire! O Banu ʿAbd Shams, save yourselves from the Fire! O Banu ʿAbd Manaf, save yourselves from the Fire! O Banu Hashim, save yourselves from the Fire! O Banu ʿAbd al-Muttalib, save yourselves from the Fire! Buy yourselves from God; I cannot avail you anything against God. O ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, I cannot avail you anything against God. O Safiyyah, aunt of the Messenger of God, I cannot avail you anything against God. O Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of God, ask me from my wealth whatever you wish; I cannot avail you anything against God. Yet you have a kinship, and I will keep it moist with its moisture (sabbuluhā bi-balālihā).'" Safiyyah and Fatimah were among the believers, and their warning was the implementation of the imperative in all its meanings, from calling to faith and to righteous deeds. Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) combined warning against polytheism and warning against sins, since he warned Safiyyah and Fatimah, and both of them were Muslims.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "When ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) climbed al-Safa and began calling: 'O Banu Fihr! O Banu ʿAdi!' for the clans of Quraysh, until they gathered. If a man could not come out, he sent a messenger to see what it was. Abu Lahab came with Quraysh, and he said: 'Tell me, if I informed you that cavalry was in the valley about to raid you, would you believe me?' They said: 'Yes, we have never experienced from you anything but truthfulness.' He said: 'Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment.' Abu Lahab said: 'Ruin to you for the rest of the day! Did you gather us for this?' Then it was revealed: ﴿Ruined are the hands of Abu Lahab, and ruined is he﴾ [Al-Masad: 1] ﴿His wealth will not avail him, nor what he earned﴾ [Al-Masad: 2]."

This hadith implies that Surat al-Shuʿara’ was revealed before Surat Abi Lahab, although Surat Abi Lahab is counted sixth in the enumeration of surahs, while Surat al-Shuʿara’ is counted forty-seventh. Therefore, it is apparent that the statement ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed before Surat al-Shuʿara’ as a separate verse. In some narrations from Ibn ʿAbbas in Sahih Muslim, it came: "When (And warn your closest kindred and your devoted family members) was revealed, and that was abrogated (nusikha)." Perhaps the verse was revealed the first time and then its recitation was abrogated (naskh, i.e., the cancellation of a ruling or recitation by later revelation), and then parts of it were revealed again within Surat al-Shuʿara’.

Al-ʿashīrah are the nearer members of the tribe. The description (﴿closest﴾) is an emphasis on the meaning of ʿashīrah, and a means of drawing their hearts to answer what he called them to, and an implicit rebuke to those among them who are culpable.

The injustice done to close kin is more painful to a person than the blow of a polished, Indian sword.

And to this the Prophet (ﷺ) alludes at the end of the earlier call: ("Yet you have a kinship, and I will keep it moist"), meaning: this is the limit of what I can offer you, when I cannot avail you anything against God. So it is incumbent upon you to keep my kinship moist with what you possess, for you have the ability to respond to me.

The mention of ʿashīrah has already occurred in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, and your ʿashīrah...﴾ [At-Tawbah: 24] in Surat Bara’ah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 215:

﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers.﴾

It is a parenthetical clause placed between the two sentences, hastening to honour the believers before the command to disown those who do not believe, and after the command to warn (al-indhar), which cannot but strike the souls with a painful impact.

Khafd al-janah (lowering the wing) is a metaphor for treating others with gentleness and humility. It has already been discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88] in Surat al-Hijr, and His saying: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ [al-Isra: 24] in Surat al-Isra. The wing is to a bird what the two forelimbs are to beasts, and it is with the two wings that flight takes place.

And ﴿of the believers﴾ is an explanatory specification (bayan) of ﴿those who follow you﴾, for what is meant by following is following in religion, which is faith (iman). The purpose of this explanation is to exalt the status of faith, as if it were said: "Lower your wing to them for the sake of their faith," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It also serves to console the hearts of the believers among his kin. For this reason, when he called Safiyyah in his supplication, he said: "Aunt of the Messenger of Allah," and when he called Fatimah, he said: "Daughter of the Messenger of Allah," to put them at ease. This is from lowering the wing. He did not say the same to al-'Abbas, because at that time he was a polytheist.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verse 216:

﴿So if they disobey you, then say: "Indeed, I am free of what you do."﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214], meaning: if they disobey your command derived from the command to warn, that is, if your tribe disobeys you, then nothing is incumbent upon you except to disassociate yourself from their deeds. This is the origin of the words of the Prophet ﷺ to them in his call: "Except that you have ties of kinship, which I will keep connected with their moisture" (ghayra anna lakum rahiman sa-abulluha bi-balalaha). So the disassociation is only from their disbelief, and this does not prevent maintaining ties of kinship for their sake and repeating counsel to them, as He said: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. He was commanded to say this to them in order to show that they are deserving of being disassociated from their deeds, so that he would not limit himself to concealing that within himself.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 217–220:**

﴿So rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Who sees you when you stand up.﴾ ﴿And your movement among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

The command to rely (*tawakkul*) is linked by the conjunction *fa'* of consequence (*fa' al-tafri'*, the particle that marks something as a result of what precedes it) in the recitation of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far. In that case it is a consequence of ﴿So say: Indeed, I am free of what you do.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 216]. This serves as an alert to hastening to seek refuge from the evil of those enemies, and as an explicit statement of the connection between reliance (*tawakkul*) and His saying, "Indeed, I am free [of what you do]."

The majority of readers recite *wa-tawakkal* with the *waw*, which is a conjunction joining it to the answer of the conditional clause. That is, "Say: Indeed, I am free, and rely [on God]." Its conjunction with the answer requires that it be a consequence of the condition, just as the answer is, and it implies hastening to it. Thus the outcome of the two recitations is one, although the method of deriving the meaning differs.

Page 204

The meaning is: if the people of your tribe disobey you, then disown them. Since disowning implies the arising of estrangement and enmity between him and them, God strengthened the heart of His Messenger by telling him not to care about them, and to rely upon his Lord, for He is sufficient for him, as He said: ﴿And whoever relies upon God, then He is sufficient for him.﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. He linked reliance to the two names (*al-'Aziz al-Rahim*, the Mighty, the Merciful), and to the relative clause that follows them, and to the allusion closing it, that He observes his words and knows his intention. This indicates that reliance upon God brings about what these attributes and their implications point to. By the description "the Mighty, the Merciful," it is indicated that by His might He is able to overcome his enemy, who is stronger than him, and that by His mercy He protects him from them. These two names have been noted more than once in this surah for this purpose, as has already been explained.

*Tawakkul* (reliance) is a person entrusting his affair to one who suffices him in his concerns. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And when you have made a decision, then rely upon God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], in Surat Al 'Imran.

His description of Himself as ﴿Who sees you when you stand up﴾ is intended for the necessary implication of its meaning, namely that the Prophet (ﷺ) is held in special care by Him, because He knows his turning toward God and accepts it from him. So the meaning of "sees" (*yarakа*) is a special seeing, namely the seeing of approval and acceptance, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48].

*Al-qiyam* (standing) means prayer during the depths of the night; this name became dominant for it in the terminology of the Qur'an. And "your movement among those who prostrate" is his prayer in the congregations of the Muslims in his mosque. This combines the sense of care for the Muslims as a consequence of care for their Messenger, and this is from his blessing (ﷺ). This wondrous, highly concise construction has gathered it.

In this verse there is mention of congregational prayer. Muqatil said to Abu Hanifa: "Do you find congregational prayer in the Qur'an?" Abu Hanifa said: "It does not come to my mind." Muqatil then recited this verse.

The position of ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is that of a justification for the command ﴿So say: Indeed, I am free of what you do﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 216], and for the command ﴿rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. So the attribute "All-Hearing" is appropriate to the speech, and the attribute "All-Knowing" is appropriate to the reliance; that is, He hears your words and knows your resolve.

The pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*) in His saying "He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing" is for emphasis.

﴿So rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Who sees you when you stand up.﴾ ﴿And your movement among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

The command to rely (*tawakkul*) is linked by the conjunction *fa'* of consequence (*fa' al-tafri'*, the particle that marks something as a result of what precedes it) in the recitation of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far. In that case it is a consequence of ﴿So say: Indeed, I am free of what you do.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 216]. This serves as an alert to hastening to seek refuge from the evil of those enemies, and as an explicit statement of the connection between reliance (*tawakkul*) and His saying, "Indeed, I am free [of what you do]."

Its conjunction with the answer requires that it be a consequence of the condition, just as the answer is, and it implies hastening to it. Thus the outcome of the two recitations is one, although the method of deriving the meaning differs.

[p. 205]

﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every sinful liar.﴾ ﴿They lend their hearing, and most of them are liars.﴾

When He had belittled their saying about the Qur'an, that it is the saying of a soothsayer (kahin), He answered them with His words: ﴿Nor have the devils brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 210], and that it is not fitting for the devils, nor are they able to produce its like, and that they have been barred from the reports of their allies, the discourse returned to describing the condition of their soothsayers, so that it would be known that what they accused the Qur'an of should not be attributed to the condition of their allies. Thus this sentence is connected in meaning to the sentence ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾.

The speech was addressed to them in the form of a question about whether He would inform them of the one upon whom the devils descend. It is a question that implies that the thing being asked about is something that would displease them, so that disclosing it requires their permission.

This interrogation is rhetorical, used as a metonymy for the fact that the report is something whose disclosure requires permission. The interrogative particle chosen for it is (hal), which indicates confirmation, because (hal) in interrogation carries the meaning of (qad), while an interrogative hamza is implied within it. The meaning is: "I inform you with a firm and established information." It is an interrogation from which no answer is expected from the one questioned, because it is not genuine; therefore it is followed by the disclosure of what was asked about, without waiting for the listener's permission. A parallel to this in the answer is the words of God Most High: ﴿About what do they ask one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1] ﴿About the tremendous news﴾ [al-Naba': 2], although there is a difference between the two interrogations.

The verb (unabbi'ukum, "I inform you") is suspended from acting on the interrogation in His words: ﴿upon whom the devils descend﴾. It is also a rhetorical interrogation whose meaning is a statement, a metonymy for the importance of the report, to the extent that it is something that those who seek and pursue information ask about. Thus interrogation is a consequence of concern.

The prepositional phrase is placed before its governing verb for the sake of emphasis on the one upon whom they descend. The original structure was: "Upon whom do the devils descend?" When the prepositional phrase was fronted, the preposition (ʿalā, "upon") came before the interrogative noun (man, "who"), because its referent is the one upon whom they descend. It is not an objection that it is customary for the interrogative to stand at the beginning of the speech, because interrogative nouns contain the meaning of nominality, which is their basic nature, and they contain the meaning of the interrogative hamza, as (hal) does. So when the preposition is required to accompany the interrogative nouns, the nominal aspect is given preference, and the preposition enters upon them and they are not placed before it. Therefore you say: "Upon Zayd did you pass?" and do not say: "Who upon did you pass?" Rather you say: "Upon whom did you pass?" The same applies to the rest of the interrogative nouns, such as ﴿About what do they ask one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1], ﴿Of what thing did He create him?﴾ [ʿAbasa: 18], and the expressions ʿalāma ("for what?"), ilāma ("to what?"), and ḥattāma ("until when?"), and ﴿In what are you concerned with its mention?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 43].

The interrogation is answered here by His words: ﴿They descend upon every sinful liar.﴾

The word (kull, "every") is used here in the sense of multiplicity, meaning: upon many of the liars, who are the soothsayers. Al-Nabigha said:

*"And every silent (sword) of the Tubba'i stock, and the weaving of Sulaym, every long-sleeved coat that trails."*

The (ifk) is a person who lies much, namely falsehood, and the (athim) is one who commits much sin. The soothsayer was only sinful because he adds to his lying the misleading of people by pretending that he says nothing but the truth, and that he receives the report from the devils who bring him news of the heaven.

The descent (tanazzul) is attributed to the devils because their connection with the souls of the soothsayers occurs through a succession of waves in the upper atmosphere, as was mentioned earlier in the sura of al-Hijr.

The phrase (﴿They lend their hearing﴾) is a qualifier of (﴿every sinful liar﴾), meaning: they display that they lend their ears at the sight of the stars, so that their devils may descend upon them with the report, and that is from their lying and their sin.

Lending the hearing (ilqa' al-sam') is intense attentiveness, to the extent that it is as if the hearing were cast from its place. The directing of the faculty of hearing toward a hidden sound is likened to throwing a stone from the hand to the ground or into the air. God Most High said: ﴿Or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ [Qaf: 37], meaning: most intent in attentiveness so that he may understand what is said to him.

This is just as it is also called (iṣghā', "listening"), meaning: inclining the hearing toward what is heard.

His words (﴿and most of them are liars﴾) mean: most of these liars are lying in what they claim, that they received it from the devils, while they received nothing from them. That is, some of them do receive a little from the devils, but then they lie about it, adding much more.

In the authentic hadith: the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about soothsayers, and he said: "They are nothing." It was said: "O Messenger of God, they sometimes tell of a thing that turns out to be true." He said: "That word is of the truth, which the jinn snatches and drops into the ear of his friend like the clucking of a hen, and they mix into it more than a hundred lies." Thus they are liars, and they vary in lying. Some of them lie in what they add to the report of the jinn, and some of them lie in the very basis of receiving anything from the jinn. Since the condition of the soothsayers may be confused, for weak minds, with some aspects of prophethood in reporting the unseen, and their rhymed prose (saj') may be confused with the verses of the Qur'an at first glance, the verse has elaborated in explaining the reality of soothsaying and has clarified that its ultimate outcome is reporting a few things that may happen to be true. How far this is from the guidance of the Prophet and the Qur'an, with what it contains of courtesy, guidance, instruction, eloquence, fluency, clarity, and inimitability, and his never presuming to report the unseen. As He said: ﴿I do not know the unseen﴾ in many verses of this meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 26, verses 224–226 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the poets—those who are astray follow them.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley?﴾ ﴿And that they say what they do not do?﴾ ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227]

Among the slanders of the polytheists that the quiver (kinanah) of their accusations contained was their saying about the Prophet (ﷺ): "He is a poet." When the preceding verses shot the arrows of their quiver and broke them, and among them was their saying, "He is a soothsayer (kahin)," nothing remained except refuting their saying, "He is a poet." Between soothsaying and poetry there was a common link in the imagination of the polytheists, since they claimed that the poet has a devil (shaytan) who dictates poetry to him, and they sometimes called it al-ra'iy. So it was fitting that a comparison be made between the falsification of their saying about the Qur'an, "It is poetry," and their saying about the Prophet (ﷺ), "He is a poet," and their saying, "It is the word of a soothsayer," just as He joined them in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42]. So here He conjoined His saying, ﴿And the poets—those who are astray follow them﴾, to the sentence ﴿The angels descend upon every lying sinner﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 222].

Since the state of poets in reality differs from the state of soothsayers, as the faculty of poetry has no particular connection with satanic souls, and this claim was merely a fabrication of some poets which they spread among the common Arabs, the verse was limited to negating that the Messenger should be a poet, and that the Qur'an should be poetry, without addressing that it is the revelation of devils, as occurred in the mention of soothsaying.

A group of poets in Makkah used to satirise the Prophet (ﷺ), and the polytheists would take care with their gatherings and listening to their words, and Bedouins would gather to them outside Makkah to listen to their poetry and their satires. The verse combined the state of those who follow the poets with their own state, disfiguring both groups and warning against both. Among these were al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Musafi' ibn 'Abd Manaf, Abu 'Izzah al-Jumahi, Ibn al-Ziba'ra, Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, and Umm Jamil al-'Awra' bint Harb, wife of Abu Lahab, whom the Qur'an gave the epithet (﴿the carrier of firewood﴾ [al-Masad: 4]); she was also a poetess, and she is the one who said:

"We have disobeyed Mudhammam, and we have refused his command, and we have abandoned his religion."

So this verse was a negation of poetry being part of the character of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a censure of the poets who took up satirising him.

His saying, (﴿those who are astray follow them﴾), is a censure of their followers, and this necessarily implies the censure of the followed all the more. The "ghawi" is one who is characterised by error (ghayy), and ghawayah is extreme misguidance; that is, those who follow them are the people of misguidance and idleness, who are eager for corruption and harm. His saying, (﴿those who are astray follow them﴾), is a censure of their followers, and this necessarily implies the censure of the followed all the more. The "ghawi" is one who is characterised by error (ghayy), and ghawayah is extreme misguidance; that is, those who follow them are the people of misguidance and idleness, who are eager for corruption and harm. So His saying (﴿those who are astray follow them﴾) is a statement, and in it there is a kinayah (implicature) for declaring the Prophet (ﷺ) free from being among them, for his followers are the choice of their people, and there is none among them of the astray. Thus this sentence includes the declaring free of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of his companions, censure of the poets and censure of their followers, and declaring the Qur'an free of being poetry.

The fronting of the predicate's subject (al-musnad ilayhi) over the verbal predicate here shows that it is for mere emphasis and for drawing attention to the subject so as to capture the hearing; and the context is independent of restriction (al-hasr), because if they are followed by the astray, then their followers have been negated from the righteous, since the custom of gatherings is that their members share a single disposition, as it is said:

"Do not ask about the man, but ask about his companion."

Al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) made it a restriction, meaning: none follow them except the astray, because it is more explicit in negating the following of poets by Muslims. This is his method consistently: fronting the subject over the verbal predicate indicates that it restricts the predicate to it, that is, the content of the predicate is confined to it; so it is a restriction of a relative kind (qasr idafi), as its explanation was previously given at His saying, ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The seeing in (ألم تر, "Do you not see") is of the heart, because wandering (al-hiyam) and valley are used metaphorically for the meanings of confusion of speech in the purposes of poetry, and that is known rather than seen.

The interrogation is confirmatory (taqriri), and the confirmation was applied to the negation of seeing in order to show that acknowledgement cannot be avoided, as previously in His saying: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18], and the address is to an unspecified addressee. The pronouns in (أنهم, يهيمون, يقولون, يفعلون) refer to the poets.

So the sentence ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley﴾ and what is conjoined to it are confirmatory of what the sentence (﴿those who are astray follow them﴾) implied of censure of the poets by way of the import of the discourse.

The state of the poets is depicted as the state of those who wander in many different valleys, because poets speak in various arts of poetry: satire, aggression against people's honour, amatory and courtly verse about women, praise of one whom they praise out of desire for his gifts even if he does not deserve praise, dispraise of one who withholds from them even if he is of virtue, and sometimes they dispraise one whom they had praised and praise one whose dispraise they had previously voiced.

Al-hiyam is bewilderment and wandering in pasture. The wadi is the low ground between two elevations. Camels graze in valleys only when the hills have become barren, while the hills have better pasture; so the state of the poets is depicted as the state of camels grazing in valleys, bewildered, because the poets are eager to speak in order to captivate souls.

(Kull) is used for multitude. It is related that some jokers slipped into a group of poets before one of the caliphs, and the chamberlain recognised the poets, and denied this one who had slipped among them, so he said to him: "These are the poets, and are you among the poets?" He said: "Rather, I am among the astray." So he (the caliph) found it witty.

He coupled their censure with the censure of lying, saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾. The Arabs praise one another for truthfulness and reproach one another for lying, and the poet says what he does not believe and what contradicts reality, to the point that it is said: "The best poetry is the most false." Lying is blameworthy in the Islamic religion; so if poetry is a lie with no indication of its speaker's intent, then it is ugly, and if there is an indication for it, it is a lie that has an excuse, so it is not praiseworthy.

In this there is a manifestation of the vast gulf between the state of the poets and the state of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said only what is true, did not flatter, and did not bring what misleads minds.

Among the anecdotes: al-Farazdaq recited before Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik his saying:

"So they spent the night beside me, prostrate, while I spent it unlocking the seals of the sealed wine."

Sulayman said: "The hadd punishment has become obligatory upon you." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, Allah has warded off the hadd from me by His saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾."

It is also related that al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi ibn Nadlah was an official of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he said a poem:

"Who will convey to the beauty that her husband, at Maysan, is given to drink in glass and in jars?"

Up to his saying:

"Perhaps the Commander of the Faithful will be distressed by our drinking together in the ruined palace."

This reached 'Umar, who sent for him to come to him and said to him: "By Allah, I am indeed distressed by that, and the hadd has become obligatory upon you." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I did not do any of what I said; it was merely a surplus of speech, and Allah, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾." So 'Umar said to him: "As for your excuse, it has warded off the hadd from you; but never work for me again, after what you have said."

The following of the astray by them is a kinayah for their being astray, and the frightful depiction of them as bewildered camels conveys the disfigurement of their condition, and that this is on account of poetry, as the attaching of the predicate to the derived noun (al-mushtaqq) indicates; this implies that poetry is viewed in religion with a sense of disparagement. The exception (﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds...﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227]) etc. is from the generality of the poets, that is, from the ruling of their censure. By this exception it is determined that the blamed ones are the poets of the polytheists, whom poetry had occupied from hearing the Qur'an and entering Islam.

The meaning of ﴿and remember Allah often﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227]: that their turning to the Qur'an and worship was greater than their turning to poetry. ﴿and defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227]: these are the poets among those who embraced Islam, who composed poetry in satire of the polytheists and in defence of the Prophet (ﷺ), like those who embraced Islam and emigrated to Abyssinia, for they composed much poetry in censure of the polytheists. Likewise those among the Ansar who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah and Hassan ibn Thabit, and those Arabs who embraced Islam later, such as Labid, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and Suhaym 'Abd Bani al-Hashhas. The mention of believing poets does not necessitate that part of the surah is Medinan, as was explained previously at the beginning of the surah.

The verse has shown that poetry has two states: a blameworthy state and a permitted state. So it is determined that its censure is not because it is poetry, but because of the meanings and circumstances surrounding it that required blame. Thus the verse opened for poetry a door of acceptance and praise; and it is incumbent upon the people of inquiry to specify the circumstances that lead toward accepting it or toward praising it, and those that lead toward rejecting it. The praiseworthy state was alluded to by His saying: ﴿and defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227], and the permitted state by His saying: (﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227]). And how, when the Prophet (ﷺ) praised some poetry containing praiseworthy qualities, and asked his companions to listen to Ka'b ibn Zuhayr's poem containing precise descriptions of excellent riding camels; and he permitted Hassan to satirise the polytheists and said to him: "Your words are harder on them than the impact of arrows." And he said to him: "Speak, and the Holy Spirit is with you." Some of this will come at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 69] in Surat Ya-Sin. He gave him a reward as he had given Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and he gave him his mantle; this is an accepted state, because he came as a believer.

Abu Hurayrah said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say on the minbar: 'The truest word, or the most poetic word, that the Arabs have spoken is the word of Labid:

"Surely everything other than Allah is vanity.'" He used to ask for the poetry of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt because of the wisdom in it, and said: "Umayyah almost embraced Islam." He ordered Hassan to satirise the polytheists and said to him: "Speak, and the Holy Spirit is with you." And he said to Ka'b ibn Malik: "Your speech is harder on them than the impact of arrows."

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi related in Ahkam al-Qur'an, with his chain to Khuraym ibn Aws ibn Harithah, that he said: "I emigrated to the Messenger of Allah at Madinah upon his return from Tabuk, and I heard al-'Abbas say: 'O Messenger of Allah, I wish to praise you.' He said: 'Say: may Allah not break your teeth.' So al-'Abbas said:

"Before it you were good in the shades, and in a repository where the leaves are woven..." — the seven verses. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'May Allah not break your teeth.'"

Al-Tirmidhi related from Anas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah in the 'Umrat al-Qada', and 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah was walking before him, saying:

"Clear the way for the sons of the unbelievers from his path; today we strike you over his revelation,
a blow that removes the head from its place and makes the intimate forget his intimate."

'Umar said to him: "O son of Rawahah, in the sanctuary of Allah and before the Messenger of Allah you recite poetry?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Leave him alone, O 'Umar, for it is swifter against them than the spurting of arrows."

From al-Zuhri, that Ka'b ibn Malik "said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about poetry?' He said: 'The believer strives with his sword and his tongue, and by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is as if you are spraying them with arrows.'"

'Ali ibn Abi Talib has much poetry, and much of it is not authentically attributed to him.

Al-Qurtubi has explained in his tafsir, in this surah and in Surat al-Nur, the discussion of distinguishing between the two states of poetry; and likewise Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani at the beginning of his book Dala'il al-I'jaz.

Part 2 of 2 of the commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 26, verses 224–226, is translated below.

It was necessary that the consideration of the meanings of poetry and the condition of the poet be undertaken, and the scholars have always given attention to the poetry of the Arabs and those who came after them. In that poetry there is an encouragement toward the eloquence (fasahah) and rhetorical power (balaghah) of the Arabic language, and this leads to a legitimate purpose, namely the comprehension of the rhetorical excellence of the Qur'an.

The meaning of ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 227] is: after the polytheists had wronged them with insult and lampooning.

[صفحة ٢١٣]

﴿And those who have done wrong will know what [kind of] return they will be returned to.﴾ Mention of wrongdoing has naturally led on from it to the threat against wrongdoers, who are the polytheists who wronged the Muslims through harm and abuse, with their words and their poetry. This verse was placed as a concluding summary (tadhyil), so its wording calls for generality in the meaning of wrongdoing (zulm). It covers disbelief, which is the greatest wronging of one's own soul, and sins that affect only the self, and likewise transgression against people's rights. Abu Bakr recited it in his testament appointing 'Umar as caliph after him. The waw is parenthetical (i'tiraḍiyyah), introducing a new statement (isti'naf).

This verse is a warning against violating rights and an exhortation to exert full effort in advising the community. It speaks with the most awe-inspiring admonition and the most terrifying threat to whoever reflects on it, because of the particle of deferment (harf al-tanfis), which indicates that the punishment is approaching, and because of the relative pronoun, which indicates that the evil outcome awaits the wrongdoers because of their wrongdoing. It is also because of the vagueness in His words: ﴿what [kind of] return they will be returned to﴾, where He left its specification unstated, by a specific punishment, so that the souls of those threatened would be dazed in every possible direction by the terror of the return. In general, it is an evil return.

Al-munqalab (the return) is a noun of place (masdar mimi) from inqilab, which means destination and outcome, because inqilab is returning. The verb of knowledge ('alima) is suspended from operating (mu'allaq) by the presence of the interrogative particle after it. The interrogative noun is in the accusative position, substituting for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) to which it is attached. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: The pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) used to admonish one another with it and warn each other of its severity.

[صفحة ٢١٤]

[صفحة ٢١٥]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat an-Naml (The Ant)

The most famous of its names is Surat an-Naml. It was named thus in Sahih al-Bukhari and Jami' al-Tirmidhi. It is also called Surat Sulayman (The Surah of Solomon). These two names are the ones al-Suyuti restricted himself to in al-Itqan and elsewhere.

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi mentioned in Ahkam al-Qur'an that it is called Surat al-Hud-hud (The Surah of the Hoopoe). The reason for the three names is that the word "an-naml" (the ant) and the word "al-hud-hud" (the hoopoe) are not mentioned in any other surah of the Qur'an. As for naming it Surat Sulayman, it is because the kingdom of Sulayman mentioned in it in detail is not mentioned in the same way anywhere else.

This surah is Meccan by consensus, as Ibn 'Atiyyah, al-Qurtubi, al-Suyuti and others have related. Al-Khafaji mentioned that some scholars held that some of its verses are Meccan (sic; this is probably a slip, and the correct form is "Medinan of some of its verses"). I have not found this statement from anyone other than al-Khafaji.

It is the forty-eighth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after ash-Shu'ara' and before al-Qasas. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Its verses are counted as ninety-five according to the count of the people of Medina and Mecca, and ninety-four according to the people of Syria, Basra and Kufa.

* * *

Among the aims of this surah

The first aim of this surah is that it opens with what points to the inimitability of the Qur'an through the eloquence of its composition and the loftiness of its meanings, as indicated by the two disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at its beginning.

[صفحة ٢١٦]

And the exaltation of the Qur'an's status, and that it is a guidance for whoever Allah makes it easy for him to be guided by it, unlike those who denied that it is from Allah.

And the challenge to know what it contains of the reports of the prophets.

And taking lessons from the greatest kingdom ever given to a prophet, which is the kingdom of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and what knowledge of the affairs of birds he attained, and what greatness of civilization his kingdom reached.

The most famous community among the Arabs that was given strength is the people of Thamud. The reference is to a great Arab kingdom, which is the kingdom of Saba'. In this there is an intimation that the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is a message accompanied by the governance of the community, followed by a kingdom, which is the caliphate of the Prophet ﷺ.

And that the Muhammadan law will be the basis of a kingdom for the community that is yet to come, just as the kingdom of Sulayman was established for the Children of Israel.

And the argumentation against the polytheists regarding the falsehood of their religion, the exposure of their gods, the refutation of the reports of their soothsayers, diviners and the custodians of their idols. And the affirmation of resurrection and what precedes it of the terrors of the Day of Judgment and its signs.

And that the Qur'an is dominant (muhaymin) over the earlier scriptures. Then the peaceful disengagement from the polytheists and informing them that the role of the Messenger is to continue conveying the Qur'an, and warning them that they will witness the signs of truth, while Allah is aware of their deeds.

Ibn al-Faras said: There is no ihkam (establishing of definitive rulings) and no naskh (abrogation) in this surah. His negation that it contains ihkam or naskh means that it does not include a fixed legislation (tashri' qar) nor abrogated legislation. Al-Qurtubi said, in his commentary on the verse ﴿And I have been commanded to be of those who submit [to Allah]﴾ [an-Naml: 91] and ﴿And to recite the Qur'an. So whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself﴾ [an-Naml: 92], that it was abrogated by the verse of fighting, end quote, meaning the verse revealed about fighting in Surat al-Bara'ah. It is called the verse of the sword. Al-Qurtubi was a contemporary of Ibn al-Faras, except that he was in Egypt while Ibn al-Faras was in al-Andalus. His statement ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾ [an-Naml: 21] and two rulings are derived from both of them, as will come.
